YRODSHAM GAS AND WATER (Dissolution of Frodsl-sam Gas Company, Limited; Incorporation of New Company; vesting in them of undertaking of dissolved Company; Re- gulation of capital, Ac., of new company; additional capital; separation of gas and water undertakings; power to supply gas and water; maintenance and extension of gas works; manufacture and storage of gas and residual products; manufacture of meters, dm. ; patent rights; construction of water works; prevention of waste of gas and water, &c. ; acquisition of lands, rates, and charges ; price, Ac., of gas and water; breaking up of streets; agreements with local authorities, bodies, and persons; incorporation and amend.

, meat of Acts, and other purnesesk NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing session for leave to bring in a Bill (hereinafter called the Bill) for all or some of the following, among other purposes, that is to say To dissolve the Frodsham Gas Company, Limited (herein- after called " the Limited Company") and to cancel or annul their memorandum and Articles of Association, and certificate Of ineefporation, and provide for the winding up of the Limited Company, and the discharge of their liabilities. To incorporate into a company (hereinafter called "the Company ") the shareholders of the Limited Company or some of them, with or without other persons, or corporations, under such name as may be prescribed by the Bill. To apply, for the purposes of the Company and of the Bill, the capital and funds of thi. Liailted Company, and to define, declare, and regulate the undertaking capital and borrowing powers of the Company, and the rights and privileges of the shareholders. To make provision for the vesting and apportionment of the shares and capital of the Limited Company, or of any new shares or stock instead thereof, in and among the shereholders of the Company. To authorize the Company to raise further capital; to bor- row on mortgage or otherwise, and to create and issue deben- ture stock. To make provision (if thought fit) for the separation of the Gas and Water Undertakings of the Company, and of the capital employed therein, and the profits and revenue arising therefrom, and for the keeping of separate accounts in relation to such undertakings respectively. To vest in the Company the undertaking , lands, buildings, mains, pipes, plant, moneys, rights, powers, privileges, liabilities, easements, agreements, and licenses of the Limited Company, and to authorise the Company to execute the works and exercise all or any of the powers, and to effect all or any of the objects hereinafter mentioned. To empower the Company to supply with gas and water for domestic trading, public, sanitary, and other purposes, the whole or any part of all °mimeo( thetownships following, that is to say, Frodshara, Frodsham Lordship, Ifelsby, Alvanley, Newton-by-Frodsham, and Kingsley, in the Parish of Prod. sham, and Sutton, in the Parish of Runcorn. all in the County Palatine of Chestier. ' To authorise the Company to purchase, take on lease, or ac- quire by compulsion or agreement, and to hold and use for the purposes of their undertaking, all or some of the following .sids, that is to say—A piece of land in Ithe said township and parish of Frodsham belonging or reputed to belong to John Higson, and adjoining the present site of the Limited Com- pany's gas works in Gas Works-road, and bounded on the south-east by the said present site of the Limited Company's gas works, on the south-west lax land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Ashton; on the north-east by an occupation road running from the Gas Works-road to the field numbered 116 on sheet xxivls of the-4-311,-a Ordnance Survey, 1873, for the Parish of Frodsham; and on the north-west by other lands belonging, or reputed to belong to the said John Higson, and to authorise the Company on those lands, or part or parts thereof, and On the lands hereinafter described as the sites of the Limited Company's existing gas works, to erect, construct, and make, and to maintain, and continue, and from time to time to extend, enlarge, and improve gas works and works for the manufacture, distribution, storage, and supply of gas, and for the manufacture, conversion, utilization, storage, and dis- tribution of materials used in and about the manufacture of gas, and of residual products resulting from such manufacture, and to empower the Company on, and from all such lands, to manufacture, store, and supply gas, and to manufacture, con- vert, ritilise, distribute, and store such materials and residual products as aforesaid. The sites of the Limited Company's existing gas works Consists of the pieces of land hereinafter described, that is to say:— (a) A piece of land belonging, or reputed to belong to the Limited Company, in the said township and parish of Frod- sham, bounded on the north-east by an occupation road running from the Gas Works-road to the field numbered 116 on sheet xxiv 15 of the .„--Arc,-, Ordnance Survey (1873), for the said parish of Frodaham ; on thenorth-westby land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Iligson ; on the south-west partly by land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Ashton, and partly by an occupation road running from the main street of Frodsham to the field numbered 167 on the said Ordnance Sur- vey ; andon the south-east partly by the bowling-green belong- ing to the Bear's Paw Hotel, and partly by garden* belonging, or reputed to belong to Halstead Clough. (b) A piece of land belonging, or reputed to belong to the Limited Company in the said township and parish of Prod- sherry bounded on the north-west by Ship-street; on the south- west by Plumbtort-lane • on the south-east by certain gar- dens belonging, or reputed to belong to Williant Hayes Picker- ing, Mrs Margaret Ashton, and John Robinson respectively ; pus oulthe north-east by land belonging, or reputed to belong to William Hayes. To authorise the Company to manufacture, purchase, sell, let on hire, or otherwise deal in meters, tubes, pipes, lamps, burners, fittings, and other apparatus, articles, and things used in the supply of gas and water, and to have, hold, use, enjoy, and exercise all powers, rights, privileges, and authori- ties necessary, proper, or convenient for the purposes aforesaid, and generally to carry on the business usually carried on by gas and water companies. To empower the Company to manu- facture, purchase, provide, sell, let on hire, and fix stoves, ranges, fittings, engines, machinery, apparatus, and appliances for lighting, for motive power, for heating, cooking, ventilat- ing, manufacturing, or any other purpose whatever, and to Supply or work the same by means of gas. To give powers to the Company to acquire, hold, use, and exercise patent rights and licenses in relation to the manufacture, storage, and dis- tribution, and utilization of gas and residual products, and in relation to the supply of water. To authorise the Company to make and maintain the water- works and other works and conveniences following, or some of them, that is to say :- 1 (1) A Well and bore hole and Pumping Station with pump- ing Engines, Engines and Boiler House, chimney and all 'other necessary Works buildings and conveniences, eaustenear the town of Frodsharn In the township and parish of Faxl- sham, in the County Palatine of Chester, in a field belonghts to Henry Linaker and in the occupation of Mary Forster, and numbered 206 on sheet No. xxiv, 16, of the Ordnance Survey, dated 1873, for the Parish of Frodsham. (2) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 1) to be situate In the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship in the said parish of Frodsham commencing at the said well and borehole and Pumping Station, above described, and terminating in the Intended Low service or Overton Reservoir hereinafter de- scribed at the north east angle thereof. (3) A Low service rectangular Reservoir to be called the Overton Reservoir and to be situated in the said townships of Frodshant and FrodshamLordshipandparish of Frodsham at or near the south east end of the Field belonging to and iu the occupation of Mrs, Martha Aston and numbered on the said ordnance Survey 334 in the township of Frodsham and 218 in the township of Frodsham Lordship. (4) An approach road to be Situate it the said townships of Frocibbam mul ertidshaft T.L`Ttiship and parish of Frodsham Coranasating by a ilitletion with Townfield Lane, ,at a point about 319 yards measured in a stmight line eastwards of the entrance gate to the Vicarage of Frodsham and terminating at the south-west corner of the said Field,number 334, in the Said township of Frodsham and 216 in the said township of Prod- sham Lordship. (5) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 2) to be situate wholly in the said township of Frodsham Lordship and parish of Frodsham commencing by a junction with the said intended aqueduct, or line of pipes (No. 1 at a point about 44 yards eastwards of the north west corner of the said field No. 334 in the township of Frodsham and 216 in the township of Frodsham Lordship and about 124 yards northwards of the south-west corner of that Field and terminating in an intended well or tank to he situate in the south-east corner of the said field. (6) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 3) to be situate in the said townships of FrodshamandFnxisham Lordship andparish of Frodsham commencing at a pond in the north-west corner of a field forming part of the Glebe of the vicarage of Frodsham in the occupation of John Pollard, and numbered 333 on the said ordnance survey and terminating in the said intended Overton Reservoir at the north-west angle thereof. (7) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 4) to be situate in the said townships of Frodsham and , Frodsham Lordship and parish of Frodsharn, commencing by a junction with the aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 5) hereinafter described at a point in the Main-street of the town of Frodsham, at the juno- Hon of Church-street with Main-street, and terminating in the , said intended Overton Reservoir at the South East angle thereof. (8) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 5) to be situate in the townships of Ifelsby, Frodsham Lordship, and Frodsham, in the parish of Frodsham, and in the township of Sutton, in the parish of Runcorn, in the County Palatine of Chester, com- mencing at a point on the highway leading from Chester to Warringtomabout 390 yards south westwards of the south west corner of the station master's house at the Helaby and Alvan- ley Station, on the West Cheshire Railway, and terminating at a point on the same road about 200 yards north eastwards of the centre of the bridge earrying that road over the river Weaver, known as Frodsham Bridge, (9) A high service reservoir, to be called the Beacon Reser- voir, and to be situate wholly in the said township of Frod- sham Lordship, at the southern end of the field or en- closure on Beacon Hill, belonging to Edward Abbott Wright, numbered 8 on sheet xxxii. 1. of the rsltiz,- ordnance survey, dated 1873, for the said parish of Frodeham. (10) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 6) to be situate in the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, or one of them, in the said parish of Frodshani, commencing in the said Intended Beacon Reservoir, on the north east side thereof, and terminating in the said intended Overton Reservoir at the south east angle thereof. (11) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 7) to be situate in the townships of Alvanley, Heisby, and Frodsham Lordship in the said parish of Frodsham commencing at is point in the highway at or near the junction of the roads in the village of Alvanley opposite Green Rank Farm House, and about 83 yards westwards of the north-west angle of the Church of St. John the Baptist in Alvariley, and terminating In the said intended Beacon Reservoir on the south-west side thereof. (13) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 9) to be situate in the townships of Frodsham Lordship; Newton-by-Frodsham, and Kingsley, and the said parish of Frodsham, commencing by a junction with the said intended aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 7) at a point in the highway in the village of Overton about 9 yards eastwards of the north-east angle of the Ring-o- Bells publichouse, and terminatingat a point in the highway at or near the junction of the roads in the village of Kingsley opposite the farm buildings of Kingsley Hall, and about 23 yards eastwards of the north-east angle of the Post Office. (14) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 10) to be situate in the said townships of Newton-by Frodsham and Kingsley and parish of Frodsham, commencing at a point In the highway in the village of Newton about 113 yards eastwards of the south- east angle of the old Manor House, and terminating by a junction with the said intended aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 9) at a point about 190 yards south-eastwards of the south- eastern angle of the Lowerhouse Farm House. To&ther with all necessary and proper embankments, walls, fences, tanks, wells, dams, drains, sluices, cloughs, valves, hydrants, air-valves, cleansing pipes. culverts. engines, pipes, buildings, machinery, roads, and Other works and conveni- ences for the collecting, storing, and distributing of water. To enable the Company to divert into the said intended waterworks, and to collect, take, use, and approPriate for the purpose of their undertaking all such underground streams, springs, and waters-as can be collected or obtained by the pro- posed works, or any of them, or as may be found in or under any of the lands belonging to, or to be acquired by, or vested in the Company under the powers of the Bill. To enable the Company to make effectual provisions and regulations for the protection of the waterworks, and other works and property of the Company, and for preventing the waste, fouling, and misuse of gas and water, and for defining and regulating the supply of gas and water by them. whether by meter or otherwise, and the terms and conditions of such supply. To authorise the Company to deviate laterally from the lines of the intended waterworks within the limits shown upon the plans hereinafter mentioned, or as may beproviclerthy the Bill, and whettrx within or beyond the limits of deviation allowed by the Waterworks Clauses Act, 1847, and to deviate vertically to any extent from the levels of those waterworks as shown upon the sections hereinafter mentioned. To empower the Company by compulsion .or agreement to purchase, acquire, and to take on lease, lands, houses, springs, streams, wells, waters, waterworks, and other hereditaments within the parishes, townships, and places mentioned in this notice, or some of them which maybe requiredfor the purposes of the intended gasworks and waterworks, or otherwise requisite or desirable for the purposes of the Bill, and to take compul- sorily or by agreement easements in or over any such lands, houses, or other property and hereditaments, and to vary and ex- tinguish all rights of way and other rights and privileges con- nected with any such lands, property, and berediMments, To exempt the Company from the operation of section 92 of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, so as to enable them to purchase compulsorily parts only el certain properties. To empower the Company to levy and recover rents, rates, and charges, differential and otherwise, for, or in respect of the supply of gas and water, and for the sale or hire of meters, fittings, stoves, ranges, engines, machinery, apparatus, and ap- pliances—to alter eidsting rates, rents, duties, and charges, , and to confer, vary, and extinguish exemptions from the pay- ment of rates, rents, duties, and charges. To make provision with respect to, and to regulate the price of water and gas to be charged by the CoMpany, and the quality and pressure of gas to be supplied by them, and the amount of profit which may be divided among the Shareholders of the Company in respect of their gas and water under- takings or either of them. To authorise the Company to lay down, maintain, take up, alter, and repair mains, pipes, culverts, conduits, sluices, drains, and other works in, through, under, over, across, and along, and to cross, break up, open, alter, divert, stop up, or otherwise interfere with, either temporarily or permanently, any roads, highways, occupation roads, footpaths, public places, bridges, canal's. navigations, towing' paths, railways tramways, works, pipes, sewers, drains, rivers, streams, brooks, and watercourses in any of the parishes, townships, and places before mentioned, so far as may be necessary or con- venient for the supply of gas and water, or for all or any of the purposes of the bill. To empower the Company from dine to time, to sell, ex- change, let on lease, or otherwise to dispose of any lands or property at the Hine belonging to them, which they may not require for the purposes of their undertaking. To enable the Comparry on the one hand, and any Sanitary Authority, Local Board, Public Body, Compaq, or persons on the other hand, to enter into, and carry into effect, contracts, agreements, and arrangements for, or with respect to, the sup- ply by the Company to any Sanitary Authority, Local Board. Public Body, Company, or person, of gaaand water, in bulk or otherwise, within and beyond the limits of supply of the Company for any public, sanitary, trading, or other purpose, or for, or with respect to, the transfer to and vesting in any such Publie Body of any part of the Company's undertakings ; and to authorise any such Sanitary Authority, Local Board, Public Body, Company, or persons respectively, to apply their funds, and to raise further moneys for the purpose of any suoh Contract, agreement, or arrangement, and to sanction and confirm any such Contract, agreement, or arrangement already made, or which, prior to the passing of the Bill, may be made with respect to he matters aforesaid, or to make other pro- visions in relation to any such matters. To confer upon the Company all powers, rights, and authori- ties which are or may become necessary for carrying into effect the powers and objects of the Bill, or are usually conferred on , Gas and Water Companies. • • ' ' '

To vary or extinguish all rights and privileges which would laana'..nUulner.impeda.,or interfere with the: ~kjects and pur- poses of the Bill, and to confer other rights and privileges. To incorporate with the Bill, with or without such variations and modifications as may be deemed expedient, all or some of the provisions of." To alter, amend, extend, enlarge, or repeal, so far as may be necessary for the purposes of the Bill, all or some of the provi- sions of any Act which may relate to or be affected by the Bill.

Here's good luck trThonest Roger, /Find his match 'at con ; He's a blunt an' true owd codger— _ Every inch a mon! 0 the cfaicent chaps 'at know him Like his witty tongue; Nowt but two-faced rascals co him, When they'n getten stung! Roger's varra good at speawtin' ; Rich i' common sense, " Though th'owd cOoat he knocks abcawt in Rod cost eighteenpence. He believes id little matters
Wod yo'n getten on, iv yer bits o' rags an' tatters Clooathes an honest mon.

Wed he says is reet, depend on't,— "Search this waurld o through. Truth'll live to win at th' end ma. Lies'll never do; Iv a chap's a deawnreet streight un, Panty though he be"— Says owd Roger—" he's a reight un, Just the mon for me." Roger likes, just after dinner, Chattin' wi' his mates— • Tonathri weyvers an' a spinner— Deawn hi t' factory gates. a bit o' good debatin', Mixed wi gradely fun, 1 Passes while they're starinin' waitin' • Till their "bell heawr's" done. Many a dispute he's decided, Mony a foight he's stopped,: ;111" He's their Judge, an' when he's tried id, Oft the case is dropped. 1 t Many a face hes he med sunny, ' Dried up many a tear, Sin' he geet thad bit a' money Left to him last year. • That's the only thing he's sly in— Dooin' good to th' poor; - Lots 'at hes no bed to lie in - Knows his friendly dooar. f Bless thi heart! owd Honest Roger, Heaven wodnd be Quite as far off earth, owd codger, Iv we'd moor like thee:! "Doctor, when do you think a man weighs most ?" asked a patient who was undergoing a course of dietary ' treatment. "When he steps on my corns," answered the doctor. Guest (rising excitedly from the table after tasting an olive for the first time) : "It's sorry I'd be to disturb the hilarity of the matin ; but I belave some joker has been salting the zuseberries." The jury brought in a verdict of "Not guilty." Hisi Honour said admonishingly to the prisoner, "After this you ought to keep away from bad company." "Yes, your Honour. You will not see me here again in a burry." Heir Hutchinson was of such a solioitine disposition that the Marquis of Townshend, when Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, said of him, "If Eneland and Ireland were given to him, he would solicit the Isle of Man for a potato garden." A domineering man said to his wife, "Remember, my dear, that you are the weaker vessel." "That may be so," she retorted; "but I'll take good care that you shan't forget that the weaker vessel may have the stronger spirit in it !" A curate and his wife had heard that the moon was inhabited; they procured a telescope to ascertain the • fact. The lady had the first peep. "I see." said she, "I gee two shades, inclining towards each other; they are undoubtedly two happy lovers." "Pooh r said the curate, looking in his turn: "these two shades are the we steeples of a cathedral." RE REACHED His DESTINATION.—A sporting-looking, chap, leading a fine Irish setter, boarded an up-car on Ridge-avenue, near Oxford-street, a few days ago, and pushed his way to the front. Presently the conductor banged the door open, and, addressing the man with the ,eetter, said: "You'll have to take that 'ere dog off this cite" "Why ?" inquired the other, in apparent surprise. "Its Wrist the rules." tersely rejoined the car man. "Is , that so?" retorted the sporting-looking chap. "I never knew that before. Funny, now. isn't it, that the com- pany won't let a nice, clean, good dog like that ride, when it makes no objection to drunken men?" "Well, I've nothing to do with that," responded the conductor, who was beginning to show signs of impatience; "rules are rules, and we have to obey them.' "You don't really mean that I've got to get off ?" exclaimed the pas- senger, appealingly. "You can't keep that dog on the ear," returned the conductor. "Oh, well, it's all right," was the reply. " Here's Twenty-fourth-street--the very place I want to get out at. Pm much obliged for carry- ing me this far. I was afraid I'd have to take another ear. Would you believe it, I was put off six cars 'tween here'n Ninth-street, but I got here just the same. Not one cent of fare, either. Fact." To his hospital patients Abernethy was uniformly kind and gentle. In illustration of this a story is told by Mrs. Stowe, who accompanied him one day through the • "wards, where a poor Irishman jumped out of bed, and threw himself at Abernethy's feet. Then he jumped up and flourished a limb, crying, " nate the leg, yer bonnet-! Glory be to God! Yer honnoes the boy for doing it! May the heavens be your bed! Long life to yer honour rec. This was a man whe had been brought in with a diseased ankle, for which amputation had been ordered. But Abernethy thought he could cure it, stopped the, amputation, and put the man under consti- tutional treatment. The result was a perfect cure, and an ecstasy of thankfulness on the part of poor Pat. The , opportunity was seized by Abernethy for giving a clinical lecture, every point of which was illustrated by • Pat's emphatic, "Thrue, yer honnor ; divvel a lie in it:" Every reference to the leg brought out the member with a flourish from under the bedclothes; and the whole affair was most, comical. But while everybody was laughing at the Irishman on his knees before the great surgeon, Abernethy was composed. Bending down over the man, he said with much earnestness, "1 RIR glad your leg is doing well, but ueyer kneel, except to your Maker." LORD MEATH ON SOCIRTHP3 FOR YOUNG PEOPLE-- Societies and organisations are lifeless abstractions unless animated by a living spirit. If that spirit be not evoked, the best societies are but an empty name. Work must be ac.comnlished by the agency of human hands, hearts, and intellects. Let our imaginary clergyman ask himself whether he instilled this life into the dry bones of the organisation; and, if he did not, let him not then be astonished if the bones are atill dry, and likely. to re- main so to the end of the chapter. 'Deb° of use, the Girls' _ Friendly Society or the Young Men's Friendly Society, or, indeed, any society for the benefit of men arid women, must thoroughly saturate the minds of its members with the spirit of brotherly love and of prac- tical Christian kindness one towards another and towards all mankind. It must give them work to do. It must prove to them that the happiest man even on this earth is he who renounces for the sake of another, and not he who passes his life in the endeavour to get the better of his neighbours. It must show them that work for others is the most ennobling of all pursuits, and that it is pos- sible for the very poorest and the very busiest to do Some little act of kindness to his fellow-man. It must furnish them with opportunities of being useful to others, and show them that their organisation is a means of accomplishing this, and is a blessing to them- selves and to others. Each member should be made to feet that it is a privilege to belong to the society, and that dismissal from its ranks would be a disgrace.' To establish such an esprit de rorps, the society should have some local habitation, where meetings may periodically take place, and where associates. and members may feel themselves to be really at home. However small may be the house or room, it should be the exclusive property of the society, and should be used for no other purpose.— The Qttiver for November. THE QUEEN AND THE GREAT AIONTROSE.—Her Majesty the Queen, on the occasion of a recent visit to the ancient church of St. Giles in Edinburgh, was graciously pleased to express surprise that it contained no memorial of the gent Montrose. The reproach implied is happily in course of being removed, and ere long the name and fame of Montrose will be adequately commemorated in the place where he is buried. The fact, how- ever, is very remarkable, that from the 11th May' 1661, when his mutilated and scattered remains having been diligently collected were with great pomp and ceremony interred, down to the present time—a period of more than two centuries—no stone or inscription of any kind has been placed to mark the spot. Surely this singular omission requires and admits of some explana- tion. The explanation is to be found in the entire failure of the great majority of his countrymen to firm an accurate conception of the career and char- acter of Montrose. By some he has been worshipped as the champion of unlimited monarchy—of the royal prerogative absolute both in Church and State. By others he has been denounced as a traitor to the Cove- *ant and the Church of which he had professed himself •a devoted adherent He has been represented as bloody, aruel, and vindictive—an intriguing courtier, fired bv an unholy ambition and by jealousy of all who did or niight stand in his way. These irrational notions and prejudices ought to have been dispelled ere now by such painstaking and impartial historians as Bur- ton and Gardiner; but much of the old misconception -still prevails, and justifies such an examination of the oonnection of Montrose with the National Church 'of Scotland on the one hand and with King Charles I. on the other, as may define to unprejudiced minds the true place which he is entitled to hold as a historical person- age in the troublous years of the seventeenth centurv.— rom Montrose and the Covenant of 1638, in Blackwitod's Magazine for Sovember,lBB7. fiAmeisTwas—whose professional labours necessitate long in- errata between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating. earaftwiling, and capable of sustaining exhausted nature as o,,Abnry's Oocoa, gam:lndeed absolutely *we. THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT CHURCH. t jn accordance with a time-honoured custom, tht Mayor and Corporation of Warrington on Sunday morning attended divine service at the Parish Church, where a bermon was preached by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's Church, Bewsey- road, who was on the previous Wednesday ap- pointed by the newly-elected Mayor, Alderman T. H. Sutton, as his chaplain for the ensuing muni- cipal year. At the close of the annual meeting, at which Alderman Sutton was chosen the Mayor, he. as is usual, invited the members of the Corporation to meet him at the Town Hall on Sunday morning for th,3 purpose of attending church, and at about ten o'clock the following members assembled at'the appointed place, where they were met by His Wor- ship :—Aldermen Pickmere (ex-Mayor), Davies, ; Webster, and Chandley; and Councillors Marsh, Ashton, Greenall, Joseph Taylor, J. Shaw Green, Heaton, Jolley, J. Pierpoint, Dakin, Blackhurst, Percival, F. A. Roberts, Wright, W. Pierpoint, Fran- comb, and Hutchinson. A procession was formed in front of the Town Hall steps. Chief Constable Hunt, and as many members of the Borough Police Force as could be spared from duty, headed it, and immediately following came the Borough Fire Bri- gade, under the direction of Fire Brigade Superin- tendent Turner. Then there walked the Mayor, with the chaplain on his right and the Deputy- Mayor on his left, the afore-mentioned members of the Corporation, the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. J. L. Whittle), the Borough Surveyor (Mr. Longdin), the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Gornall), a number of representatives of the Ratepayers' Association, and various members of the general public, amongst whom were Messrs. T. Morris, D. Jones, D. W. Finney, Noah Legge, T. Birchall, W. W. Westwell, J. Smethurst, T. Paterson, T. Reid, J. Fair- hurst, jun., J. Hesketh, T. Jones, T. 0. Speakman, and others. Alderman Harrison drove to church. In the course of his sermon, which was preached to a large congregation, the Mayor's Chaplain said that on that day, throughout the length and breadth of the land, mayors and members of corporations were attending their parish churches. Surely it was a good thing that the rulers of the town should as their first public act meet together to worship God in the house of prayer. The office of mayor was of ancient date, and they would learn from the history of their country that on many °e- vasions mayors and corporations had lent important ser- vice to the State. The mayoral office was one of dignity and responsibility; and to be elected mayor was the' greatest honour that could be bestowed on any inhabi- tant of the borough, because it showed that not only the Council, but the inhabitants also, respected and honoured him. As well as being an office of such dignity, it was one also of responsibility, because not only had the mayor to mete out justice, but he had also to preside over the meetings of the Town Council, and did not they find that the conduct of anybody was regulated by the man at the head. But these duties were not the only ones that were in the present day expected of a Mayor. They looked to the Mayor to take a leading part in mat. tees of philanthropy, and all matters which were intended to benefit the sick and the poor. Dangers surrounded us on every hand; and one of the greatest of these dangers was that of lawlessness. He was not going to preach a political sermon, nor to give instances of lawlessness. Rather would he speak of the spirit of lawlessness which on every hand they saw manifested. Were the children of the present day as obedient to their parents as they ought to be ? Did young men and young women always show the same respect to their elders? He was afraid not. These were serious failings, and he was afraid they were faults which would increase unless they were nipped in the bud. Could their mayors help them? They could do something to teach the people their duty. They could help them by having the same law for the rich as for the poor, and by showing fair play all round. There was also a danger of having only a superficial knowledge of things. Everyone in these days wanted to learn, and there was a danger of trying to obtain a smattering of everything, and knowing nothing well. They must encourage schools of science, and other means of acquiring knowledge, and thus the generation would be made wiser, better, and holier. The great tendency to divide mankind into different classes was another clan-

....... ger. Those classes were supposed to fancy that their in- terests were opposed the one to the other, but that wasa mistake. Here again, the chief magistrate could en- courage them by endeavouring te bring class and class together, byihemselves associating more with them; and trying to teach men and women that they were brothers and sisters in Christ Jesus. He had, he thought, said enough to show that the duties of a Mayor were difficult and onerous. How was a Mayor to accomplish this work? He could only do it in one way, and that was by Divine help. The Mayor and Corporation had that day acknowledged that, and their dependence upon Ai- mighty God, by coming there that day as their first pub- lic act. It was an especial pleasure to him to address the Mayor and Corporation for the first time that day, , because their present Mayor was not only his own , churchwarden, but also his own personal friend. It was, indeed, a glad thing for them all to meet together that morning, to ask God to pour his blessing upon the Mayor and Corporation, so that they might be able to do their duty as Christian men and good citizens. Might God go with them during the year, and they might then de- pend that it would be a successful one. •

45.1 WARRINGTON LEAGUE OF THE CROSS. The hall of the Warrington League of the Cross, Bewsey-street, having recently been closed for the purpose of cleaning and decorating, the re-opening was celebrated on Sunday evening by a public meeting. There was a large tittendance. The chair was taken by Father Flanagan, chaplain of the League, and he was supported on the platform by Fathers Sumner and Brown, Councillors Dixon and Fleming, Messrs. J. F. Quinn (of Manchester), Miller, Cavanagh, Drury, D. Houghton (president of the League), T. Kilgallon (vice-president), J. Mul- lins (secretary), I'. Lane, J. Kilduff, T. Houghton, 3. Richardson, M. Burke, T. O'Brien, T. Griffin, Keating, Seahill, and Flanery. Mr. D. HououTorr, who WSW received with ap- plause, said he had received a number of letters of apology for non-attendance, but he thought they might take them as read with the exception of one from Father Thompson. The latter gentleman regretted that he could not well be present at the meeting, but he sent his best Wishes for a successful gathering, and enclosed a donation towards meeting the expenses of painting and decorating. (Ap- plause.) The other letters, Mr. Houghton added, were from gentlemen whose entire sympathey they had, and who wished for the success of the League. (Applause.) The CrrAruarArsr, who was cordially received, said he was proud in looking round from that platform to see to many before him. He was proud of .their good, self-sacrificing president. and of their hard- working committee; he was proud of those who, after a day's hard work, came there and laboured to make that hall beautiful, and be was proud to be able to declare that hall of the 'League of the Cross to be re-opened on that night. (Applause.) Mr. J. F. QUINN next gave an earnest and effective address on temperance. Commenting.on the improved condition of the hall, he said it looked that night the home of a newly-married couple, so clean and beautiful was it. (Applause.) He was sure that if they would only encourage their worthy president and the council they would go on making that a home wherein they might assemble and enjoy themselves in a manner that would bear the morrow's reflection. All credit was due to the council of the League, and he hoped they would rally round them and encourage them by doing their share in the work of removing from Warrington that terrible block on their progress—intoxicat- ing drink. (Applause.) He wanted to draw their attention to the enormous waste of money upon intoxicating drink. At the present the

country was undergoing a terrible depression in trade; hundreds of men were standing idle at the street corners, and looms and foundries were in many towns silent. And why? Some of them said because the labour mar- ket was overstocked, others said it was due to foreign competition, but the late Mr. Wm. Hoyle stated—and he thought they would admit he was somewhere near the truth—that one of the reasons of the depression of trade' came from the fact that such a terrible amount of money was taken from the channels of commerce and spent in intoxicating drink. Last year £120,000,000 was spent in intoxicating drink, and that meant that £120,000,000 'were taken directly from the channels of commerce. A calculation had been made that if the married women of 'Manchester alone were to expend BS each on a given Saturday night in purchasing twelve yards of calico it would so reduce the stocks in the warehouses in Man- chester as to give such an impetus to the cotton trade of Lancashire that the looms that are now idle would be fully employed, and the men who wish to work could find 'employment. (Applause.) That money' spent on drink was drawn from the channels of commerce was proved in this way. If they spent £1 on cotton goods, from 14s to 15s went back to the labour market, on fur- niture 14s, on men's clothing 16s, and on ladies' apparel 15s; but if they spent £1 on drink only4d went back into the labour market to find employment for workmen. (Hear, hear.) No wonder trade was bad and looms standing idle, and no wonder their streets were filled , with men looking in vain for employment. Having quoted medical opinion to refute the arguments that drink was good for health, and that it helped to keep up the heat of the body, he asked them not to be deluded by a fallacy ottlmt kind. If they wanted good health they should keep from intoxicating drink. (Hear, hear.) Speaking to those who came from Ireland, he asked them not to forget the teaching of their native land, and not to fall away from the love of home and love of re- ligion through intoxicating drink. Let them give up the drink and give not a chance to those who were only too ready to add insult to their creed and reproach to their country. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Their duty was not only to give up the drink themselves, but to in- duce others to follow their example. They need not wait for Acts of Parliament, for Sunday Closing Bills, or Permissive or Local Option Bills. Let each man act for himself, and let each man pass his own Sunday Closing till and his Permissive and Local Option Bills. (Loud applause.) • Father SUMNER moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Quinn for his address. In the name of their homes, their health, their wealth, their happiness, and their religion he advised all present to give up the use of intoxicating drinks. (Applause.) Mr. MILLER seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried by acclamation, and Mr. Quilne briefly responded. A similar compliment was paid the chairman, OR the motion of Councillor DIXON, seconded by Father BROWN, and the proceedings closed.

This is a pitiful satire on royalty, but on the whole is more harmless to the people than the extrargiffices and high-handed selfishness of Otto's predecessor, King Ludwig. The new Lord Mayor of London is; in accordance with custom, eaten up by a desire to do something that shall outvie the glories of his predecessor's reign. Mr. de Keyser has a difficult task in com- peting with Sir Reginald Hanson, who, in addition to many personal advantages, had the great oppor- tunity of the Jubilee Year. The new Lord Mayor is not well advised in the course he is understood to have laid out for himself. The coming year, it ap- pears. will be distinguished by two events, one the jubilee of the Queens Coronation, the other the silver wedding of the Princeof Wales. Lord Mayor de Keyser, faute de mieux opportunity, is,tit is understood, going to 'pan out" upon these occa- sions, which it is thought may contain within themselves the possibility of a baronetcy. It is, however, safe to predict that he will lack that popu- lar support and approval which is essential to suc- cess in these enterprises. One jubilee in a lifetime Is enough for ordinary people. The nauseous taste of the surfeit of Jubilee in 1887 Will not have left the public mouth by next year. If the Lord Mayor is well advised, he will enter into honourable com- petition with his predecessor in other and newer helds. No one will grudge Mr. Henry Northcote the new honour bestowed upon him by his late father's col- leagues in the Government. It will take much more than the bestowal of a baronetcy upon one of his Sons to wipe out the debt of indignity and ingra- titude which Lord Salisbury's present Government

incurred to Lord Iddesleigli. But there seems something undesirable, if not indelicate, certainly ill-advised, in Mr. Henry Northcote's going out of his way to take upon himself the more illustrious name of his father. Sir Stafford Northcote had a reputation almost unique in Eng- lish politics. A man of ability which was never fairly recognised. he preserved amid singular temptation and influences the character of an Eng- lish gentleman. For the House of Commons there is, and ever can be, but one Sir Stafford North- cote, and it will not like to find, masquerading under that name the amiable but not con- spicuously able young gentleman who has now ap- propriated the title. It may be all very well for the next generation. We to-day do not feel the sacri- lege of the gentleman who lately represented Tam- worth going about under the name Of Sir Robert Peel. But the 'present House of Commons would certainly have liked fiirStafford's name preserved for the identity of its old,triend and companion. ' There is always a certain amount of mystery as to what Mr. Irving a next production is likely to be. He is one of the few managers who can keep a secret. Of course *4 Faust," now running so trium- phantly in New York, will be put on on his return, till its popularity is exhausted. But a great run, once broken, rarely Starts with much vigour, and the management will have to be ready. I know I I am not revealing any secret when I say that Just before leaving Liverpool Mr. Irving commis- I sioned Mr. Willis to dramatise Don Quixote as quickly as it could be done. Mr. Willis has long east hungry eyes at this subject. and, lam told, has repeatedly suggested it to Mr. Beerbohm Tree who has thought of employing Mr. Grundy on the same theme. As every reader of Don Quixote will know the difficulty about the adaptation for the Lyceum stage of the immortal work 18 to find a fitting part for bliss Ellen Terry. Mr. Willis's ingenuity will. I believe, have been found equal to this.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT.

The decision arrived at last night ,by the Metro- politan Radical Federation lifts a cloud from the public mind. Up to the date of this meeting there seemed a certainty of the conflict of last Sunday be- ing repeated on Sunday next, with greater delibera- tion and increased force. Those struggling for vin- dication of the right of public meeting were, naturally enough,. aggravated by the action of .he authorities and the condnct of the police. The events ot last Sunday already belong to ancient history, but those in the neighbourhood of Trafal- gar-square, on Sunday afternoon, are not likely ever to forget it. One of the most animated narrations I have heard is from the lips of a French visitor. This is M. Andrieux, a gentleman who has taken an active part in French polities. He remembered the streets of Paris at the time of the coup detat, and was an eye-witness of many of the scenes that marked the epoch of the commune. Happening to be in London, and his hotel being in the neighbour- hood of Trafalgar-square, it occurred to M. Andrieux that it would be interesting:to see the very rare spectacle of a London crowd in open and organised revolt against the police. His oPportunities for ob- servation were limited by an important circum- stance. He had scarcely taken up his position at the northern corner of Northumberland Avenue, when the police, horse, and foot, bpre down upon the crowd amid which be serenely stood. The intel-
ligent foreigner was one of the jarliest victims of order, being beaten about the head and shoulders by two infuriate policemen. _ _._. . . .

M. Andrieuks cue is doubtless that of hundreds of other equally inoffensive, but injudiciously curi- ous persons. In justice to the police, it must be admitted that nothing else could be expected. Their orders were t•-i clear the Square, and among fifty or sixty thousand persons it is impossible for a police- man to distinguish between professional agitators and innocent onlookers. The simplest way out of the difficulty was to use their batons right and left, and this they certainly did. The case is quite differ- ent with those responsible for the instructions given and the general line of policy taken in this matter. That it has been fussy, tyrannical, and dis- astrous is written in every record of the proceed- ings. There wail a very proper outcry against the interference with business by the blocking up of Trafalgar-square and the approaches on week days. Then it was proposed to hold the meeting on a Sunday, If the Home Secretary and the Chief Com- missioner of Police had only refrained from inter- ference, the Sunday meeting, if it had done no one any perceptible good, would not have effected any particular harm. But the instincts of a Tory Gov- ernment prevailed. If the people in any large num- bers want to do a particular thing, the people are wrong, and must be " put down." Thus came about the fight of last Sunday, with promise of renewed battle seven days' later, a propect averted only by the attitude assumed by Mr. Gladstone and other Liberal leaders, and the prevalent good sense of the mob.

_ There now remains no shred of hope for the Crown Prince. The only question is whether he shall undergo an operation almost certain to prove fatal. or whether he shall linger on to the inevit- able end. .The utmost expected is that his life may be extended over a period of two years. That is the most sanguine expectation, and beyond it there is no hope. This is a fearful position 'for a man to stand in. Beside it the sudden death of Lord Wol- verton, and, yesterday, of Sir William McArthur, is a happy consummation. The nearest approach to the present position of the heir of one of the greatest thrones in Europe is the case of a man con- demned to death under the law of the United States. What with appeals and postponements of trial, a man irrevocably condemned to death may, in that favoured country, exist for at least two years in the condemned cell. For all practical purposes such is the tate of the German Crown Prince. To those who saw him riding in the procession through the streets of London on the Jubilee Day, there is some- thing peculiarly pathetic in the reflection of the secret he concealed under his gallant bearing. He must have been ill then, with sure forebodings of the worst; and perhaps not more than one of the myriad pair of eyes that looked on admiringly knew that be was a doomed man. The German Royal Family, with its many ramifi- cations, is not the only one in deep distress just I now. The state of mind of the Queen of Sweden, aunt of Prince Leopold's widow, which has excited much pained attention of late, has reached a crisis 1 in which it is impossible to deny insanity, and her Majesty is at the present moment in strict confine- ment. ling Otto of Bavaria, the mad successor of a maniac king, grows worse and worse. In his best moments he occupies his time by turning over pic- ture books, peeling potatoes, and making cigarettes. In his worst moods; he wants to kill somebody. A man a day is his minimum desire, and his mood is cunningly gratified without anyone being a penny the worse. Every day his Majesty calls for his rifle. A gun containing blank cartridge is placed in his hand, and he strides forth into the grounds sur- rounding Nymphenburg Palace, which is his prison house. div.head: SUSPECTED MURDER OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: SUSPECTED MURDER OF A WARRINGTON
GIRL.

The police are engaged in an investigation of the circumstances under which a young servant woman. formerly of Warrington, met her death in the neighbourhood of Old Trafford a week ago. On the evening of Wednesday, the 9th inst., Elizabeth Ellison, who for the past six years has been in the employ of Mrs. Colton, hairdresser, Chapel-street. Salford, received the permission of her mistress to visit the Boyll Jubilee Exhibition. She had pre- viously informed Mrs. Colton that a young man named Samuel Evans, calico printer, living in lodgings at Pendleton, with whom she was on friendly terms, would accompany. her. It was about six o'clock when the woman left, and as she did not return within a reasonable period after the closing of the Exhibition. Mrs. Colton became slanted. About one o'clock in the morn- ing the young man _Evans came, saying he had missed the girl, and despairing of finding her had come away without her. In answer to Mrs. Colton's inquiries, he stated that they went to the Exhibition together, that they there had some refreshment, and that on coming away they called at the Dog and Partridge Hotel, situated near the principal entrance to the Exhibition, in Chester-road. As they were leaving the hotel, about a quarter to eleven. Ellison, he said, mysteriously disappeared. He spent a considerable time in try- ing to find her, ancl then made the best of his way home. Evans remained at Mrs. Colton's home until between three and four o'clock, to see if Ellison would come. Inquiries were set on foot the next day to discover' what had become of the young woman, but no tidings of her movements after leav- ing the hotel could be met with until Tuesday, when her dead body, shockingly mutilated and stripped of all clothing except the stockings and boots, was found in the Bridgewater Canal, Throstle Nest, Old Trafford. The right arm is off and the left arm is broken. There are also large cuts across the breast and forehead, and injuries ,in other parts of the body. Of course, all these injuries may have been caused by boats after the immersion of the body in the watkr. The question now engaging the atten- tion of Mr. Supenntendent Bent and the detectives is—How came the young woman into the canal? Pending the result of their investigation p the police have deemed it right to place Evans under arrest. He was apprehended on Wednesday evening at Mrs. Colton's shop, where he had gone presumably to learn if any further light had been thrown on the mysterious occurrence. Mrs. Colton states that the' deceased girl, who was in her 23rd year, left her home on the evening in question in the best of spirits, and that there was nothing in her conduct at any time that would point to the idea of suicide. She was expecting in the course of a few weeks to be married to a young man in Warrington, where her mother and other relatives reside. THE INQUEST. _

On Wednesday evening Sir. F. Price. district cor- oner, opened an inquest touching the circumstances 0 the young woman's death. Mrs,Colton said that Evans went to her house the worse for drink about one o'clock last Thursday morning, and asked if " Lizzie" had come home, meaning the deceased. She told‘ him she had not, and asked where he had left her. He said that after coming out of the exhibition they went to the Dog and Partridge Hotel, at Old Traffordt Thti de- ceased left the hotel about a quarter to eleven, and he stayed a short time longer, expecting that she would be waiting for him outside. When he came out, however, he found that she had gone, but where he did not know. Ile searched about the neigh- bourhood for an hour and a half, and not being able to find her, he went to Mrs Colton's shop. Mrs Col- ton added that Evans sat up until three o'clock on Thursday morning waiting for the deceased, aid then went to bed. Deceased was to have left her place on Saturday next to be married. Bridget Ellison, of 36, Dial-street, Warrington, sister of the deceased, said that Evans went over to Warrington last Friday night and told her parents that the deceased was missing and must be dead. The deceased was about to be married to a jroung man at Warrington named John Welsh.—Questioned by the Coroner, witness said she knew the deceased had been keeping company with the " printer " (meaning Evans) about two years, but she did not think Welsh knew it. The inquiry was adjourned until Wednesday next, and the Coroner ordered a post-mortem examination to be made.

CHAPTER X. . THE INQUEST. The inquest was being held in the farmhouse parlour. The room was crowded with people and every chair in the house was brought into requisi- tion. At the head of the table, placed at one end of the room, sat the Coroner; ranged beside him were the jurors in their rough tweedbsuits or black Sunday coats, farmers of the neighbourhood and small trades- . _ .

men Irv' Tavistock. At the opposite end of the room sat Anne and Martin side by side, dressed in as much mourning as was possible to them at such short notice—Martin with a band of crape round his left arrn, Anne in a plain black' silk gown which had seen some service. Behind them were the old labourer, Richards, his wife, and their darughter Eliza. The latter looked very pale, and seemed in a state of terra that was quite uncalled for. Several farmers of the place arid their wives were present, and at the door of 'the .room stood Watkins, the policeman, in all the solemnity of his official helmet and uniform. Just as the proceedings were about to begin, Captain Stambrxlge walked into the parlour. Iris shoulders were bowed, his face was white and haggard, he looked like a man stricken down by grief. Many were the pitying glances directed towards the .bereaved bridegroom elect. Ho bowed gravely to Anne as he entered, but he did not speak, or hold out his hand to her, and she observed that he did not even ,look at Martin, but appeared to keep his eyes carefully turned away from the farmer, to whom, at any rate, thought his sister, was due some small civility, as he was the master of the house where they were all assembled. After the jury had viewed the body, and Mr. Prior had stated the exact cause of Susan's death, Anne Derrick was the first witness called upon. The questions put to her she answered with the supreme calmness of one who had her nerves strung up to their highest tension. Perhaps her self-possession was almost teo perfect to be natural; at all events, it gave the coroner the idea that there was some hidden danger against which she was guarding herself. The fact that a man was actually concealed in the house when she entered it haiurally caused ,a great slasation in tho room. Every eye was fixed upon her as she answered the Minute inquiries of the Coroner. "Could you discern any person as you entered the house?" he asked.
"No, it was too dark," replied Anne. • "Don't you keep a light of any sort burning in Pip entrance hall ?"

"Yes, always." "How did it come not to be lighted last Friday evening then?" "I can't tell. I had been out all day, perhaps it had been forgotten." Here a sobbing and gasping was heard from the servant Eliza, in the background. "It warn't ni fault. I lighted it all right enough— " Then fo- lowed a warning " Sh, sh !" from her mother. "You say, Miss Derrick, you had your hand on this person's arm. Could you tell, from the sense of touch, how he was dressed ?" "I felt a man's cloth coat," replied Anne, speaking rather slowly, and knitting her •brows 'a little, as if she were taxing her monitory to the ut- most extent, to recall every circumstance of that dreadful night, " a thick cloth, so far as I can tell from just that one moment." "The sort of coat that a man in well-to-do circum- stances would wear ?"

".1 should say so." "Was there anything in that momentary touch that reminded you of any person you knew?' Anne became conscious at that momeat that Stambridge's eyes were fixed upon her with a sort of stealthy suspicion. A sudden thought made her thrill, and he could hardly refrain from saying, "It will just such a coat as Captain Stambridge is wear- ing.. But she quickly recovered her presence of mind, though her momentary change of colour and hesita- tion in replying did not escape notice. "There must be hundreds of coats made of the same sort of cloth," so she answered the Coroner. "'Your own coat, sir, if you will excuse my saying so, looks as though it, would feel like the one I touched." • There was almost a titter In the room, and the Coroner, not best pleased, went on abruptly, "Are you prepared to swear that you did not recognise this man as anyone you know ? ' "Certainly, I can swear to Anne was then called upon to describe, the find- ing of her sister's dead body in the parlour, and she answered still in the same unkltering manner. "Preciously strong-minded female Mat," whispered one of the jury to another. "But a rare pretty one, though, all the same,' said the other, admiring Anne's bright hair and complexion and her tall, finely developed figure, set off by the simple folds of her black silk gown—ad- miring her with all the amazement which a true Briton feels at the combination of good looks and good sense in a women. • Here the foreman of the jury asked a questiOn," Is there anybody who has had a quarrel with your sister, who may have wished to injure her ?" - "No—except, that is—" here Anne stammered, her pale cheeks flushedoind for a mernentshe lost her self-possession. " Try to remember now," said the Coronetre Anne looked down and made no reply. ' "I ask you on your oath "—the Coroner went on, sharply— 'do you know whether the deceased, Susan Derrick, had a disagreement of any sort with any. person whatever?" "I only know what she told me, eir, the morning before she died." Anne raised her head again, and spoke firmly, but she had turned very pale. "She said she had had a quarrel with Captain Stam- bridge. I don't know any particulars." "That's a lie!" came a hoarse cry from a corner of the room. Everybody started and looked to- wards Stambridge, who had started from his seat, his face purple, his small eyes blazing. "Sit down, Mr. Stambridge," said the Coroner authoritatively, "we shall call you as a witness presently. "I ain't going to sit here and listen to flat perjury," muttered Stambridge, resuming his seat, however. "We all sympathise with you in your sad loss," the Coroner went on, "but you cannot be allowed to in- terrupt the witness. I do not think we have any ' further question to ask you, Miss Derrick. Richards, as being the next person who had seen the corpse, was then called upon to give his evidence, which was only a repetition of what had gone before. One new fact was elicited. "Did you see or hear anything of the man that Miss Derrick found in the house?" asked the Coroner: "Well, sir, as you've asked me, Phave called to mind," replied the old man, in the slow, deliberate manner of his kind, " that as I was in the stable un- harnessing the brown horse as the missus had druv into Tavistock, being market day, I believe as how I did heal sunimat like a man's footsteps go quiok across the yard towards the gate. The master's come home, then,' thinks I to myself; where's he off to again in such a hurry? Y,To, it b'aint the master, then,' thinks I; it be Captain Stambridge as comes courting Miss Susan,' and just then the missuS comes cryins, oat for me, and I runs indoors, and the shocking sat .I seed there druv everything else out of my head; and I never thought no more about ahem footsteps till yesterday morning, when I was talking the matter over with my missus here." ' "You cannot say for certain whose footsteps they were ? " " Lord, no, sir; I was busy with the horse, as I be a-telling of you, and I didn't take no particular notice one way nor another. I just says to myself, there's the master, then, or else its Captain Stambridge. But you know now, sir, as well as I can tell you, that It warn!t the master, for he was a long ways up on the moor all the time." "And it certainly was not me," growled Stara- bridge, but he dared not say so aloud. 'Anne sat perfectly motionless while this morsel of evidence, which was quite new to her, was given; but the mention of Martin's name made her writhe inwardly. " Why did Richards say what his fancies were about the footsteps? Fancies are not evidence," she thought. Watkins, the policeman, was the next person summoned, and after a few questions had been asked and answered he thrilled the greater part of the audience by producing the revolver, and stating that he had found- it on the table in Mr. Derrick's room, with one chamber discharged, and the rest loaded. The Coroner and the jury handled the weapon cautiously. The bullet which Mr. Prior had two days before extracted from the death wound was corn- spared with those still in the revolver ; they correa-

ponded precisely, and this part of the chain of evi- dence was complete. Anne kept her eyes fixed on the Coroner, she dared not look at her brother whilst the ordeal proceeded. She felt as though 'a single glance in his directior might betray that he was in any special way affected by the testimony they were hearing. But she knew by the instinctive sympathy she had with' him that Martin was bearing himself with the most perfect composure. Nearly every man in the room disliked and disapproved of him ; not a man amongst them except old Richards could he rely on as a friend. Everyone else regarded him with suspicious,or coldly hostile glances, every one else would take it as a matter of course if some damning fact were brought to light against him. But be sat calm, unmoved through it all. Every moment he expected to be summoned to give evidence, but the Coroner, for reasons of his own, had determined that the master of the house should be the last witness called. Eliza Richards, sobbing, gasping incoherent, who required pulling and pusoing up to the table by her father, and who appeared to regard the Coroner and the ceremony of oath-taking with as much anguish as if a dentist and tooth-drawing were in question —Eliza Richards next declared that Miss Susan had sent her out about four o'clock that Friday after- noon, with a 'message to Miss Taylor, the village dressmaker. "She wanted her brown silk' dress trimmed with two rows of lace on the body instead of one, poor Miss Susan did, and I was to be sure to say the lace must be fulled on,, or 'twould look so skimpy, if you please, sir," said Eliza with a fresh burst of grief. "Well go on, my good girl; what time did you get back to the house? "Please sir, no time in special, because, Miss Susan she said so particular I was not to hurry hack, she didn't want me. I might stop and have a cup.of tea with a friend if I liked:" "So the unfortunate young lady was left entirely alone in the house that evening. Was it dark when you returned home?" "Yes, sir, dark as a wolf's mouth, and terrible foggy, I'm sure o' that much." Try your best to remember now. Did you meet any man when you were coming • along the lane towards the farm ? " "No, sir, that •I didn't; there's ne'er a man to meet,' cried Eliza, with a howl of anguish. "Did you hear anything out of the common as you were coming along ? " persisted the Coroner, who felt sure there was some deeper reason for the girl's terror and misery than the mere fact of having to answer a few simple question. "1 did, sir—yes, I did—" she sobbed, "but ra rather not say anything about it, if you'll please to excuse me, sir." - "But I insist on your telling me," was the Cortiner's quick reply; and now there was a general increase of interest amongst the audience, a sense that some- thing startling was about to happen, Eliza only sobbed on ; tier fattier, Who was stand• ing close behind her, ova & secret, savage, tweak to the girl's arm. tut the Coroner detected him, and fancied that he had seen the old man trying to fate signs to his daughter before. • " Stand back there!" he said, sternly. " How I dare you attempt to tamper with a witness! Now ray good don't be frightened, nobody wants to do yafl at' harm," he went on in a gentler tone. "But 'you are on your oath, yea know: and you must tell me the whole truth, about what yeti heard last Friday night when you were coming home, or I shall have to send you to prison." "Oh, oh I but father told me I wasn't to say word about it. Whatever shall Ido ? " "Good Lord! if the girl b'aint enough to drive one mad ! " groaned Richards, mopping his red face with a yellow cotton handkerchief. "Speak" out, then, you darned idiot, you! You have gone and made a precious mesa of it !" "If you speak another word,sir," said the Coroner, in high wrath, "I will have you removed by the police." Richards merely gave a defiant and "Come on, ' then D" sort of glance in ' the direction of Wat- kins, whom he regarded . with some of the good- humoured contempt bred of familiar acquaintance. Eliza, after a good deal more choking, proceeded, "I was coming along the lane, and I was just going, to step into mother's house to have a bit of a talk, when I thought I heard Miss Susan a-screeching—" "Where is your mother's house ? " interposed the Coroner. "Just by, if you please, sir; you can see it from that there window."- "Well, go on," and everybody listened, scarcely breathing, with all eyes fixed upon the girl. "I heard Miss Susan give two great screeches— 'Martin, Martin ! ' she cried—l heard the words quite plain, and then, lwasn't a minute after,l heard something go off like a gun." ' There was a dead silence in the room while you might have counted ten. Then a deep breath seemed to go through the crowd. "We are getting near the truth new," was the meaning of the sound. • Martin gaVe a great start as Eliza spoke. He elevated his brows and fixed his, eyes 'on her for a minute; then be looked down again Sand be muttered to himself with a heavy sigh, "Poor girl ! " Everyone observed that' he was deeply moved In some way by this fresh piece of evidence. But as for Anne—the report of the firearm which had killed her sister seemed to have sounded in her oars—she felt deafened, stunnefl;; for a minute she almost lost consciousness.. "Did you go and see what was the matter?" asked the foreman of the jury. . Ne sir, because poor Miss Susan had told me so paTticular she didn't want me. So I went and stopped with mother, until I heard Miss Derrick come driv- ing home from Tavistock. Then I ran along here, but the missus wouldn't let me stop in the house tllat night, but sent .me home again to mother's to sleep, because she thought I should be frightened. And that's all I know about it, sir; and if Mr. Watkins was to take me away at once, I couldn't tell you In more, if you please, sir." The girl was dismissed ; and -again Martin looked un, expecting, and extrerneiy anxious to be summoned:- But once more lie was forced to NPltit. (2'o be coatintied.)

IRELAND.
Three National League meetings were held at Macroom on Sunday, and were addressed by Dr. Tanner and Mr. Giffin°ly. Three warrants have been issued for the. arrest of the last-named gentleman.

Mr. Balfour. Chief Secretary for Ireland, left London on Saturday evening for Dublin. Mr. Balfour returned from visiting Lord Salisbury at Hatfield only just in time to take the Irish mail from Euston at 8 20. By an explosion, on Saturday, in the stillroom of Mr. Cossidy's distillery at Monastervan, near Maryboro, Ireland, one man was killed and several others injured, one of whom has since succumbed.
The Dublin Queen's Bench on Monday granted the application of the Crown to remove the place of the trial of the men charged with the murder of Head-Constable Whelehan from Cork to Wicklow.

Fifteen young men were sentenced at Kilrush, on Saturday-, to one month's imprisonment with hard labour each, for offences against the Crimes Act The prisoners, after being sentenced, cheered for Mr. O'Brien and the Plan of Campaign. - - •

Constable Thomas Thompson, having served eight years in the Royal Irish Constabulary, on Saturday evening handed in his resignation to the officer com- manding the Limerick district, as a protest against the prison treatment of Mr. O'Brien, M.P. Mr. Wilfred Blunt has taken proceedings in the Superior Courts against the Chief Secretary, Mr. Byrne (divisional magistrate), Inspector Ward, and Sergeant Walpole, for assault and false imprisonment. Lady Anne Blunt sues the Chief Secretary and Mr. Byrne for assault. The Lord Mayor and Mayoress of Dublin have counter- manded invitations to the Mansion House ball fixed for Friday, as it would be repugnant to the feelings of the citizens of Dublin to engage in any festivities, consider- ing the peril in which Mr. O'Brien's life is placed. On Sunday, a meeting in furtherance of the plan of campaign was held at Liscilla, on Lord Dillon's estate. Mr. Fox, M.P., and Mr. Conway, M.P., spoke. It was stated that all the tenants on the adjoining Murphy estate had paid their rents at Bs.. 6d. in the pound reduc- tion.

• It is stated on very good authority that the Govern- ment has decided to abandon the Press prosecution against the Lord Mayor of Dublin, M.P., and Mr. O'Brien, M.P.. for having, with a view to promoting the objects of the National League, published notices of certain sup- pressed branches.

Intelligence from Cookstown, in the north of Ireland, on Saturday, states that a Roman Catholic priest, on intetfering with an orange drum and fife band, which was marching to Lissan House, at the invitation of Sir N. Staples, by kicking a drum and striking ane of the drummers- with a stidk, was attacked by an •excited crowd, who gave hien a severe thrashing. In the Queen's Bench Division, Dublin. on Saturday, Mr. Carson, for the Crown, applied, under the ,Crimes Act, for an order for a special jury in the case of three men charged with a murder in Longford, arising out of a private quarrel. The order was granted. A similar order was granted in an assault case in King's county. These were the first applicationsnf the kind made.

Lord and I.cly Edward Cavendish, whoare at present staying at Lismore Castle, county Waterford, spent a considerable time in visiting various places of interest in the locality on Monday, including the new cathedral, towards the cost of the erection of which the Duke of Devonshire subscribed £l,OOO. 'Lord Edward Cavendish will spend a couple of days this week in shooting over .the Duke's preserves. The audited amounts of the fund for the defence of Messrs. John Dillon, Wm. 'O'Brien, Sheehy, Wm. Red- mond, Crilly. and Harris, M.P.'s.' in the abortive prosecu- tion for the Plan of Campaign conspiracy, show that the sum of £2.693 was stibscribed,,of which .£2,082 was paid for the coat of the trial and proceedings in the Dublin Police Court, the balance being handed to Mr. Dillon for the Evicted Tenants Fund. A large demonstratien of various branches of the Natiooal League was held on Sunday evening at Lisfinnv Castle, where Mr.. Pyne, MX. has fortified himself. Replying te a congratulatory address from the Youghal Branch Mr. Pvne, who spoke from an aperture in the castle about 80it. from the ground, said he wa,•: perfectly safe there, and lie would not like to be the first police- man who would attempt to effeat an entrance into it.

div.head: SERIOUS "RIOTINO T KILMUSH.
div.p: SERIOUS "RIOTINO T KILMUSH.

The 17 prisoners convicted under the Crimes Act at Kil- rush, on Saturday, were removed on Sunday by steamer to Limerick. They were escorted from the gaol to the quay by armed police. A large-crowd assembled, cheer- ing the prisoners u they wero marched to the wharf. The prisoners responded by singing "God !Pave Ireland." Then the crowd commenced stone throwing, upon which the Riot Act was read. The police then charged the people. severat of whom were injured, five scrim-My, and one policeman received a severe cut on the face from a stone. As the steamer left the prisoners gave cheers for Mr. O'Brien. the people ashore singing "God Save Ireland." Further rioting took place during the night. and the Riot Act was again. read. The police arrested eight persons, and considerable excitement prevailed.

ARREST OF ItYPlk'f" TclF! T.:*.nt:trlp• proclamation was received at Tullamore on foaturue. from the Lord Lieutenant, proclaiming that district and prohibiting a demonstration announced to be held there yesterday, to sympathise with Mr. O'Brien:Mr. Doughty, an English labour delegate, who was announced to speak at the meeting, was arrested in Dublin on Satur- day. Mr. Doughty was appointed a short time ago by a meeting of working men in Hyde Park, at whici a considerable sum of money was subscribed, to visit Ireland as their representative for the purpose of le- porting to the English working men the condition of affairs in Ireland. He arrived about a month ago, and proceeded immediately to Mitchelstown, where be spent several days. The charge against him is based upon a speech delivered at Six Mile Bridge, county Clare. Mr. Doughty was subsequently taken to the Kingsbridge railway terminus, and conveyed by the night mail train leaving Dublin at a quarter to eight to Ennis, which was reached at four in the morning.

div.head: CRITICAL CONDITION OF tIR. O'BRIEN.
div.p: CRITICAL CONDITION OF tIR. O'BRIEN.

Mr. O'Brien's clothes were taken from him on Satur- day morning by a, warder who entered his room to light his fire whilst ho was in betend suddenly ruithed away with them. Mr. Wm. O'Brien in the evening made a declaration to Dr. Moorland, J.P., which this Magistrate, at his request, eommitted to writing. "They intend to kill me,' he said. Subsequently, in an interview with Mr. Andrew Connolly, Mr. O'Brien said, " They Mean murder. They have acted like dastards. ii feel R 1 mll never leave the place alive. I ask you as a favour to let the public know what is being done." Pointing to the blue suit of hospital clothes, he added, "II I the here, I shall never put these on. I cannot say any- thing more, until I see Dr. Ridley and speak to him about the breach of faith." Mr. O'Brien states that Dr. Ridley had promised him that his clothes would not be interfered with.

Dr. Muirhead, in his entry in the 'Tuliarnore Prison visitors' book, describes an interview with Mr. O'Brien, during which he seemed most excited and coughed. He complained of a breach of an honourable understanding with Dr. Ridley on the question of his clothes, and re- peated, " They brought me here to murder me." Dr. Muirhead adds—" A bright hectic flush was burning in his cheek; his hands perspired with the cold clamminess of a tubercular subject; he coughed frequently; his breath was fceted ; and there has undoubtedly been a fresh secession of tubercular deposit in his system." The prison suit for Mr. O'Brien is stated to have been made in Mountjoy Gaol. Dublin. and sent to Tullamore last Wednesday. Unlike the original prison suit, it is of blue material. The prison tailors are working extra time at 100 suits of the same description—apparently intended for prisoners under the Crimes Act. The Freeman's Journal appeals to Englishmen to pro- test against Mr. O'Brien's treatment, which stirs the blood of Irishmen aflame. Mr. O'Brien on Saturday de- liberately charged the Executive with compassing his death. He may be labouring under excitement : but does not this treatment mean either loss of reason or life?
