div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1887.
ME TRAFALGAR-SQUARE MEETINGS.

--SUNDAY'S DEMONSTR4IIOS.—YHE GUARDS CALLED OUT.—PROCESSIONISTS DISPERSED. On Saturday afternoon, a deputation composed of Mr. Cuninghtme Graham M.P., and representatives of the Radical Federation and other bodies, waited a. the some Office upon Mr. Matthews, who declined to see anybody but Mr. Graham. In reply to Mr. Graham, who stated that Sunday's meeting was a, bond-fide political one, similar to those which he had stated would be permitted, Mr. Mattrzums said i--" It is the intention of her Majesty's Government that this meeting shall not be allowed, and we believe that we are within our strict legal rights. The public are only allowed in the Square on sufferance by her Majesty." Mr. Matthews also stated that he wished that the question should be tried in a legal manner before the Courts, to remove any doubts from the mind of the public.--Mr. GRAHAM said he regretted to hear this decision, as a very grave responsibility would lie with her Majesty's Government, as the meeting would be held at all hazards.

The agitators who designed to set Sir Charles Warren's proclamation at defiance by holding a meeting in Trafal- gar-square on Sunday afternoon were ignominiously repulsed by the police, who defended their purpose, and remained when night closed in masters of the situation. But Lilo authority of the Mei Commissioner was not vindicated or the aoitators baffled without a scene of disorder and tumult' disgraceful to the metropolis and dishonouring to the Day of Rest. The anticipation of a riot attracted all the roughs of London, who were ready for anything. To their sufficiently large numbers were added thousands of decent men, who, without any riotous intentions, came to see what was going on, and by their presence added considerably to the difficulties of the pohce, To distinguish between roughs and specta- tors was impossible, and many a too curious sightseer thus venturing into bad company, learned from the heavy hand of a constable that it is the duty of all good citizens, when disorder begins, to go home. Between sixty and seventy persons were treated at the• Charing Cross Hospital, mostly for bruises on the bead, arms, and legs; but the majority of the cases were slight enough to permit of the patients returning home, after treatment. The surgical staff of the hospi- tal was taxed to its utmost capacity for work; many a local surgeon also had his Sunday evening's rest broken -by bleeding and limping patients, who were brought to him by their friends on their way home.

In addition to the large number of wounded people., twenty set-foils cases were treated at St. Thomas's Tfospital, so that the number of hospital patients can he stated at onehundred ; but this, of course, bears a small proportion to the' total number injured, the individuals in the crowd who received hurts avoiding the hospitals wherever possible, so as to prevent their being identified as having taken part in the disturbance. The chief of the divisional-surgeons of the Metropolitan Police states that a policeman was stabbed in the bark with a swordstick : another police officer also was stabbe,i, and of the injured lying at St. Thomas's Hospital it is feared that two Will terminate fatally. The worst of these is a boy, who was knocked down by the mOb at Westminster, and is suffering from concussion df the brain and internal injuries, and it was feared that he could not live through the night. 'Police-patrol floon was thrown from his horse and sustained a fractured leg and other injuries, which render his case a,serious one. Amongst ,the injured is a young woman who had been visiting . a friend, a patient in an hospital. It is stated 'by the authorities that 'just' before 'the people came in contact with the police in the Strand, at the corner of Wellington-street, a eart-load of wood was driven ,up and shot. down into the street, to enable the pmeessionists to arm themselves. Many of these timber weapons appeared .as it they had formed part of wooden jointing wrenched asunder, and with the nails still projecting Many of the crowd, the police also state, pelted them with iron nuts. Altogether five thousand police were on duty in and around the Square, end at rho, mints at. which the processions were eapected to approach. In the tirst instance the number of arrests was very large, amountivg. it is *said; to over 400: but a great number were speedily liberated. At nicht there were iu detention-26 at King-street. 23 at Bow-street, and three at Nine-street. The charges entered against their were, in general. riotous conduct. One, however, was accused of violently stabbing Police-constable Wood- house. Several were detained for throwing dangerOus missiles, a few for breaking windows, and one, oddly enough, for being in unlawful l possession of an undarella. MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS. —7O PERSONS IN

THE DOCK. The only unusual feature in Trafalg.ar-square on Monday was the number of police on duty. These patrolled the pathways, and allowed no person to loiter in the centre of the :Square: but, notwithstanding their ewertions, the pavements became inconveniently crowded. The disturbances were the all-absorbing topic of co%ver- sation in the Metropolis, and were eagerly discussed. At Bow-street Police Court, on Monday, about 70 per- sons were charged with having, in company with divers other persons, unlawfully and riotously assembled in Trafalgar-square, on Sunday. and with a series of assaults on the police in various parts of the metropolis. The court was crowded. In the majority of the cases the prisoners were punished with fines Short terms of im- prisonment, orbeing bound over to beef good behaviour. The precincts of the court while these and subsequent cases were being 'beard presented a remarkable spectacle: The corridor from the cells was filled with police in uniform and in plain Clothes, many of them _wearing bandages round their .heads.

Thos. Morris, baker, WHO was cnargea wttn assatt..- the police with a stick, was sentenced to six months' hard labour. R. C. Cuninghame Graham, M.P., was next charged before Mr. Vaughan with conspiring against the Queen's peace, and assaulting the police.—Mr. Poland appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Asquith. M.P., for the defence.—lt was rumoured in. court tha* Sir as. Russell, Q.C., M.P., will defend Mr. Granatn at a later stage.—Sir A. Stephenson, solicitor to the Treasury, and Colonel Strachey occupied seats on the Bench. The defendant, who entered the dock in company with. John Burns, had a brindseo rnurv-1' his head.,--Mr. Poland stated that he appeared, instructed by the solicitor to The Treasury, to prosecute the two defendants on a tharge of haying assaulted the police in the execution of their duty, on Sunday afternoon, in Trafalgar-square, and be read the police proclamation recently issued by Sir C. Warren.—The cases were adjourned for a week, the defendants being liberated. Graham in £2OO and Burns £lOO, in addition to personal sureties to the same amount.

LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE. Mr. Gladstone having received from Bermondsey G'sd- stone Club a resolution condemning the conduct of the police on Sunday, in Trafalgar-square, and recommend- ing the holding of another meeting, has replied as fol- lows "Hawarden Castle, Chester, November I& Dear Sir,—l think you will expect me to meet your j request by an explicit answer expressing the best udg- ment which, while absent from the spot, I am able to form on the deplorable disturbances of yesterday. As I understand the matter, the Rome Secretary stated on Saturday for the information of the public that he in- tended to prevent yesterday's meeting in Trafalgar- square, and that he believed this prevention to be within his legal power. The question is one of great moment So the inhabitants of London, and particularly to those who at present are unhappily in circumstances of distress; and it will be generally felt that the state of the law in regard to it ought to be promptly tested and ascertained ; but it appears to ins indisputable that until a decision can be had it is the duty of every citizen to refrain from all resistance to the Executive Govern- ment, which is clearly entitled to administer the laws according to what it may be advised is their true con' struetion. Such abstinence is, I think, due alike to the high character of London for maintenance of public order, and to the respect we owe both to the law and to the mode in which it is usually applied through the medium of the admirable police of the. metropolis. But 1 must add that the appeal to Parliament and the nation on the grave and solemn issue now raised by the pro- ceedings of the Government in Ireland would suffer disastrous prejudice were it to be associated, in any manner, by those who make the appeal wiNi the metro- politan disturbance.—l am, &c., W. E. GrAnsroNs. "J. IL Johnson, Esq."

Mr. Gladstone, in another letter to a London corre- spondent on the same subject, but written on Sunday before receiving news of the disturbance, said :—" I am unable to pronounce upon the law of the question raised by Sir Charles Warren, but if it is on his side (and I am bound to assume he has examined it), I should be slow to question the exercise of his discretion."

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. Goschen was, on Satin%jay. elected Lord Rector.of Aberdeen University by 455 votes, to 314 given to Mr. John Morley. The Queen has been pleased to confer the dignity of a baronetcy upon the Hon. Henry Stafford Northcote, C. 8., M.P., who will bear the name of Sir Stafford North cote.

The Rev. E. J. A. Fitzroy, vicar of St. Jude's, West Derby. having written to ask Lord R. Churchill whether in advocating free schools he meant to allow parents to choose whether their children should bo educated at voluntary or board schools, has received a reply to the effect that Lord Randolph Churchill's answer to the question is most certainly in the affirmative.

Mr- Labouchere, M.P., was present on Monday at the annual dinner of the Eleusis Club, Chelsea, and formally opened a considerable addition to the premises. In proposing the toast of "Success to the Club," he con- demned the proceedings of Sir Charles Warren and the Rome Secretary with regard.to meetings in Trafalgar- square. and pointed out that that kind of tyranny was only what might hare been expected from the result of the last general election.

The Colston banquets were held on Monday night at Bristol. Mr. B. H. Fowler was the principal ~peqker. He deplored the difference which had arisen respecting the Irish question, and contended that the policy of the Government was doomed to end in failure. A wise and safe measure of Home Rule was the best, solution of the Irish problem that could be found. To separation in any degree, or under any pretext, he and his friends were prepared to offer the most strenuous resistance. Tho work of the Liberal party had been de- stcnctivet it must now be constructive.

MR. GLADSTONE ON RECENT EVENTS.—At a meeting of the electors of Midlothian, held at Loanhead last night, the following letter was read from Mr. Gladstone : Hawarden Castle, Chester, Nov. 15, 1887. Dear Sir,— The lateness of your meeting is in some respects advan- tageous, for things which were disputed have, with time, become clear. We said that the Government and the majority would waste the session, that coercion was the alternative to Home Rule. Our opponents said the re- verse. Experience has judged between us. It has taught even more, for on the side of the Government co- ercion has passed into illegality, and a comparison of Ireland now with Ireland eighteen months back shows that it has produced insecurity and disorder, and has aggravated the disease of Ireland—hostility to the law which England mainly dictates. While all this is going on, the dissentients have also helped to clear our vision, for they tell us plainly that nothing can be done for the government of Ireland until Irish nationality, which has resisted the oppressions of 700 years is renounced and extinguished, though even Lora Carirarvon told us we ought to give reasonable satisfaction to the national as- pirations of Ireland. Everything, in short, is helping the public mind towards right conclusions, and a great solution.—l remain, dear sir, your faithful and obedient , servant, W. E. GLADSTONE MR. JOHN MORLEY AND THE UHIONISTS.—A meeting of the electors of the Western Division of Edinburgh was held on Monday in the Music Hall in support of the can- didature of Mr. T. R. Buchanan,.M.P. The hon. gentle- man was accompanied. to the platformilay Mr. John Morley, M.P. The hall, which accommodates about 2,000, was crowded.—Mr. Asher, as an elector in the division moved a resolution approving the course taken by Mr. ;Indianan, and adopting him as the Liberal can- didate for the division.—Mr. John Morley, who was re- ceived with prolonged cheering, said Mr. Buchanan had played the part of an upright and honourable man. His opponents had not denied that. The change that had • taken place in Mr. Buchanan and the place he now oc- qupied was not an atom more serious than the change that had taken place in the position of Lord Hartingt& himself. (Cheers.) The change in Lord Haztington s opinion explained how it was that elections were won by Liberal Unionists in July, 1886, and why, as he (the speaker) ventured to think, no more victories were going to be won by them. It had been pointed out that the whole of the policy which was announced to this country by the present Government had gone. They announced a measure of local government, but it had gone. They were told there was to be a measure of land purchase, and they were told so still, but he did :not expect to see a line or clause of it.

MR. GOSCREN AT MANCITESTER.—Mr. GOSCherl ad- dressed a great Conservative and Unionist gathering in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday night. The right 'hon. gentleman paid a hearty tribute to the Chief Secretary for Ireland, who, in the van of the struggle in which they were engaged, was battling bravely against the forces of disorder." He recalled the great conflict in America, in which the sympathies of Lanca- shire, in spite of much suffering, were with the North, and In "favour of the maintenance of the Union. The present struggle was one in which the vital interests of the country were involved. He insisted on the mainten- ance of law and order both in Ireland and in England as a primary condition of the country's prosperity. "We have," he said; "the same duty in London as in Ireland, and the same duty in Ireland as in London." The authority of the law would be asserted, and all attempts to gain unworthy ends by a policy of wearing out one's patience would be answered by the British nation with the declaration that they would never surrender to crime nor time. Mr. Goschen, besides being entertained by the Mayor of Manchester to luncheon on Wednesday, and receiving a congratulatory address from the Cham- ber of Commerce, was present at a banquet in his hon- our at the Conservative Club, when he replied to the toast of his health. On Thursday Mr. Goschen fulfilled three engagements, in the first place receiving an address from the bi-metallists of Manchester. He afterwards lunched at the Queen's Hotel, Manchester, with the Liberal Dissentients and at night delivered an address at Ashton-upder-Lyne.

div.head: EXECUTIONS AT (3A RLISLE AND OXFORD.
div.p: EXECUTIONS AT (3A RLISLE AND OXFORD.

Hunter, is blacksmith's striker, was executed in Carlisle Gaol, on Monday, for the murder of a child. mimed Isabella Steel, by the wayside. The condemned . man, who was atiout 30 years e age, had conducted him- self very quietly in the prison. lie had to be wakened at six o'clock in the morning, and at ten minuted to eight he submitted to be pinioned by Berry. When he left his cell he shook hands with several of the warders and nodded to reporters and others near. He walked steadily to the gallows, with a half smile upon his face. When the chaplain, who was reeting the Litany for the dying, came to the words "May he rest in peace," the bolt was drawn, and the man died apparently instantanfemsly. Hunter had stated that he did not kill the child wilfully, hut he preferred being hanged to passing his life in penal servitude. Hunter received his sentence of death at the fast Cumberland Assizes for killing the (laughter of a woman with whom he cohabited. He was (ormerly a blacksmith, but for three mouths prior to the crime had been on tramp with a woman named Mary Steel. tie ill-treated her daughter (Isabella), and finally caused her death by kicking her on the roadside. The execution of Joseph Walker, who was sentenced to death at the Oxfordshire Assizes for the murder of his wife, on Sept. 16th, at Chipping Norton, by cutting her throat, took place yesterday morning, at the county gaol, Berry being the executioner. During the past fortnight. a petition fort a commutation of the sentence was en- tensively signed, on the ground of the provocation the condemned man had continually received from the deceased. Walker had been visited by his brother and by his two children, for whom he had a great affection, and the parting scene was especially painful. Walker appeared resigned to his fate. Yesterday morning there was a celebration of the Communion at St. Frides- wide, in order to pray for the unhappy man. Several hundred persons assembled to witness the hoisting of the black flag, but tio expression of feeling was mani- fested. Walker was 46 years of age, and weighed 16 stone. The drop which Berry allowed was only 2ft. Win., which the executioner said was the shortest he had ever known. There was not the slightest movement after the drop fell, although the pulse beat feebly for a short time afterwards. The culprit had frequently alluded to the crime, but declared that it was not premeditated. He expressed a hope that, the public would not visit his sin on his children, but would help them to lead sober, in- dustrious, and Godly lives. He displayed throughout the utmost fortitude, and partook at breakfast-time of a slice of bread and butter and a cup of tea.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

lAlrolaty!a 144 amount of unemployed labour has 1 been placed fit the service of Mr. T. A. Walker, the gentleman who has undertaken the construction of , the Manchester Ship Canal. From an early hour on 1 Monday morning until the middle of the afternoon the quiet turnpike road between New Ferry and Eastham presentedan unusually animated appear- ance, hundreds of persons traversing it in the hope of securing work at or near the Eastham terminus of the canal. A large proportion of the unemployed of Liverpool, together with a few from Manchester, proceeded frora Liverpool to New,Ferry by steamer andwalked the remainder of the distance, trusting they might obtain, at the end of thpir• journey, either initnediate work or a promise that their ser- vices would be utiFted on the following day. This expectation proved, however, in most instances to have been ill founded. Mr. Manisty, the contrac- tor's agent at Eastham, is still engaged in making further arrangements for proceeding with the work of excavation on an extensive scale, and un- til these preparations are completed it is useless taking on a very large staff of workmen. The con- sequence was that nearly all the applicants for work came away disappointed. Under any circum- stances the great bulk of them would have done 60 because they did not appear suited for rough out- door labour. The others may reasonably hope to stand a fair chance of obtaining remunerative em- ployinent when everything has been put in ship ' shape, which will probably be in about a week. Since• the first sods were cut a considerable amount of work has been done near Eastham.., The railway along the bank of the Mersey has been ex- tended, and brought as far down the river as Job's Ferry, where a large quantity of timber and other materials required by the contractor is being lan- ded. In the field adjoining the spot where the East- ham locks are to be made a branch line is being rapidly constructed, along which the soil to be shortly excavated will be conveyed and tipped on the low-lying land near the south bank of the Mer- sey. The huge excavators or "steam navvies," which have been lying in pieces on the ground for several days, are being put together so as to be 11 ready for immediate use, and several locomotives are standing in a row with everything in readiness except the requisite steam pressure. Joiner's and smiths' workshops are being erected, as well as a place in which various kinds of materials will be stored which are likely to be frequently required. There is but little lodging accommodation at East- ham, and it is reported that all the accommodation available at Ellesmere Port has already been applied for. Active Operations have not yet commenced at the latter place, but the requisite material is already there, and a beginning will shortly be made in the neighbourhood. One reason for this brief delay is found in the fact that that portion of the land be- tween Eastham and Ellesmere Port which has up to the present time been in the hands of the Shrop- shire Union Railway and Canal Company has not yet been formally transferred to the Ship Canal Com- pany. The necessary formalities are expected, how- ever, to be completed shortly. From what we can learn, the directors of the company hope to be able at the beginning of each month to complete the purchase of additional land. As soon as this is done the Contractor will be informed of the fact, in order that he may, if he likes, at once begin opera- tions there. , We believes however, that it is Mr. Walker's intention to confine his attention during the remainder of the present year to the two lower sections of the canal.

Although some 20,000 men will ultimately find work on the Manchester Ship Canal, only 2,500 will be engaged on I the first section of the canal, in Cheshire, and the bulk of the hands will not be taken on for some months. In a short time the Eastham section will be in full swing, giving con- stant employment to over 2,000 men. The rate of wages fixed by the contractor is 4d. per hour dur- ing the winter months, when the hours worked daily cannot exceed nine; but in consequence of the increased number worked in the summer, the average wages will be about £1 per week. Quite a village of huts is being erected to accommodate the men employed, and Cheshire workhouses are full of men expecting to get on the job. At Eastham, on Thursday, the excavations were pro- ceeding, a staff of some 350 men being at present em- ployed'. Materials and machinery are still arriving, and the principal work now going on is that of preparation for future operations. Of the total length of the Canal (34 miles) 23 or 24 are in Cheshire, the boundary being crossed near Thelwall, The next centre of operations I will probably be Frodsham, where matters are nearly ripe for a start. Runcorn will probably be the next place where work will be begun. The contracts for the length of canal extending from Eastham to the mouth of the Weaver, in Cheshire, will be pushed on most rapidly, the object being to join the Weaver navigation as early as possible. At the mouth of the Weaver a large basin and docks will be created, and here ships carrying salt will be loaded from the flats which have cdme down the river from the salt works of the Nortliv•-ich and Winsford districts. In this way an almost immediate income will be secured to the company, as it is hoped to complete this branch of the work within the next two years. At present the flats have to be taken down the Mersey to Liverpool, where the tran.shipment of the salt is made. The alternative plan will be that the ships will proceed up the Ship Canal to the mouth of the Weaver, where they will take in the salt. The canal will be entered close to Eastham by tidal locks. By next April it is hoped that the Eastham and Ellesmere Port section will be in full swing with the work. Large numbers of applicants continue to come into Eastham in search of work, but comparatively few of them can be taken on at the present stage. It is really pitiable to watch the faces of the men as they turn away disappointed of work after their weary trainp.

div.head: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.
div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.

The luckiest "find" ever made in California, was made i by a man named Finney, who "turned up" a solid lump ' a gold near Downieville. in 1868, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 18.00 dols. per ounce, which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget of pure gold ever discovered. . Heretofore the Australian nugget found in the Ballarat gold fields has been considered the Largest. It was valued at £15,000. This man Pinney, or "Old Virginia," as he was called, went to Washoe, California, and there he made the great silver discoveries, where the " Comstock " lode was located, and where Virginia City, which was named after him' stands. He died in great poverty. Ile was cele- brated for his wonderful head of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of golden tints, and which fell in heavy curls over his stalwart shoulders. He was very proud of his head covering, and always carried in his " outfit " a brush, comb, and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his "camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great care. When misfortune overtook him, and he continued "pitying in bad luck "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hair, and it became frowsy, began to turn gray, and fall out, so that a few years before he died he was nearly bald, and his few remaining hairs were quite white. Had he added to his " outfit " Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he lived, for it never fails to strengthen and invigorate the I hair, restore its colour, and render it soft, glossy and strong. It can be found at any chemist's or perfumer's in the world. It is the best and most agreeable hair dress- ing known. Try it.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. Seely, as a memorial of his deceased father, has made a gift to each of the Isle of Wight tenants of half a year's rent due at Michaelmas last. The total of this gift amounts to nearly £5,000. Ii the Crown Court at the Liverpool Assizes on Mon- day, Henry Hou(grave, 50, labourer, was found guilty of shooting Frederick Read, a gamekeeper, with intent to murder him, and was sentenced to penal servitude for life.

The London and North-Western Railway Company have in contemplation an important railway improve- ment at Bolton. At present Great Moor-street is the terminus and it is proposed to carry it forward to Church-street, Little Bolton.

In the Appeal Court, on Saturday, the appeal was heard of D. E. Bensaude against an order of Justice Charles, pre- cluding him from molesting or interfering with his wife, Miss Violet Cameron, contrary to the provisions of a covenant contained in a deed of separation.

At Bolton, on Sunday afternoon, an elderly man named William Bradley, who had for close upon five years con- ducted a night school in that town, committed suicide at the residence of his married son, with whom he re- sided, hanging himself with a clothes-line attached to the banister. _

THS QUEEN'S ENVOY TO TER POPIC—A special envoy will be sent to the Pope early in the ensuing month to express to him, on behalf of her Majesty, a sense of the courtesy shown to her by the mission of Monsignor Raffo Scilla to congratulate her on her Jubilee. The en- voy will be the Duke of Norfolk, K.G. • •• • - - - ---••

'Sir M. Hicks-Beach, presiding at a meeting of his Wilt- shire tenan try, at Netheravon, on Saturday, said he wished he oould see some remedy for the present agricultural distress, but frankly acknowledged he could not. Some of the proposed remedies would, he thought, entail evils greater than those actually existing. Be should be sorry to see anything that would make food dear.

THE THIRLMEIZE WATERWORKS.—It is stated that this work proceeds very slowly, and with the approach of winter the workmen have been further thinned., about fifty having just been discharged. Boring is about to be begun in the Rydal Park portion of Nab Scar to meet that already well advanced from the opposite direction. A great number of men have been attracted to the dis- trict in search of work, and are thrown into great dis- tress. _

Justices Stephen and Charles, sitting as a Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench, on Monday, ordered Charles Thomas Hill, solicitor, of 52, Chancery-lane, to be sus- pended for three years, on the ground that he had been guilty of gross misconduct in the libel action against the Pall Mall Gazette in connection with the Eliza Arm- strong case. Mr. Reid, Q.C., who made the application, Mid Hill got up the action, and then delivered extor- tionate bills of costs.

ACTION FOR FAIRS IMPRISONNENT.—In the Queen's Bench, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Mathew and a special jury, the case of Sharley v. Bayfield and another was heard. In this case Alice Sharlev, domestic servant, sued the defendants, Dr. Bayfield and Mrs. Darling, for false imprisonment and malicious prosecution, theaction arising out of the charge which was preferred against her in February last year, of putting opium into tea in- tended for her mistress. The hearing of the case was opened on Saturday and concluded on Monday, when the jury found a verdict for the defendants. _ _ _

Early on Saturday morning, a quarrel took place be- tween two brothers, named Fidele, in Cardiff, in the coUrse of which one was shgt, The elder brother, Joseph, •had advanced a considerable sum of money to the younger, Carnini, to purchase a rig-out for a voyage. On Friday, Joseph heard that his brother was squander- ing the money on loose characters, and went in search of him. Meeting him in Nelson-street, he commenced to upbraid him for his conduct. whereupon Carnini pulled out a revolver and shot his brother in the breast, inflict- ing terrible wounds. _ . .

NEW USE FOR A WOODFN LEO.--Efarry Smith, n native of Leicestershire, a man with a wooden leg, was en Monday, at Whitehaven, committed for trial at the Cumberland Quarter Sessions. Smith, early on Saturday morning, met a policeman and asked to be locked up. The policeman refused his request, whereupon Smith said he would soon do something that would get him locked up. He then went to the Crown flotel, unscrewed his wooden leg, and with it smashed five large plate glass windows, causing damage estimated at £B. Before being removed to his cell, the prisoner shouted to the magis- trates, "Help the landlord; the other I will put up with." .*. .

HIGHWAY ROBBERY WITH VIOT,F.NCE.—A terrible high- way robbery took place at Llanelly, on Saturday morn- ing. Thomas Davis, an employe in the Dafen Tin Works, was returning to the works with a bag contain- ing £370, workmen's wages, when he was attacked by some person or persons unknown, who stole the money, and murderously assaulted him. Ile was found at one o'clock in an unconscious condition, a huge blood- besmeared cleaver being by his side, and when he was taken to the hospital it was ascertained that his skull had been gashed in several places, and that he had nearly bled to death. He succumbed on Monday. One arrest has been made. • SHOCKING CAB ACCIDENT AT BOOTHSTOWN.-- On Sunday, a party of Bolton gentlemen went nut for a drive in the Worsley district, in a four-wheeled cab. They were together for several hours, and did not com- mence the return journey until late. The driver, George Dawson' an experienced man, missed his way, and went In the direction of Boothstown at a furious rate. Eventually the vehicle was overturned, and the cab became a total wreck. Dawson was thrown violently from the box, and killed nistantly ; and all the occupants of the conveyance were badly out and bruised. They included Mr. James Entwistle, poor-law guardian for Bolton; Mr. John Glaister, bleacher, Mr. Chadwick, a watchmaker; and another Bolton gentleman. 411 were conveyed home in cabs, and received prompt medical attendance. Dawson's body awaits an inquest. HEXTFIORPE DISASTER: ThIAL OF DRIVER AND GUARD.— At the Yorkshire Assizes, held at York Castle, on Mon- day, before Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, Saml. Taylor, 39, engine driver, and Robert Davies, 28, fireman, were indicted for the manslaughter of Jane Rail, James Win. Beaumont, and other persons, at Hexthorpe, on the 16th September last. Mr. Coltman and Mr. W. S. Loft. house appeared for the prosecution; Mr. E. ' Tindal Atkinson, Q.C., and Mr. Kershaw represented the pri- soners ; and Mr. Mellor watched the case on behalf of the Manchester Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. Both prisoners pleaded not guilty. The prisoners were in charge of the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire train. The theory on which the prosecution was based WRS that the accident was caused by their culpable negligence in not looking out for flag signals, which were plainly eahibited. SHOOTING A SWEETHEART.—At Winchester Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Wills, George Prior Wa.s charged with shooting with intent to murder Alice Maud Mary Gamblin, at Portsmouth, on the-12th ult. The prisoner lodged with a Mrs. Ward, to whom Garnb- lin acted as servant, but was under notice to leave, and on the day in question it was stated that he pawned his clothes and purchased the revolver. Be then returned !tome, and entering the kitchen, where Gamblin was alone, he is alleged to have fired the revolver, the bullet striking her in the groin. She ran out screaming, and two more shots were fired, but did not hit her. It is Supposed the prisoner had some affection for Gamblin, for a few weeks before the occurrence he stated he i would kill her. He admitted firing the shots. Ile was • found guilty, and sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude, the judge intimating that the prisoner was morally guilty of murder.

CONFESSION OF A MURDERER : A MORBID MIND. —The convict Joseph Morley, who was sentenced to death at the present Chelmsford Assizes for the murder of. Mrs. Dodger, at Dagenham, in confessing his guilt, states that the crime was not premeditated, but that in cutting Mrs. Hedger's throat he yielded to an uncon- trollable impulse. Ile also states that he was led to commit the crime in cOnsequence of his reading an account of the recent clerical murder in Suffolk, and that he had for a long time taken a morbid interest iu perusing narratives of murders and crimes. The con- fession has been forwarded to the Rome Secretary, to whom an application has been made for a commutation of the sentence to pne of penal servitude for life. The grounds upon which the appeal for mercy is based are the youth of the convict, the absence of motive for the crime, and the existence of insanity in his family. Mean- while the execution has been fixed for Monday next.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN SHROPSHIRE.—EarIy on Sunday morning a labourer named George Houckley, an elderly man, living at Ironbridge, Shropshire, attempted to mur- der his wife and afterwards committed suicide. The couple retired to bed as usual on the previous night, and about midnight the deceased got up and committed a murderous assault on his wife with a pickaxe, severely fracturing' her skull and breaking one of her arms. Having thus maltreated her, he forced her out into the street, and threw the hatchet after her, striking her on the head. A few minutes afterwards he committed suicide by cutting his throat. He is supposed to have been insane. An inquest was held on Monday, rela- tive to the death of George Bouckley and his wife. The evidence of their daughter, aged 16 years, was that early on Saturday morning the man attacked his wife with a chopper, inflicting fatal injuries, and then throat. cut his The jury returned a verdict of felo de se in the case of Houckley. THE EXTRAORDINARY YORKSHIRE DIVORCE CASH.— In the Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty Division, on Saturday, Sir James Thinner' and a special jury resumed and concluded the extraordinary suit of Driffield v. Driffield. Clark, and White.—The petition was that of Mr. William Driffield, of West Huntington Hall, York- shire, a gentleman of independent means, for the disso- lution of the marriage on the ground of the misconduct of his wife with Major James Alston Clark, a retired officer of the army, and also Mr. Edward Charles White, a private inquiry agent (who had previously been engaged to watch Mrs. Driffield). There was also a charge against Mr. Leeman, formerly a solicitor, of York, but he had died some time before the institution of the present suit. —The respondent and the two co-respondents answered, denying the charge. 'lhe jury found against the respon- dent with Major Clark and Mr. White, hut not with Mr. Leeman. His Lordship granted a decree nisi, with costs, with custody of the children. It was also arranged that the costa of the supplemental petition in regard to White should not be charged against Major Clark.

When the ancient empire of Atahualpa existed in all it glory, and before its overthrow by the rapacious Pizarro, the extraordinary virtues of the " Pearl of South America " were as well known to the then natives as to, the Peruvians of the present day. Indeed, its great and admitted worth led to its being used in all public ceremonies as an acceptable offering to their deity—the Sun God. The leaves of this marvellous shrub. when ready for market, are transported on mules up the steep mountain sides, across the icy and desolate plateaux • and through the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many of them 13,000 and 14,000 feet above the level of the sea, and then downwards on the other side of the mountains Into Pero for shipment from the port of Callao (Lima.) And so terrible- is the icy rigour of the climate amidst the lofty heights of the mountains, especially of the icy plateaux of Lipes, that the muleteers find the chewing of these leaves alone enables them to withstand the icy rarefied air, and to support the long night- watches to prevent the mules they are transporting to Pena from straying. Several natives, who, never allowing a day 60 pass without chewing the leave,, of the "Pearl of South America" at least three times daily, attained the truly pate* archal age of 130 years.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1887.

MR. GOSCHEN has been delivering his soul before the Tories and Liberal Unionists at Manchester, • and it is due to him to say that he shows himself much more at home amongst the Tories than ever he did amongst the Liberals. The than who was more Conservative' than the Conservatives them- • *elves in opposing the extension of the franchise in boroughs, and, more recently, in counties, is in ' ' his place, futile though his efforts may be, in -trying to stern the tide of democracy. His speech ef Tuesday abounds in fallacies and misrepresenta- tiobs from beginning to end; he has no case, but he displays considerable skill in abusing his oppo- nents. What can be more misleading, for instance, "Oen his referenee to the part that Lancashire played during the cotton famine which resulted • from the great civil war in the United States? Lancashire," he said, "suffered in that cotton , ,famine, but Lancashire looked on with sympathy st the struggle of a country for unity, the struggle ' of a country against disintegration." The infer- ence he draws is that Lancashire, for a similar • reason, sympathises with the Government in their ; struggle with Ireland. But dare he put the matter .• to the test? Will he, as a member of the Govern- ment, recommend an appeal to the country at the , 'present time and abide the issue, knowing, that - Lancashire will lead the way? Why, it is notori- 'oijs that Mr. GOSCHEN aid Lord SALISBURY have " swallowed every principle they formerry professed, 7and all because they were afraid, with regard to the last Land Bill, that, if they did not eat their own words, the Dissentient Liberals would desert - them, and there would be a dissolution of Parlia- ment. They are both hollow and inconsistent; but it would seem that— A merciful Providence fashianed.them hollow, In order that they might their principles swallow. Lancashim sympathised with the North, because she believed that the war was a war against slavery, just as she sympathises with Ireland to-day because of the tyranny of the Government. Nobody knows better than Mr. GOSCHEN that it is th,e veriest clap-trap to talk about disintegration. Fifty years ago Canada was in revolt because the Goschens of the day resisted her demand for self- ., , government. After a bitter straggle, in which many lives were lost, Home Rule was conceded her; but not even the CHANCELLOR of the Ex- , °stemma. will say that it has resulted in disinteg- ration. Canada is loyal and prosperous under her constitution—just as Ireland will be when she is granted Home Rule. It is ludicrous to hear Mr. Ciaseim talk of "the powei of making the laws that you want" as one of -the essential conditions 'ef prosperity—ludicrous because if it is good for England it is equally good for Ireland. Thepower to make their own laws is exactly what the people -of Ireland demand; and, as this is an essential condition of prosperity, and as, too, it is refused by the Government, the conclusion is irresistible that the Government do not desire the prosperity 'of Ireland. Mr. GOSCHEN cannot forgive Mr. GLADSTONE for having, by describing him as a Tory, lost his election at Edinburgh; and he neglects no op- "Portunity of venting his spleen upon the chief of the Liberal party. Like most persons who are vin- 'clictive, he is reckless in his statements 3 and reck- less statements always recoil upon their author. Re quotes Mr. GLADSTONE'S letter on the Trafal- gar Square disturbances, and tries to make it out that, in the matter of obedience to the law, the ex-Premier has one voice for Fngland and a wholly different voice for Ireland. An assumption of this kind is as far from the truth as it can possibly be. Mr. GLADSTONE has in no single instance counselled resistance to the law, either in England or in Ire- land. What he has done, with great force arid with statements that carry conviction with them, has been to point out that the authorities were themselves the law-breakers in Ireland, and that they ought to be held to account by the nation for their lawless conduct. The meeting at Mitchels- town was legally constituted; it was not even pro- Claimed; and, as the police had no more right than any other body of men to break in upon it, they axe responsible, legally and morally, for the lives that were lost through \a disturbance which they themselves had created. Because Mr. GLAD- *worm points these facts out, how can it tte said that he countenanees an infraction of the law? R. is demanding that the law shall be observed by tsnervants of the Government as well as by • ary citizens. We need hardly say that it is quite in harmony with • Mr. GLADSTONE'S career' that, so long as there is a doubt as to the law, he should advise every citizen to "refrain from all l'egistance to the Executive Government ;" but, once let it be shown that the Government are in the wrong in denying the use of Trafalgar tivare for public meetings, and not, even Goeonew doubts that he will be emphatic in his demand that those who have broken the law shall be made to- sufter the penalty cf the law. There is this much, meantime, to be for the men who sought to hbld a meeting in ,Lndalgar Square, on Sunday last—that the meet- Was a purely political one of which notice had "sen given weeks before; that the oonveness were

fbllowing a custom which has been observed from time iinmemorial in deciding to hold it in the Square; and that nothing could justify the police in striking Mr. CUNNINGHAM GRAHAM, M.P., again and again, when as leader of the movement he iiralked, unarmed, to the Square to assert what he believed to be his right. Whateverthelaw as to the matter may prove to be, it is nonsense for the some Secretary to say that "the public are only itllowed in the Square on sufterance by her Majesty." It is a degradation of the Queen's name to introduce it in such a connection. It is not less offensive on the part of Mr. GOSOHEN to say that the meeting was not being held to establish free speech, but the right of intimidation. If this monstrous teaching is to be permitted, the Gov- ernment which is blessed with such an adviser will soon be tempted to put down every political meet- ing where there is any likelihood of anything being saki which is disagreeable to them. It would be a simple matter for them to plead that what was disagreeable to them was in the nature of intimi- dation. This old, bad Tory doctrine, the sort of doctrine which led to the massacre of Peterloo, is the latest wisdom of the Tory Ciremaira.on. of the ExclisQuEß who poses as a Liberal Unionist.

IT Is a common thing for those who are opposed to any scheme of Home Rule to deny that there is such a thing in a really strong feeling in Ireland in favour of self-government. , , What the Irish want ttiey say, is not freedom to govern them- selves, but power to oppress others by taking pos- session ot the land. There can bei no doubt that the Irish question is more or leas an agrarian question, but this does not necessarily mean that Irishmen wish to live rent free. What they ask, and what they have a right to ask, is that they shall not be robbed of the value of their improve- ments by evicting landlords who demand impos- sible rents. But beyond this practical view of their grievances, there is the sentiment Of nationality, that love of independence which Eng- lishmen admire so much when it shows itself in the breast of a Pole or a Greek, but which is pooh- poohed as something not worth considering when found in the heart of an Irishman. Still, the sen- timent is there; it is a factor to be dealt with, and those who do not know how powerful it is in its in- fluence upon the life and character of the people of the Emerald Isle have 4 good deal to learn about Ireland. We have beenlecl into these observations by the perusal of a volume of Irish Minstrelsy, pub- lished in the Canterbury Poets series, by Mr. Wal- ter Scott. It is quite a garden of choice flowers and we purpose to pluck a sower here and there by way of showing that love of fatherland is the prevailing genius of the Irish race. There is a song on songs by THOMAS DERMODDY, one stanza of which runs :

0, glorious songs! That rouse the brave 'gainst tyrant wrongs, Resounding near and far; Mingled with trumpet and with drum, Your spirit-stirring summons come, To urge the hero from his home , And arm him for the war. This 4 in the right vein; it has a martial ring with it, suggestive as it is of Shakespeare's "spirit stiffing drum and ear-piercing fife." The ever- popular "Wearing of the Green" is one of the street ballads of 1798. The versemost quoted is as follows
I met with Napper. Tandy, atici he took me by the hand, And he said— How's poor Old Ireland, and bow does she
stand r (axe's the most distressful country that ever yet was
• Ben; They are hanging men and women forthe wearing of the

green. Nearly a century has elapsed sinoe this song was written, but some of our rulers have learned nothing and forgotten nothing in the meantime. Politicians of the HAITINGTON-SALISBUBY school have no letter way of dealing with Ireland than "hanging men and women for the wearing of the green." . In England, the word " Paddy " is used as a term ot reproach; bnt not so across the Chan- nel. There is one song with the title of "Paddies Evermore." We:give four lines of it:—

The strife for freedom here begun We never will give o'er, Plor own a land on earth but one— We're Paddies evermore. The adage that "Knowledge is power" is put in this effective way in "Rory of the Hill" :- 01 knowledge is a wondrous power, and stronger than And th—nes shall fall, and despots bow, before the might

, of mind. This is a poetical notice to quit," and we do nob doubt that in the long run it will be followed by a series of evictions of an. entirely new and quite a wholesome kind. Here is a grim joke—one of several—from "The Blacksmith of Limerick" : The .nnt that topped the rampart, he NM a colonel
bold; Right through tb3 murk of battle his helmet Sashed with
gold. - "Gold is no match for iron," the doughty blacksmith
said, As with that ponderous hammer he cracked the foeman's head.

" The Union," a song by Sliabhlinn, reminds us in its etnphaaia of the reference which Mr. GLAD- worm made in one of his speeches to the passing of the Act of Union. The song begins : How did they pass the Union ? • Ily perjury and fraud; lily slaves who sold their land for gold, , As Judas sold his God. Then we have, finally :

And shall it last, this Union, To grind and waste us so P O'er hill and lea, from sea to sea, All Ireland thunders, No! The Union will not, of course, last to "waste and grind ; " it is to be so changed by Home Rule that the Union may become a blessing instead of a curse; and it is a hopeful sign that Englishmen as well as Irishmen new perceive and acknowledge that this is not only possible, but probable., In this connection we cannot do better than qudte from a pathetic poem by Miss Fanny Parnell (sister, of the Irish leader), who died in 1883, at the age of 28. It bears the title, "After Death," and would seem to have been written with a fore- boding of the approaching end : Shall mine eyes behold thy 'glory, 0 my country? shall mine eyes behold thy glory? Or shall the darkness close around them ere the sun- , blaze break at last upon thystory ? Ah ! the tramp of feet victorious ! I should hear them 'mid the shainrocks and the mosses, And my heart should toss within the shroud and quiver as a captive dreamer tosses. What consuming energy there is in these lines! Who can read them and doubt that the writer was possessed of a passionate love of her nation as a nation? In the song, "Patrick Sheenan," we have a stirring account of an eviction. Poor Pal says :

" My father died; I closed his eyes ONtside our cabin door; The landlord and the sheriff, too, Were there the day before! And then my loving mother, And sisters three also,, Were forced to go with broken hearts From the Glen of Aherlow. The informer is a character in Irish history alike prominent and odious. In view of the use recently; made of this personage by the Government, it is interesting to note the reference to him by Lady Wium in her beautiful poem of "The Brothers"
Before them shrinking, oowering, scarcely human, The base irtformor bends,

Who, Judas-like, could sell the blood of true men While he clasped their hands as friends. , Ay, could fondle the young children of his victim, Break bread with his young wife, At the moment that, for gold, his perjured dictum Sold the husband and the father's life. • We have quoted sufficient to show that no student of Irish song can be ignorant of the fact that is so constantly ignored by a certain class of politi- cians—namely, that national feeling, national aspir- ation, is the bed-rock of Irish character. We had marked a number of passages by way of exhibiting the humorous side of Irish life, but must content ourselves with a single quotation from "I'm Not Myself at All," by SAMUEL LOVER : Th' oth ir day I went confessing, and I asked the father's . blessing, "But," says I, " don't give me one entirely For I fretted so last year, but the half of ma is here, So give the other half to Molly Brierley." , A tit-bit like this will set the reader's mouth watering, if he is not devoid of taste ; but if he Wants more we mUst refer him -to the full dish itself. "Irish Minstrelsy" is a volume of over 300 pages; • it is well printed and well bound, and is to be had for a shilling.

The. Rev. H. Gibson Smith.i•eacl an interesting paper on Plato at the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society on Tuesday; and it was not its smallest merit that it led a few of the mem- bers out to the border land of debate. Dr. White gave a lively turn to the after-proceedings by knocking down a few of the argumentative Frops of previous speakers, and was in turn dealt with by Mr. Robert Davies. If the Philosophers would only follow this up, and improve on it, the pro- ceedings would be more interesting than they usually are, and the members would be more truly benefited. An intelkictual debate is a healthy mental stimulant.

The sudden and lamentable death of Captain Reynolds brings painfully to everybody's mind the fact that Warrington has singularly suffered within the last twelve niontlisi by the loss of so many of its most prominent men. We have had to record the death of Mr. Peter Rylands, Mr. Warrington Wood, Mr. C. Broadbent, Mr. George Crosfield, the Rev. It, Tilcher, and noW. of Captain Reynolds. "One woe cloth tread upon another's heels, so fast they follow." It was only the other week that Captain Jackson, of Latchford, was seized with a sudden and fatal illness while on his way to visit Captain Rey- nolds. Both are now laid in the earth, and we are made to feel the full force of the meaning of the phruse--" In the midst of life we are in death." :

Captain Reynolds impressed all with whom he came in contact with the feeling, that his val an upright and kindly nature. Those who, in political matters, were his opponents are as' em- phatic in their testimony as his nearest friends, and, than this, what more can, be said? Sudden death is appalling from its suddenness; but he who lives a good life may be said to be at all times prepared for death. Such men are Nature's noble- men, for, after all, "Kind hearts are more than coronets."

SELLING COAL BY MEASURE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, William Stanway, coal dealer, Lowland-road, was. charged with having sold coal by measure instead of by weight. His assistant, Robert Barber, a youth, was also similarly charged. Both de- fendants pleaded guilty, and P.C. 298 gave evidence. The defendant said th bags were made specially to hold a hundredweight rf cnl, but they would hold more. On the morning in question Barber could not get the scales into the waggon' and as he thought it would be all right if he gave plenty of weight it would not matter for weighing the coal. He therefore filled the bags, and if the whole of them had been afterwards weighed, the result would have been in the customers' favour. Barber had no interest in doing wrong, and he had never advised him to do so The Bench dismissed the case against Farber, and fined Stanway Is and costs, 8s 6d.. ROBBERIES AT WIDER/J.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Peter Twist, collier, Park-road, St. Helens was sent to goal for one month with hard labour for having stolen two-picks, value 4s, the property of John Ed- wards, collier, Collins Green. The prosecutor brought the picks out of Bold Colliery on the 4th inst. to be shar- pened, and when he went to work again on the Bth he missed them. On Saturday, the 12th, he saw prisoner bringing one of the picks out of Old Boston coalpit, New- ton. He then gave information to P.C.Vardy, who appre- hended him that morning at half-past five.—Margaret Ellen Lally, a respectably dressed woman, of 12, Char- lotte-terraen, Farnworth, pleaded guilty to stealing a mlantity of female clothing' value 9s, the property of Ann Edwardson, widow, of Liverpool. The goods were St proseeutrix's mother-in-law's, where prisoner fre- quently went as a visitor She was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. Isnimesriox ()TIMED by one box of Howell's Golden Herb ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN CoNsram.E.--Joseph Hayes, a rough looking fellow, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Ellesmere-street, and also with assaulting P.C. John Hulse.—lt was proved that about five o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner was drunk and disor- derly at the bottom of Ellesmere-street. The constable asked him to go away quietly, when he made use of very violent language. At length the constable arrested the prisoner, who then struck him with his fist, kicked him and hit him, and a violent struggle took place upon the ground. A numberof persons formed a circle around them, and several men rescued the prisoner and took him away. Subsequently Inspector Millington appre- hended the prisoner in a lodging-house in Mersey-street. —The prisoner denied the charge of drunkenness.— Superintendent Hollingsworth said the constable was new to the town, and the Apectators, instead of helping the constable in the execution of his duty, rescued the prisoner. He must ask the Bench to protect the police. The prisoner was fined 108 and costs in each case, total £1 Pi 4d, or a month's hard labour. ' BR-UTAL:ASSATILT BY A WOMAN AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. George Pilkington and Colonel Gamble, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mary Jane Keegan, a middle- aged woman, of 35, Water-street, was charged with having caused grevious bodily harm to an elderly , widow named Ellen Godfrey, aged 62, of Sankey-street. It was alleged that about eight o'clock on Saturday the prisoner followed Mrs. Godfrey down the street, and upon getting near to her knocked her down. When she attempted to rise the prisoner knocked her down again, and then kicked her and jumped upon her. Mrs. God- frey shouted." You have given me enough. You have broken my arm," and the prisonerthen desisted from her violence : Several by-standers assisted Mrs. Godfrey , home, where she was attended by Dr. Hutchinson. She was generally bruised about the body, and the shoulder blade on the right side was dislocated.—The prisoner I was on Monday apprehended by P.C. Worsfold, who charged her with the offence. She replied "Nothing of the sort."—Dr. Hutchinson certified that Mrs. Godfrey was in a dangerous state, suffering from fever, cones quent uponthe shock.—The prisoner was remanded for- a week. EDwanns-Moss, M.P.—An ac- cident of a serious nature has happened to Mr. T, C. : Edwards-Moss, M.P., in the hunting field, near Crewe.. !taking a fence his horse landed and fell ; in an opertAirain. and, in getting up the horse trod on-Mr. Edward Moss's face. The gentleman who picked hini.up thought he was killed. He was un- consciolik ft:lr a considerable time, and suffered from slight concussion. The doctor pronounces ; himself satisfied with the progress Mr. Edwards- 1 Moss is making, and does not apprehend any ill 1 effects to his eyesight. He has had a marvellous escape, and we trust he will suffer no permanent ' • iniury from the accident. , LANCASHIRE ITUSSARS ANNUAL DINNER.—The 1 annual dinner to the members of the "C " troop 13 (Newton) of the Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry was held at the Pied Bull lintel, Newton, on Saturday night; when between 80 and 90 gentle- ; men sat down to an excellent 'repast provided by 1 the host and hostess. Mr. and Mrs. H. J. Bond. The ( chair was occupied by Mr. J. E. Pardey, and among those present were :Messrs. P. Dodgson. George 1 Clarke, R. H. Wright, E. Wright, Sergeant Major Hughes, Quartermaster Howard, &c. After dinner 1 the evening was spent in a convivial manner. The loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured, in- ,cluding " The tenantry of Mr. W. J. Legh," " Sue- I ceos to the troop," &c. The proceedings were plea? santly interspersed with selections ot music by Sergeant Major Hughes, Quartermaster Howard, I Sergeants Ritchie and Carr, Privates S. Swann, i Sherlock, Ellam, Gorse, and others. At the close cordial thanks were tendered to the host and hostoss. • THE LIBER,ATION SOCIETY; ANNUAL MEETING. 1 —The annual meeting of the Manchester and Dis- trict Branch of the Liberation Society was held on 1 Tuesday afternoon, at the offices of the society, in St. James's-square, Manchester. Mr. Hugh Booth presided. The committee, in their report to the , • subscribers, expressed regret that their public ap- pearances have again this past year been limited , ,by the political crisis Their activity had been I spent in operations which, though not seen, were I essential, and which would eventually be fruitful. • Thus, the periodical distribution of literature, the ; delivery of lectures whenever. practicable. and the ' constant correspondence with inquirers had been 1 • systematically attended to. The Government Tithe ' ' Bill, the Patronage Bill, and the Cemeteries Bill 1 were dealt with privately in their assemblies. At other meetings of the committee resolutions were• ' passed and published es to the movement for the Disestablishment of the Church of Scotland and of the Church of Englknd inlWales. On the motion of I Mr A. R. Raynor, seconded by the Rev Thos. Green, ' the report was adopted, and ordered to be printed under the direction of the committee. Votes of thanks were awarded to Mr 11. Lee, the president; to Mr. Hugh Booth, the chairman ; and to the other members of the committee. LIVERAL MEETING AT ASIITON.—MT. French, QC., the Liberal candidate for the Newton Division, ad- dressed a meeting of his supporters.at Ashton-in- Makerfield on Saturday night, Mr. Roberts in the chair. Mr. French's address was entirely devoted to the Irish question. He said the deCision of the elec- tors at the last election was given upon what had turned out to be a false and misleading issue. The Coercion Act was passed in breach of the under- standing upon which the present Parliament was elected, and the Liberals gave and intended to give as much trouble as they could to the Government in carrying out their present policy. They sympa- thised.with the people of Ireland in the active and patriotic opposition they had offered to that policy. The tide was turning in favour of the Liberal party, and if an election should be precipitated. it was felt that in many cases the pollings at the last elec- tion would be reversed. He should have been a.slialned of Mr. William O'Brien had he given any other advice than that he had. The Tories were lisp* their Coercion Act to break the spirit of the Irish people, but they would fall. He condemned coercion, and said the end of the land question in Irelan.l would be the abolition of the landlords and the creation of a peasant proprietary throughout the land. The time had come when the whole policy of the Government should be revieweci,when, with the larger experience and knowledge the people of England had of the Irish question, they should have another • opportunity of pronouncing their opinion upon the question that was put in 1885 —shall it be conciliation of coercion? A resolution protesting against coercion and expressing confi- dence in Mr.•Glarlstone was adopted. Poor Liverpool! There is a total deficit of £50,000 to add to the £20,000 of last year. Ah, that is an "exhibition "—but of what

Mr. Henry S. Northcote has been hdnoured by her Majesty with a baronetcy. It is tinderstood that he will be known, like his father, as Sir Staf- ford Northcote. But why not Sir Henry by way of distinction? Can it be that he thinks he will not otherwise arrive at distinction?

The young brewer at Barnes, who committed suicide because he was a rejected suitor-, and left a note asking that the photograph of the lady of his love should be "pinned into the flesh over his heart," was certainly suffering from temporary insanity. 0, love, love, love, it's just like a dizziness, And won't let a poor body go about hi* business.

The Rev. Charles Berry, of Wolverhampton, has been definitely called to Plymouth Church, Brook- lyn, at the annual stipend of 10,000 dollars; It is not abad salary-22,000 a year ; and we can well be- lieve that the reverend gentleman will listen to the call. This extraordinary success is a feather in the cap of Lancashire. Mr. Berry was born at Leigh, and educated at Ormskirk.

Mr. French, Q.C., who made such a good fight of it for the Liberals of the Newton Division at the last election, has been giving an address at Ashton. It is to be hoped that this is the first step in the direction of again paying his addresses to the con- stituency. The electors are wiser to-day than they were a year ago; they know what Coercion means, and have come to say, as Mr. Chamberlain once said .that "they hate the name, and hate the thing."

Mr. Fronde, the historian, is pretty candid as to his view of the Irish question. His remedy for the present state of things is "a military or quasi-military authority." He adds, to his cor- respondent, "You have never yet succeeded in governing them constitutionally, and you never will." According to his doctrine, our present government of Ireland is the best possible govern- ment; or perhaps we ought to amend the state- ment by saying the worse things get in Ireland the better it will be.

Lord Derby makes short work of the contention of those who argue that the English ',Church in Wales cannot be disestablished because it is part of the English Chkirch. Ile'says :—" The right of the Legislature to deal with the question of Church establishment and endowment in Wales is not affected by the fact that Wales is for ecclesiastical purposes one with England. The power that united them can separate them." Precisely, a church established by law can be disestablished by law.

Mr. Gladstone takes I the same view. In a letter written on Monday he says :—" It is quite true that in the Church law and order the Welsh dioceses are simply dioceses of the Province of Canterbury; but so fax as a statute can go the Church of Ireland wt(s made one with the Church of Scotland. The political union was completed." Ergo—the Church of Ireland having been dis- established, the liegislatin-e is competent to dis- establish the Church either in Wales or in Soot- land.

It is natural that great interest should be taken in the condition of the Crown Prince of Prussia— so much depends on his life---but, on the other hand, it is not difficult to understand why the Prince is somewhat hurt at the five way in which certain newspaper correspondents discuss the chances of an operation. It is not pleasant to be dissected befote death. It has now been decided that there shall be no operation; and it is gratify- ing to learn that there is a distinct improvement in the health of the Royal patient.

'At Newton, on Saturday, a dozen constables were presented with certificates of proficiency as members of an Ambulance Class, while two bronze claret jugs were presented to Dr. Valentine for his valuable services as instructor. When is there to be a move made in Warrington for training the borough police in a similar. way ? We are quite sue that the medical men will be ready to give their services, with a view to the police being put in a position to*render first aid to the injured. A word to the wise should be' sufficient.

P.C. Smith, of Rainford, has come Off second best in a curious encounter with William Roth- well, who is the captain of the Star Recreation Football Club. He found Rothwell the other Saturday night at the door of a public-house, and said he should charge him with being ,drunk and disorderly. But Rothwell was awake, and believ- ing he was "as sober as a judge," or P.C. Smith, he immediately presented himself at the surgery of Dr: Murdock, who attended the police court on Monday, and testified that his visitor was sober on the night in question. There were other witnesses ready to corroborate, and there was nothing for the bench to do but dismiss the case. P.C. Smith was told thai he had made a mistake. If he would-be even with Rothwell he must take a doo- tor with him next time.

Speaking at Manchester, on Tuesday, - Mr. Goschen said :---" Apparently when Mr. Parnell pronounced the word 'autonomy,' a transforma- tion soon took place, and the army which was marching through rapine suddenly came to a halt under that magic word." Now, it is very wrong of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to jeer at the use of that blessed word "autonomy for diti not Sir Gilbert Greenall (or somebody on his behalf) in- troduce it into the address which was issued when he sought the suffrages of the Warrington electors in 1885? It is true that Sir Gilbert was at that time depending upon the supporters of Mr. Par- nell. But what of that ? " Autonomy " has not ceased to be a blessed word. Dean Finegan, chairman of the School Management , Committee, gave a report of the work of the Cookery • Classes in connection with the Board Schools during the past twelve months. The children on the rolls were: Simm's Cross, 182 • Warrington-road, 54; West Bank, 119; making a total of 355 on the' roll. The members who had made the attendances requisite to enable them to be examined were: Simm's Cross', 141 • Warrington- road, 46; West Bank, 77; so that a total of 264 were presented for examination, and the grants earned were as follows :—Simms Cross, £2B 4s. • Warrington-road, .£9 45.; West Jsnk, £l5 Bs.; total, £52 16s. With regard to the expenses of maintenance purchase of I flour, potatoes, meat, etc., there had -been a loss of 2s. 9d. at Simms Cross! School, and at West Bank School of 7s. 50. At Warrington-road School there was a profit of Is. The teacher of Cookery received a salary of £BO ,a year, and against this was to be planed a Government grant of £52.165., so that there was a total loss on the Cookery Classes, of £27 13s. 2jd. ,The only thing that was not satisfactory in regard to the Classes was that there were 355 'children on the rolls, whilst only 264 had been examined. A hundred more should have been examined but the end of the year was dis- astrous to the attendancei.the epidemic of measles being the cause of the children's absence. The committee had no control over this, and the work of the class must be considered very satisfactory.. In reply to Mr. Bond, Dean Finegan said the teaching of cookery could be extended' to other schools. Mr. Wareing asked whether others than children connected with the s-heels would be permitted to join the Class of Cookery, treatise it seemed to him if facilities were offered,. the Board might to a great extent reduce the loss upon the classes. There were' many people who would• be glad to pay a fee for tuition in cookery. Dean.Finegan replied that the ' law would not permit outsiders tojoin with theeliildren. Mr. Wareing'S ideewould behest met by a night School of Cookery. The Committee were willing to encourage the teaching of cookery. The Chairman moved, and Dr. O'Keeffe seconded, a motion thanking the Committee for their services in carrying on, the Classes.
FINANCE,

The Finance Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £505 11. 3d. Since the last report the sum of £606 4s. Wk. had been received, including the Government grant of £447 3s id. for Warrington-road School. The minutes were approved. GOVETINMSNT INSPEcTORIB ItIePORTS. _
