div.head: ' RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD; LIVELY DISCUSSION.
div.p: ' RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD; LIVELY DISCUSSION.

A special meeting of Runcorn School Board was held at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon for the purpose of appointing a head-master to the , greenway-road Sehool at a salary of £l2O per annum. Mr. J. Plitchard presided, and there were present /:/r. McDougall, Messrs F. A. Lake, S. C. Beckett, J. R: Fritl4. and G. Moss (Clerk). Dr. MacDougall moved that Mr. John L. Fletcher, of Gloucester, be appointed to the headmastership of the Greenway-road Board' Schools. In his judgment, Mr. Fletcher was the most suitable in point of age, and had a larger practiearexperience with the best results, of any of the candidates that were invited to appear before the Board. They had had 381 candidates for the post, and the Committee had spent several evenings in wading through the applications, and had now before them some really excellent men, one of whom, as a teacher had exceptional abilities. That gentleman, Mr. Fletcher, had had five years' training as a pupil teacher, two yl-ars at one of the best colleges in the kingdom—Batter- sea—was a Queen's exhibitioner, had passed in the first division when he entered and in the first division when he left, and had sineethen been an assistant master at a. school in which. the " excellent " merit grant had been received in four successive years, passing 98, 97, and the present .year they had passed 99.3, and he had also, which was an additional criterion of his exceptional abilities, passed the matriculation examination of the University of London in the first division. He had also passed the intermediate examination for the B.A. degree, and anyone knowing anything about education, and what would be required by that body, knew well enough that only men of first-rate ability were able to pass the examinations of the London University, as those were test. examinations of the highest order. Mr. Moulton, of the Brunswick Wesleyan School, was a local man, and'might be a good teacher as far as they knew; but they had had to deal with each individual ' application on its merits. Had the Chairman proposed Mr. Moulton without advertising, he should have sec- onded the proposition had no one else done so. It would have saved a great deal of valuable time and trouble, and they would not have spent the anxious evenings they had done in doing what they believed to be justice to edueatibn, to the ratepayers, and to all the candidates. It was the greatest farce and the biggest insult that could be offered to the candidates who came from such distances, as well as to some members of the Board, who had spent five or six evenings wading through those applications, and who had entered upon that sacred duty free from bias, and anxious and wishful to do their duty, in the interests of education, as well as to do justice to the large number of applicants, to ask the Board to appoint a man because he was the son of a ratepayer, and the son of his father, and who had only passed in the second division on entering college, and in the second divisibn on leaving college. • If they elected a teacher upon his merits, there was no alternative but to appoint Mr. Fletcher, who lie believed to be the best man of the seven candidates. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Imison seconded the proposition. He came, he said without prejudice—but he did not come without deter- mination—to elect the best candidate, and not consider whether he was a Churchman or a Tory; but rather to consider the results of the candidates'. examinations, and allow them to be a determining factor in the decision he should come to. (Hear, hear.) /low, according to the arguments used in committee that day, it appeared that an accidental majority of that Board were going to ap- point a man, who, according to his testimonials respec- ting ability and educational acquirements, was decidedly inferior to the six best men they had before them that afternoon. (Hear, hear.) He had no desire to say any- thing of the rival candidate, Mr. Moulton who studied at Westminster ;but ho must remind the Moulton, that Mr. Fletcher had passed in the first division in his college, and Mr. Moulton second in his. He had higher honours tan Mr. Moulton, and had a full certificate for art, mu- sic' chemistry, and for subjects which it might perhaps be fairly urged they were not called upon to teach. Al- though he had gained such honours they were told to lightly cast hinr aside for the kcal candidate, purely be- cause of his local claims. He considered it to be a glar- ing shame that their time should have been wasted as it had been. Here he had been kept three hours from his business that afternoon in endeavouring to settle a question which might have been settled before. He should second Dr. MacDougalFs motion, and whatever the result ihight be, he felt sure the ratepayers would bark them out in what they had done. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. Beckett alleged that Dr. MacDougall was annoyed because he could not have it all his own way, as he had often had it before.—Dr. MacDougall: I deny it most emphatically. I challenge you to prove a single instance at this Board. With one exception, in which Mr. Beckett has played a prominent and somewhat undignified part, there has. been practically unanimity on all questions that have come before the Board since I have had the honour of a seat.—Mr.. Beckett: I have never heard such strong language as you have used whilst in commit- tee, and I repeat what I have stated.—Dr. MacDougall: I simply challenge you to state the occasion or occasions when I endeavoured to have my own way. If you don't do so, I shall have my own opinion as to the value of what you say.—Mr. Beckett replied that he was refer- ring to the strong language which Dr. MacDougall had Used that day in committee. Dr. MacDougall, whilst a member was speaking, had jumped up from his seat, and had said "It was a perfect farce to come there and lis- ten to such rot."—Dr. MacDougall stated that if Mr. Beckett was going to adopt the dishonourable tactics of revealing what had taken place in committee, for his in- formation he would repeat that it was not only rot, but he 'would emphasize certain statements that were made in committee as unmitigated rot. (Laughter).— Mr. Beckett was sorry to say it, but Dr. MacDougall had forced him to do so. He was actuated, quite as much as Dr. MacDougall or Mr. unison • were, with the best motives, and with a desire to look after the interests of the ratepayers. He agreed with a good deal which had been said with regard to the qualifications of the various candidates, particularly those Dr. MacDougall had named; and if they were there to appoint a master to a college he would have no hesitation whatever in sup- porting one of those candidates; but it did not follow that because a man was a learned man and had obtained high honours he was the best man to take charge of such a school as the Greenway-road Board Schools were at the present time. With regard to Mr. Moulton, whom he proposed as master, he had been brought up in a school where every inquiry could be made; he had been a pupil teacher in that school before he went to college, and when he came back he had worked in it, and had been the means of gaining the " excellent " grant in connection with it. He had taken the personal super- vision of three upper standards, five six, and seven, which passed very well indeed. He hlel also had charge of the pupil teachers for nearly twelve months, and all those pupil teachera had done very well under his

tuition. When he knew something about a man, about his qualifications, and that he was a capable teacher, he thought he had a right to propose him for the appoint- ment. Simply because he did so, he was accused of be- ing a party man, and of coming there to take part in a farce. (Dr. MacDougall: Hear, hear.) He denied the assertion in tote, and Mr Imison hag). no right to say that he came there for party purposes. He was sorry that. Dr. MacDougall had made use of such strong lane, as it looked as though he was exercising a party spirit. He moved an aniendment that Mr Moulton be appointed. —Mr Frith seconded Mr. Beckett's amendment. It was a question of opinion whether Mr. Fletcher was the best- person to fill the office or not. He considered his opinion to be quite as good as any one else's, and as a member of that Board he should express himself by voting for Mr. Moulton.—Mr. Lake supported Mr. Fletcher's appoint.. meat on the grounds pointed out by Dr. MacDougall and Mr. liaison. No doubt Mr. Beckett thought that his man was the beet; but what he (Mr. Lake) complained about was that if he and Mr. Frith had stated that they were going to support Mr. Moulton all along it would have saved a great deal of time and expense. If they had said, "We are going to support this man," they would have fallen in with it, and done away with that disturb- ance and annoyance i but to come there and go through the solemn farce of advertising, and to sit night after night with the apparent intention of picking out the best man, and then to be told that it was known that Mr. Moulton would be appointed, was not an edify- ing spectacle.—Mr. Beckett and Mr. Frith denied that they knew that Mr. Moulton was going to be a candidate before the advertisement appeared...... Mr. Lake said there was something peculiar in the mat- ter, and until Mr. Beckett disclaimed any knowledge of Mr. Moulton's candidature. and that his mind was not made up before the advertisement appeared, it looked as though the members were parties to something worse than a farce—hypocrisy. They were bound to support Mr. Fletcher if they went on the principle of teaehing qualification.— Dr. MacDougall asked the Chairman whether it was his intention to sPeak on the subject be- fore he (Dr. MacDougall), as the mover of the resolution? —The Chairman replied in the negative.—Dr. Mac- Dougall then said he was charged by Mr. Beckett with displaying an acrimonious spirit. No man with a grain of sense could bring his mind thoroughly, openly, and. honestly to bear upon a question of that kind without feeling indignant at the turn events had taken. It was quite evident now, but not until that afternoon, althoughs some had a shrewd suspicion as to what was likely to: happen, that they had been playing and made to play at a solemn farce in trying to unravel the special merits of the various candidates who were applicants for the appointment, which reminded him of the Msopian fab/e of "Behold the mountain was in labour, and brought forth a mouse." He denied that there was any acri- monious spirit on his part, or any desire to support Mr. Fletcher's candidature on any other grounds except that he believed him to be the most suitable candidate. Mr. Frith had said that he had a right to his own opinions and to vote for the man whom he thought was the most suitable. No one would deny Mr. Frith's contention; but it would be rather a surprise to some to know; that Mr. Frith's qualification to form an opinion was that he had only attended two meetings since his appointment., and had spent a couple of hours one evening in wading through the 361 applications.— Mr. Frith : I object to Dr. MacDougall dealing with that matter. It is not the business before the Board.—Dr. MacDougall : It is my business to refer to it.—Mr. Frith: I object to it, and appeal to the chairman.—Dr. MacDougall: You can appeal as much as you like. That is your privilege: but it is equally my privilege. to refer to Mr. Frith's former assertion.—Mr. Frith: You will bow to the chairman's decision.—Dr. MacDougall made some further remarks, in the course of which he said that, as far as he was concerned, the successful can- didate should have his cordial support after he was ap- pointed; but they all knew they an'ere taking a new line of departure at these schools, and the material that had to be taught there was not of a very tempting kind.— On the amendment being submitted, the chairman, and Messrs. Beckett and Frith voted, whilst the proposition received the support of Dr. MacDougall and Messrs. Ind- son and Lake.—The Chairman said he was very sorry that it had devolved upon him to give the casting vote, as he should have been glad if they had been there unanimous in a matter of that kind. He must certainty give the casting vote in favour of Mr. Moulton. The Chairman was proceeding to add a few remarks, when Dr. MacDougall said he had no right to do 90 after they had voted. He should have done so before the vote was taken.—The amendment was, therefore, carried.—Mr. Frith expressed the opinion that the chairman ought to have been better supported than he had been, and ought to have been allowed to proceed with his remarks.—Dr. MacDougall said he was not going to be dictated to by Mr. Frith. The chairman, he maintained, had had ex- perience, and knew no privilege that would permit him to make any remarks after a vote had been taken, and after he had been previously invited to express his views and had declined to do so. The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: VOLUNTEER CONCERT AND PRESENTATION
div.p: VOLUNTEER CONCERT AND PRESENTATION
AT RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn detachment of the Earl of Chester's Rifle Volunteers, a concert was held in the National School, on Monday evening. and an audience of large proportions assembled. The principal reason for arranging the musical enter- tainment was to enable the Volunteers and a few • friends to publicly show their appreciation of the ser- vices of their bandmaster, Thomas Woods, by the pre- sentation to that veteran of a handsome prototype cor- net; valued at £2l. The instrument, which had been. made by Messrs. Beason and Co., of London. was suit- ably inscribed, reference-being made to Mr. Woods' 30 years' connection with the volunteer movement. The chair was occupied by Quartermaster-Sergeant nankin- son, who had been asiced to take that honourable position because he was the oldest member of the Runcorn de- tachment. In opening the proceedings, Mr. Hankinson remarked that Major Hazlehurst, when he was captain commanding the F and G companies, did his utmost to keep up the corps, both as regarded numbers and effi- ciency. Capt. Jolliffe, who had taken his place, was equally as anxious to keep up the prestige of the com- panies. but he could not well do that without the co-op- eration of the sergeants and other members of the Volun- teers. He urged the young men present to join their ranks, stating that men became more smart, and had a more manly appearance, and were improved in intellect and in manners by taking part in the Volunteer move- ment. (Applause.) The programme commenced with a capital performance by the band, and then Miss Jones and Messrs Morris and Birkett were associated in the trio "Come, sail in our light canoe." With the addition of Mss Birkett the same party rendered the quartetto "Come where My love lies dreaming" in a manner that secured an encore. Messrs Morris and Pownall sang the duet " Albion "in pleasing style, and later, Mr. Pownali gave a sweet interpretation Of "My sweetheart when a boy." A brilliantly executed pianoforte solo by Mrs. W. B. Kay was loudly encored, and the rendering of the song, "Alice, where art thou," 'by Captain Tim- mins, met with a singularly deserved encore. Mr. J. Pennington, who possesses a good voice, essayed the. song "The wolf," and he was recalled. Mr. Rodars contributed A couple of humourous songs in fine style. That quaint song, Darby and Joan," received full justice from Miss Simpkin ; and "I cannot tell—can you?" was well sung by Miss Ainsworth. The two last named ladies also sang the duet "Two merry hearts." Mr. Holland, of Frodsham, sang the "Storm Fiend with good effect. Mr. Outhwaite performed a eupho- nium solo, and Sergeant James Woods a cornet sob, both clever instrumentalists being recalled. During a break in the programme, the Chairman made the pre- sentation to Bandmaster Woods, accompanying the gift with a few appropriate observations. In the place of a speech, Mr. Woods, who had a flattering reception, played a solo on his new instrument. The duties of ac- companist were ably fulfilled by Mrs. Kay and Mr. J. Ravenscroft.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

HELSBY CHI:TECH.—The fourth of the series of" Pleasant Sarurday evenings,"originated by the Vicar for the in- struction and amusement of the working people of Helsby, took place last Saturday. A most interesting lecture on Scotland and Scotch scenery was given by Mr. Ewen, of Chester. The school children sang, very sweetly, a number of Scotch songs. FOREIGN MISSIONS, FIVE Caossas.—Two sermons, in aid of the foreign missions, were preached in the Wes- leyan Chapel, Five Crosses, on Sunday, afternoon and evening, by Mr. C. E. Norman, of Runeern ; and on Wednesday evening a public meeting was held in the chapel, presided over by Mr. J. B. Isaac, of Warrington. The Rev. A. A. Shipharn (a missionary from Ceylon) at- tended as a deputation, and gave an interesting address on the work of the mission in that island. The amount of collections received at this meeting, together with those of Sunday, was £7 4s. 9d. ' PARISH MISSION.—The last service in connection with this mission, which has extended over a period of twelve days, was held in the Parish Church, Prodsham, on Wed- nesday evening, when the missioner, the Rev. R. "D. Mourn, MA., having briefly thanked the members of the choir and others for their extra services rendered during the mission, preached from the text, "That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.' At all the services, conducted by the missioner and Mrs Monro, and the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley, there have been large attendances of all classes of the parishioners.

PRASIWTATION OF PRIZES.—A special meeting of the members of the Pride of Earlestown Juvenile Temple was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge-street, on Wednes- day evening, when there was a large attendance, and Brother E. Newman S.J.T., presided. A programme of songs, recitations, was nicely gone through, and during the evening Brother J. Barnard, P.W.T., of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge, presented handsome books to Sister Eliza Lord and Brother W. Williams for goOd attendance and conduct, and also a book to Sister Sarah Ann Lord for having introduced the most new members to the lodge. Thanks were tendered to Brother Barnard and the chairman, and the proceedings closed.

div.head: WHO IS TO BE CHAMPION?
div.p: WHO IS TO BE CHAMPION?
THE COMING CONTEST BETWEEN BEACH AND HA.N- LAN--SOILETHING ABOUT THE FORMER.

Englishman and sportsman are almost synonym- ous terms the world over, and one of the best results of thia fact is that other fact—that an Eng- lishman, by reason of his sporting proclivities, be- comes hard in muscle, sound in body, and mentally superior. If we were a nation of laggards and midnight pleasure seekers, only a few generations would be necessary to show a decadence of physical and moral strength that would soon do away with the boasted glory of the thoroughbred Englishman, who asks no favours he cannot earn. We are fond of amusement, but with it we like a mixed good. Hunting, racing, cricket, yachting, or rowing are all amusements, but of that kind that improves the. physical and mental condition while it relaxes and freshens all parts. These are the universal amuse- ments of Britain's seas in all countries and in all climes, and a word or line about them, or any dis- tinguished exponent of them, whether professional or amateur, is always accepted or listened to with pleasure by all Englishmen. In view of his past successes, and his approaching contest for the World's Championship with Edward Hanlan on the Faramatta river, a few words regarding champion Wm. Beach will be read with interest by our people. Beach is an Englishman, born in Surrey in 1851. When he was yet a lad his father moved to Australia, and the stern necessities of life required that the coming cham- pio is should "earn his bread by the sweat of his brow," and he was put to work in his father's smithy, and it was while engaged here that the bone and muscle so useful to him at present was developed. Like all Englishmen, Beach took advantage of every opportunity to engage in athletic pastimes, and his in- clinations turning to aquatics, he could occasionally be seen in his skiff rowing through the waters of the Illa- warra lakes near his home. It was not until he was 23 years of age that he engaged in a regular contest, and that was in heavy boats, for the munificent sum of five shillings, his opponent being a publican. Beach won. From this time on Beach, as an amateur, rowed against all corners, and was so successful that he was finally handicapped out of all races. His racing weight i 4 stone, and it is at this weight he will again contest with Hanlan, who has just sailed from San Francisco for Syd- ney. Beach has, as a professional oarsman, in the last seven years, engaged in about twenty-five contests, win- ning all but six, and being second in three of these. Beach's style of training is very severe, involving as it does a run of about three miles before breakfast, a. walk of half-e4ozen miles afterwards, a pull in his boat over the course. After dinner another walk and a long pull over the course again, still another walk, and to bed promptly at nine o'clock. Necessarily this constant strain on mind and body will "knock up" the strongest constitution, and Beach, with all others, has found that during the period devoted to training for a race that his liver and kidneys have given him a great deal of trouble, and he has been at times in a position where to give up training would lose a race, and to continue would probably ruin his health. A phy- sician was necessary to be on hand nearly all the time, and strong drugs were required to make quick relief possible. Nature requires an aid to keep his physical condition up to the highest possible point, and it is not surprising to hear Beach state that during the time he was training to meet Hanlan in his last race, that his trainer procured for him some of Warner's SAFE Cure, and that he "was most agreeably astonished at the great benefit which followed its use." It is a wonderful medi- cine, and he finds it the best possible aid to a command of all his natural powers, because it does not first goad and afterwards weaken the system, but works in perfect harmony with nature's laws. It not only gives temporary relief, but lasting benefit, and this fact has caused thou- sands of athletes all over the world to use Warner's SAFE Cure, not only during the time of training, but at all times when they feel that depression of spirits, nausea, lassitude, or other symptoms of disordered liver or kidneys, from whence spring nearly all the ills flesh is heir to. Any unusual or long-continued strain put on either the mind or the body will result in a weakening of the vital parts, and the liver and kidneys being so susceptible to injury, need constant care and attention, and if the same remedy used by Beach and others was taken advantage of by all the people, they would then be able to almost defy disease. Sedentary occupations, like too much activity, are likely to produce similar results on the liver and kidneys, and to each class Warner's SAFE Cure is an invaluable assistant to nature in pre- venting disease, and often a premature death.—The Sportsman.

div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington and Colonel
Gatnile.

DRIINIC AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Francis, a negro, of no settled residence was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Widnes-road—Sarah Ann Tay- lor, of Cow-lane, Ditton, made her. 25th appearance, and

was fined lOs and costs on a charge of being drunk and incapable.—For a like offence, Thomas Humphrey's, of Halton, Runcorn, was fined 7s 6d and costs.—Thomas Rrett, of Midwood-street, was charged with committing a breach of the peace on Sunday afternoon, the 30th. There was a doubt in the case and the defendant, was dis- missed. _ _ _

HARD TlME.9.—Mary Collins, a middle-aged woman, was dismissed on a charge of begging in Albert-road and William-street —The prisoner stated she was only begging for a piece of bread. Her husband had been out of work a long time, and had only obtained work at Ilutchinson's works this week. FIGHTING . wrra A BROTHER.—John Jones, a crane driver at West Bank Dock, who resides in Irwell-street, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting with his brother named Hugh, at half an hour past midnight on the 6th inst. Hugh Jones was locked up at the time and fined. The defendant said his brother was drunk, and as he was making a disturbance in his house he turned him out of the back door. At that moment a constable appeared on the scene.—The magis- trates adjourned the case for a week to allow the , defen- dant to produce witnesses.

McGinis found the prisoner in a public-house in Widnes-road, and as he could not pro- duce a pass, the constable took him into custody.—The prisoner, who said he was persuaded by some friends to drive to Widnes in a trap, and was unabje to get lick before he was apprehended, was remanded to Walton Gaol to await an escort.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
FSlDAY.—Before Messrs. T. P. Norris, W. Long, and C. Lister.

A Puinacki FlNED.—dohn Southern, landlord of the Star Inn, Statham, was charged with having, on the 6th November, kept his licensed premises open for the sale of drink at prohibited hours, viz., at 11-30 on Sun- day; Elijah Monks, Peter Atherton, and Abraham Or- ritt were charged with having been.on the said premises at the time referred to. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, of War- rington, appeared for the defence. It was stated by P.C. Dutton that while near to Southern's house, on the morn. r ing stated, he saw a lad apparently on the look-out, and when he saw witness he ran in the direction of- the back door. Following the lad in, witness found the three latter named defendants each of them having a pint of fresh-drawn beer before them. Southern alleged that the men were travellers, but it was ascertained that they had only come from Martinscroft, which was not three miles distant.—ln defence it was stated that the three defendants, Monks, Atherton, and Orrit, had borrowed an old volunteer tunic and two forage caps to dress themselves in at a local festival at Martinscroft, and when they brought these back on the Sunday named Southern asked them each to have a glass, which they did, but no money was paid.—The Bench, however, con- sidered the charges proved, and fined Southern 20s and costs, 17s 6d, and the other three defendants Ss and costs each.

SWINTON (A TFax) V. Lim/coax (A Team).—At Swin- ton. A very fast and pleasant game. Result—Swinton, 1 try (Tetlow), and 3 minors ; Runcorn, 1 try (Abrahains) and 1 minor. RUNCORN OLD BOYS V. HALTON.—Runcom Old Boys played their first match with Halton on Saturday, on the grouna of the former. The score was—Old Boys, 1 goal, 1 try, 1 minor, to one dead ball. RUNCORN FREE WANDERERS V. RUNCORN JUNIORS.— This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and after a very evenly contested game resulted in a draw. Score :—Wanderers, four ipain9rs ; juniors, six minors. All the home team played I well.

WATVIIINdteix WA-abEntitS V. SAM-lan, Tvf.bEstsv.— This match was played at Tyldesley. and after a very eant game resulted in a win for the visitors. Ow- agw to the late arrival of the visitors. Only two fifteen minutes were played. At the call of time the score was—Wanderers, 1 goal and 4 minors ; Sale-lane, 2 minors. WIDNES v. Sr. HELENS RECEESTION2ND TEAM).— These teams met at St. Helens on Saturday, with the following result :-,Widnes, one try (scored by Youde) and seven minors; St. Helens Recreation, three minors. One of the " Rec.s. " men, named Edward Taylor, was hurt during the game,:and died on Sunday evening from the effects. _ . .

FRODSHAM V. WIDNES Tams HLUES.—Frodsham met the Blues at Widnes on Saturday. After the Blues being thrown out for the Junior Cup by three minors, a good game VMS expected. When One was called Frodsham were left victors' by 2 tries, 2 minors, to 2 minors. For Frodsham the forwards all played well. The backs played a good game, Darlington and Goodall (full back) putting in grand kicks. WIDNES V. ST. HELENS RECREATION.—The Recs. jour- neyed to Widnes on Saturday full of confidence as to the result of their me,etisg, but the result showed how vain were their hopes. Both the teams were strongly repre- sented, and a fine game was witnessed by about 3,000 spectators, the result being a vicitory for the home team by one goal, one try, and three minors to nil. Witnes played against the slope in the first half, but, notwith- standing this disadvantage, they pretty soon assumed the upper hand. Unfortunately, Hughes, who was play- ing a splendid game forward for the home team had his leg sprained early in the game, and was in consequence prevented from playing during the remainder of the game. Directly after he retired Gandy obtained a fine try. Farrell failed at the place. The home team con- tinued to have the advantage, but nothing more was scored before half time was called. After' the recom- mencement, one of the visitors, Langley, had to retire through injury, which made the teams equal in numbers. Farrell subsequently ran well, and a smart combined rush having been made by the forwards, Barber secured the second try, which Farkell transformed into a goal in I admirable style. The principal features in the game up to the call of time were a splendid drop at goal by Plumpton, which missed the mark by an ace; and a smart run by Parkinson, also of Widnes, who grounded the leather, but the try was not allowed in consequence of alleged informal play. All through the interest was kept up by the fine combined play of the Widnesians. They kept their opponents constantly on the defensive, and never once gave them an opportunity of equalising matters, Individual criticism is unnecessary, as every man on both sides played splendidly. Teams :—Widnes : —S. Bingham, back; F. Plumpton, R. Barker, arul J. Parkinson, threequarter backs; E. Farrell and T. Wilkin- son half backs; W. Kiddie, T. Hughes, J. Hardman, G. Woods, W. Barber, T. Pennington, J. Gandy, J. Bing- ham, and J. H. Smith (captain), forwards. Recreation: A. Tickle, back; W. Lund, W. Matthews, and H. Gerard, .threequarter backs; James Pilkington and A. Smith, half backs; W. Parr (captain), J. Dolan J. Pyke, J. Mousdale, R. Langley, H. Greg,son, J. Ready, W. Dean, and A. N. Other, forward. RUNCORN V. SWINTON.-oViillg to the county fixture between Lancashire and Cheshire, neither side were able to put representative teams on the field last Saturday at Runcorn, Runcorn being the greatest sufferers; but the game was keenly contested from start to finish, and watched with considerable interest by several thousand spectators. The home team, who were worsted by a goal to four minors, must be accounted unfortunate in not scoring a telling point, as, without doubt, they. had somewhat the best Of the game throughout. Swinton won the toss, and Hughes started the ball. No return was effected, and Runcorn for a time strenuously strove to score. Buxton at last got well away, and pa.ssing on to Coulthwaite. the latter ran in and grounded, Paul do- ing the necessary to the place. This put the home player's on their mettle, and some very fa.st and exciting play was shown. Following the re-start from the centre, Wainwright made a grand run, the ball having previ- ously been handled by Davies and Clarke, a minor being noted to the home side, Paul kjcking the leather dead. The forwards on either side continued busy, and then Andrews, Broady, and Hughes made a good passing dis- play, which led the Runcorn men up to the Swinton line once again, the ball being scrimmaged close on the cor- ner flag. Play was shifted to the front of the visitors posts, when a great struggle was at last removed by Bullough running to mid-field, where Davies stayed fur- ther progress, and half time arrived with Swinton lead- ing by a goal to two minors. After facing over, Bum- by put the ball in motion, and some fine exchanges were indulged in between the opposing backs the ball finally settling down just within Swinton territory. Wainwright, Davies, and Broady strove hard to further improve matters, but the visitors' backs were hard to pass and Davies made a long punt, which Paul negotiated with interest, tho play locating once more in the home 25. Here Davies made another great effort, btit was checked by Paul and Sharpies. , The home players, however, came
-zhe

again, and the Swinton line was again in jeopardy, but a mistake was made by kicking the ball dea4. Ttje,drop- out saw Riley again to thc ford, Onlythlbo biougfit 'down by Bumby. The home forwards again showed up. and from centre Riley once more came out and passed to , Wainwright, who made an excellent drop, but his well- intentioned effort went the wrong side of the post, . . .

. . . _ though for the moment everyone thought that Runcorn had at last equalized the score, and hats were sent up in delight. Consternation and alisappointment, however, was shown on many faces when the ball was brought _ _ _ . .

forward to be dropped out instead of taken to the mitre mark, and not a few were feign to believe that the re- feree had given a wrong decision, but on appealing to Wainwright after the match was over he settled the matter by admitting the fairness of the referee's judg- ment by saying it was no goal. Afterwards the play was fast and exciting, but without any material advantage to either side, and time left the game in favour of Swill- ton as above. Teams i—Runeora Brazendale, back;

Davies, Riley, and Wainwright, threequarter backs; Andrews and Whitby, half backs; W. Hughes, Broady, Lewis, Clarke, Hoffiand, Gatley, P. Riley, Stubbs, and Barnes, forwards. Swinton : Paul, back ;J. W. Buxton, Bullough, and Sharpies, threequarter backs; Bumby and G. Buxton, half backs; Coulthwaite, Kenyon, Hotchkiss, Honey, Pollit, Worsley, Bothwell, Banks, and Clayton, forwards. LITIMPOOL v. Rettcoms. This fixture, which had been looked forward to with a large amount of interest by the supporters of the Runcorn Club, was decided on Monday at Aigburth, :in dull and threatening weather, notwithstanding which there was a good attendance, the bulk of the people evidently having accompanied the visiting txxim. Runcorn was represented. by their best fifteen, but Liverpool being short of their usual players had the assistance of players from the Old Boys, Man- chester Free Wanderers, and Birkenhead Park. It was 25 minutes to four when W. Hughes kicked off in the

direction of Withers, who, havircig returned, scrimmag- ing commenced in neutral ground. Alternately Pernie, Leigh, and Rertie Melly came to the front, and gradually the ball wa,9 worked within the visitors' half. The Run- . _ _ _ .

cornians now got away in a fast dribble to the line, the ball eventually finding its way to touch-in-goal. Shortly afterwards A. L. Melly, being prassed, touched down, whilst a moment later Speakman had a splendid drop at goal, the ball falling the merest shade short of its mark. From the subsequent lino out the same player taking the ball splendidly, inaugurated a vigorous attack upon the Liverpool line. At length A. Melly relieved, and again the play located in neutral ground. Some ac- curate passing now ensued from left to right of the Run- corn three-quarter lino, but still little if any ground was gained by the movement, as Bertie Melly dashed through in beautiful style. After further scrimmaging, the Run- .

„ corn forwards again broke away, and on Davies punt- ing to the lines Wainwright gained the fiat in the run-up with Melly, but the try being in a difficult position, Broady failed at goal. The game had no sooner beers re- newed than Andrews gained a second try, close to the posts, and Woods experienced no difficulty madding the mazervalue.Barelya minute hadelapsedbeforeWainwright again crossed the Liverpool line, and closely following Woods' failure at goal, half-time was reached with Run- corn leading by one goal, two trial, and three minor points, to nil. Kenworth havini; restarted the ball, Woods returned into touch at the half-way flag, further ground being gained by Davies on the right. Withers now dashed off on the opposite side of the ground, and. looked like cleaving a passage through the opposing backs until Speakman appeared on the scene and brought the aggressor to earth. Later on, Melly, taking advan- tage of a lull in the play, nearly effected a coup, on the failure of which Speakman passed over to Wainwright near the line, when the latter for the third time placed the ball behind. With the failure of the place-kick some vigorous play ensued within the Liverpool 25. At length A. Melly gave welcome relief, although a moncont later the Runcornians were swarming in front of the Liver- pool posts. During a return rush Hughes saved in ',pant style. Again Wright took on the ball in a ronining dribble, when A. Melly got up, and with a flying kick propelled the ball into touch. Davies next got away, only, however, to fall into the same hands. Fernie, who had been quiescent for a length of time, now put in an abortive run which Davies replied to in brilliant style. Chapman tackled Speakman in midfield, and thus ar- rested a movement full of danger to the opposing side. Central play prevailed until Chambers broke away in a spanking dribble, and thus for a moment an advanced footing was gained in the Runcorn half. Steadily, how- ever, the home players were borne back within their own half, where the ball was when the official whistle signalled ” no side," Runcorn being the victors of a fast game by ene goal, three tries, and three minor points to nil. Teams : Liverpool—A. L. Melly, back; F. C. Withers, A. Melly, and R. K. Fernie, three-quarter backs; W. B. Leitch ana P. Bright, half backs; H. Chapman (Liverpool Old Boys), H. Neill, C. Anderton (Manchester Free Wanderers), J, lieuarortiy.W .IL-t!zh,H. Harvey, F. Chattiterg (1117erpool Old Boys 3, P. Williamson (Birken- head Park), and H. Melly, forwards. R.uncorn—T. Broady, J. Lewis, and J. Clarke, forwards, WAARINGTON v. l'tecnies.te Hort:sem (" A" Teams).— This match Wlayed on the Wilderspool ground on SaturiLl In Rae weather, and as the fixture has been looted forward to for several weeks past as deciding the championship for "A" teams of Lancashire, fully 5.000 spectators assembled to witness the contest, the Hornets bringing a good number of supporters with them. Bam- ford won the toss, and 35 minutes being the time agreed 'upon to play-, the home captain kicked off at 3-30, Stott returning with a flying kick to Evans, who was tackled before he could-part with the ball. Whittle passed to Evans, who threw to Appleton, this .player kicking to the Hornets' 25. The visitors, however, broke away with a dribble to the centre. Whittle stopping their progress. Antrohus passed to Whittle, who got nicely away from I the scrimmage and passed to the forwards, but the Rochdale men again took play to mid-field. Pilling now , passed to Bamford, who was promptly collared by Evans, and the Warrington forwards, by a splendid dribble, took operations to the visitors' goal-line. Stott by a sharp punt relieved to the quarter-flag, but from the line out Bandies put in a neat dribble, Thorpe saving by dropping on the ball. For a considerable time War- rington pressed their opponents severely. Nuttall even- tually got possession 'and passed to Stott, who relieved the pressure by a short kick into touch, Rhodes, Ash- worth, and Rowes further improving matters by a fine I dribble. From a scrimmage near centre Antrobus got possession and passed across to Whittle, who transferred Ito Evans, this player making a splendid run in, crossing the line with two of his opponents clinging to him. This piece of 'play elicited tremendous cheering from the spec- tators. Isherwood took the place kick, but failed. Baum- ford restarted, and Boardman not making a very good re- turn, the ball was scrimmaged in the centre of the field. The Rochdale men worked the ball into the Warrington ter- ritory,echere Nuttall threw to Pennington, but Evans in- tercepted the pass and threw to Thornley. Stott, how- ever, succeeded in kicking into touch. From the lino out the Hornets dribbled over the line, but Jolley saved by kicking dead. Jolley kicked out, Stott fading to return. Pilling now secured possession, and passed to Bamford, this slayer passing to Pennington, who was tackled by Boardman. Good passing between Antrobus, Evans, and Apploton next took place, but Pennington was safe, and preyented Appleton from becoming dan- gerous. The Hornets worked the ball into the Warring- ton 25, and Bamford dropped at goal, but the kick was charged down by Craghan, and Pennington was collared by Boardman before he could got in his kick. By a grand rush of the Warrington forwards the hall was taken to the visitors' full back, who kicked to Evans, and this player, making his mark, kicked to Thorpe, who sent the leather into touch near the quarter-flag. Whittle next passed to Antrolms.who had his kick charged down, and play was taken to centre, Jolley saving nicely. Thorpe next put in a kick, Jolley. making a good return, but the ball was ruled in touch, and from the line-out the visitors worked the oval to near the Warrington goal line, the home team saving by touching down. Half time was called, with the score standing—Warrington 1 try, to the Hornets 2 minors. On change of ends the visiting captain kicked off, Isherwood returning to Bam- ford, who kicked to the Warrington quarters. The home forwards, headed by Molyneux, Dillon, Eyes, and Thornley, dribbled to centre, Bamford being allowed a free kick, and RandalLs returning well into touch. The visitors worked the ball into Warrington quarters, and Pennington put in a fine kick to Jolley, who returned with interest. Nuttall next passed to Pennington, who put in a strong run, but he was well tackled by Boardman. Evans gained a lot of ground by a long kick into touch, and the Warrington forwarcts made a splendid dribble to the Hornets' goal line, the ball going dead. Bamford dropped out, Whittle return- ing. The Hornets went away with the ball, but Evans ' neutralized by a judicious kick into touch. The best [passing of the day now took place between Whittle, Antrobus, Evans, and Appleton, the latter player making a grand run, being pushed into touch near the line. The visiting forwards dribbled splendidly up the field, but Jolley picked up the ball clean from their toes and-put in a long kick into touch. By degrees the Hornets worked the hell away to centre, and Nuttall passed to Bamford, this player putting in a dodgy run, but fell when a chance of scoring seemed possible. Good runs by Ftvans, Appleton, and Antrobus took play to the Hornets' line, Antrobus succeeding in getting over, but the hell was ruled back, play being located in Rochdale quarters when time was called. Warrington thus won a hotly-con- tested game by 1 try and 1 mina, to Rochdale Hornets 2 minors. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Appleton, Evans, and Boardman; half-backs, Whittle (captain) and Antrobus; forwards, Molyneux, a ' aghan Dillon, Eyes, Randalls, Thornley, Jones, Donohue, and Isherwood. Rochdale Hornets: Full back, Thorpe; three-quarter hacks, Stott, Bamford (captain), and Pennington; half backs, Pilling and Nut- tall; forwards, Rowe, Ashworth, Rhodes, Sugden, Foster, Sharpe, McHugh, Parkinson, and Holman. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE HORNETS.

These teams met at Rochdale on Saturday. The home team mustered their full strength, whilst Warrington were minus the services of Massey, who is still on the injured list, and for the greater portion of the first half they had to play 14' men, Daniels failing to make the journey in time. During his absence Speakman went three- quarters, whilst Turner played half. It is only fair to

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, TCOVEMBER 19, 18i7.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, TCOVEMBER 19, 18i7.

state that it was whilst playing short-handed that Roch- dale were enabled to secure their only try. ', The home team' haileg woti. the tOSS, Frank Turnei' was deputed to start_ the game, and a poor return being made by Hastings, the first scrimmage was formed at mid-field. The Hornets broke away to the Warrington quarter, but Barnes stopped their progress by a timely kick back to neutral ground. Loose play followed,' the ball being gradually worked to the visitors' lines; but Nevins relieved his side by a good kick to mid-field. From the line out a neat pass was made to Barnes, who put in a good run to the Hornets' 25. The Warrington team took play to the line, but the home forwards re- lieved the pressure by a neat dribble to centre field, Jolley saving. Nolan tried hard to get away, but Barnes neutralised his efforts by a good run and kick back to the home team's line. Pretty passing by Warren and Speak- man looked like seering, but a rash pass let in J. Leach, who put in a good run to the Warrington line, Jolley stopping him opportunely. A pass by Barton to White- head gave him a chance, but he took his drop at goal, a minor only securing. A poor reply to the drop out set- tled play at mid-field, and Smith got in a lucky kick, but Jolley ran the leather back out of danger. Barnes after- wards got away, and by a neat pass to Speakman the latter put in a good kick over the visitors' line, and Frank Turner, following up well, grounded the leather ; but this was disallowed, a dead ball only being regis- tered. Wild dropped out, and pretty passing by the Warrington barks threatened danger, but a movement was started by the Hornets forwards, in which Scholes, Groves, and E. Luck were prominent, and ended in the latter getting over, after plain cases of both off-side play and the ball being thrown forward. The decision was against Warrington, but Whitehead failed at the place. Daniels had now arrived, and the teams were evenly balanced. Frank Turner re-started, and smart following up by Fair. Turner, Littlewood, and Dillon pre- vented a return. Warren made a neat pass to Barnes,. and the latter transferred to Daniels,but Whitehead safely held him before becoming dangerous. Jolley put in a strong run to the Hornet's line, and from the succeeding scrimmage Speakman made a nice Pass to Barnes, who, finding himself pressed, kicked to Daniels, and that player signalised his appearance by safely grounding the oval over the line. Frank Turner failed at a difficult place. The drop out brought little relief to the home teani, for the Warrington forwards, who played a splen- did game all through, bore down on theßochdale citadel, but the home team rallied, and took play to neutral ground. Daniels got in a nice run and kick tq the Hor- nets' 25, but this effort was neutralised by is neat dribble to the Warrington quarter flare Barnes, however, was equal to the occasion, and made away to thehomeieam'a territory. Daniels afterwards got away, being hold on the line, and bestafterwards good forward play by Povey, Ashton, and Littlewood was shown. The gnme was trans- ferrod to the Warrington line, and pretty passing by Speakman. Barnes, and Jolley, enabled the latter to put in a huge kick to Hastings, the latter kicking dead. Nolan failed to reply to the drop out, and from the sub- sequent scrimmage Ashton broke away, being well held by Whitehead. Half time was celled with the score-- Warrington one try and one minor, to Rochdale Hornets one try and two minors. Wild recommenced operations. and the ball travelled with great rapidity from one end of the field to the other, but when play had settled, down Warrington asserted their superiority, and completely „penned their opponents. Hastinge was the first to show up with a short run, but found more than a match in Jolley, who safely brought him to mother earth. The Warrington forwards, by dint of hard work, forced the Hornets back on their line, and Nolan (who had gone to half back) relieved grandly to mid-field, Nevins replying with a splendid kick back to the Rochdale line. Some loose play followed, and , Warren securing possession safely grounded the leather over the line, but on appeal this was dis- allowed—a very unsatisfactory decision. A five yards' scrimmage being ordered, the home, team relieved to neutral ground, but Dillon, Rigby, Povey, and Little- wood again ran the ball back. 'Whitehead got a pass intended for Barnes and made tracks for the liVarringten line, but ho was safely held before becoming too danger- ous. Jolley get over shortly after, but this was also dis- allowed, and from a scrimmage formed in the Warring- ton quarters Littlewood and Pony came away with a grand dribble, and what seemed a certain chance of scor- ing was spoiled by the leather going in touch. The ball was gradually worked to the line, and the Hornets were again forced to act on the defensive. It was fast be- coming dark, and was a hard matter to distinguish in- dividual play. Barnes almost got in from a zigzag run, and it was decided to finish the game immediately after on account' of the darkness, there being fully a quarter of an hour to play. The game thus remained drawn, the score being equal, both sides scoring one try and two minors. To speak of individual play wOuld be impossible, for one and all played their level bast. The Warrington men showe,d great improvement on any previous form this year, the splendid combination of the whole team deserving the highest praise. On the Rochdale Hornet's side, Smith, Nolan, Barton, &holes, and Leech were the pick. The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full back, Nevins: threequarter backs. Jolley, Barnes (cap- tain), and Daniels; half hacks, Warren and Speakman; forwards, Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Dillon, Littlewood. Hayes,Davim, Povey, and Rigby. Rochdale Hornets: Full back, T. Smith ; threequarter backs, Hastings, Whitehead, and Nolan; half backs, Barton and W. Smith: forwards, Brierlev, Groves, Mellidew, E. Leech, J. Leech, Holt, Wild, Griffiths, and Scholea. Um- pires, Messrs. Gilbert and Brierley. Referee, Mr. E. M. Rhodes, Rochdale Hornets' Football Club.

div.head: REYNOLDS.
div.p: REYNOLDS.
FATAL ACCIDENT TO CAPTAIN

Intelligence was received in Warrington early on Saturday evening of an accident that had occurred to Captain Reynolds, of ' Raddon Court. Latchford, while that gentleman was shooting over Pasfurlong Moss, in company with a friend—Mr. W.ll. Brook, the Town Clerk of Warrington. All that was publicly known was thatthe Captain had been acci- dentally shot in the knee, and, although what had transpired was not generally supposed to be of so serious a nature as in reality it was, great Uneasi- ness was.felt.l4 a large number of friends and ad- mirers of Captain Reynolds in the neighbourhood ; and on Saturday night, when the sad accident had become a topic of general conversation, universal regret was expressed. On Sunday morning, when news came that the accident had terminated fatally, it was a severe shock to all who had known the deceased gentleman, for a fatal termination had not been anticipated, except, perhaps, by the medical gentlemen who had been called in. As the sad information rapidly gained currency a gloom was spread over the district, and especially over the neighbourhood of Latchford, where the name of Captain Reynolds had become a household word. As a mark of respect to the memory of the deceased flags were floated at half mast from above the two political clubs, from above the Town Dail, and at other less prominent places. The place where the accident occurred—Pasfur- long Moss—is situate near Culcheth; it is a con- tinuation of the Chat Moss, and for a considerable number of years Captain Reynolds had had the right of shooting over it. In order to gain as ac- curate an account of the lamentable accident as was possible a representative of the ' Examiner" on Sunday made 'inquiries in the neighbourhood in which it occurred. From what could be gathered, it appeared that early oil the afternoon of Saturday, Captain Reynolds and Mr. Brook arrived at the shooting box, and were accompanied on to the Moss by a keeper named Jackson. At about three o'clock in the afternoon Captain Reynolds was cross- ing over a wire fence, in order, it is said, to take aim at a hare that had just been started from among some twigs, when he fell, and the gun went off, shattering his left knee. The injured gentleman, with great presence of mind, then fired off the second barrel of his gun, and also shouted, in orde to attract the attention ' of his friend and the keeper, who were on the op- posite side of some willows. They at once went to his assistance, and Mr. Brook divested himself of his shirt, with which he bound up the leg, in order to, as , far as possible, arrest the hemorrhage. An ,improvised stretcher was obtained by making use of some rails, and Captain Reynolds was conveyed in a spring cart to the house of Mr. Sankey. Dr. Sephton, whose residence is not far away, was in waiting at the house, and took all possible measures for the safety of the captain, who had by that time lost a great quantity of blood, and was suffering from collapse. Mr. Brook lost no time in driving to Warrington to obtain further medical aid, and to give informa- tion of the accide'nt to those most deeply concerned. Dr. Whitehead. of the Manchester Infirmary, was also summOned, and there were soon in attendance, in addition to that gentleman and Dr. Sepliton, Dr. White, Dr. Starkey Smith, of Warrington. Dr. Rich- mond, late house-surgeon at the Warrington Infir- mary, and Dr. Smith, the present house-surgeon of that institution. It was deemed necessary by these gentlemen that the injured leg should be immedi- ately amputated, and the operation was performed by Dr. Whitehead, the patient haring had chloro- form administered to him by Dr. Sephton. He sur- vived the operation, but only lived until three o'clock on Sunday morning, when 'he died from exhaustion: Mrs Reynolds, on being on Saturday aternoon apprised of the accident, immediately drove to the house of Mr. Sankey, where she re- mained until her husband's death. The wound re- ceived by the dedeased gentleman was of a very , serious nature. The contents of the gun lodged in the left Icaec joint, shattering it to pieces. The head of the tibia, and the inner condyle of the femur were blown way, the soft parts were exten- Eively lacerated, and the knee joint was blown open. The wound bled copiously, and the sufferer lost a

great quantity of blood before he was seen by a medical gentleman. In the course of conversation with Dr.Bepbton Captain Reynoldstold that gentle- man that the trigger of the gun caught in the wire of the fence, and this caused the weapon to be dis- charged.

The lace Captain Reynolds wa4 a son of Mr. Thos. Reynolds, of Raddon Court, Devonshire, and he came to VVarrington to be with his uncle, Mr. William Reynolds. at the Mersey-street tannery, in June. 1846. He afterwards became partner with his uncle, and they continued to carry on business to- gether until the year 1868, since which time Cap- tain Reynolds bas held the Latchford tannery him- self. The deceased served with the Warrington Volunteers for Borne years, but was 'compelled by business calls to resign his command. Mrs. Rey- nolds was one of the daughters of Mr. Thos. Banks. of Hill Top, Latchford.

The deceased gentleman was very prominent among his fellow townsmen, and by his amiability of disposition and kindlines of feeling he had en- deared himself to all his friends and acquaintances. while his business tact and energy, his honest and straightforward dealings with his fellows, his con- duct as a magistrate and as a public man, gained for him the confidence of all who knew him, not excepting those who were opposed to him in mat- ters political. He led a busy and a useful life, and whatever he took in hand he did it with a determi- nation to succeed. He was well-known and much esteemed in commercial circles. Besides being the owner of the large tanning establishment at Latch- ford, he was chairman of Arthur Waring and Co., Limited,- 4uffalo hide, glue, and sizing manufac- turers; chairman of the Castle Rubber Company; and chairman of the Lion Hotel Company, Limited. He also took part in other business undertakings in the town. In 1874 he was placed on the commission of the peace for the borough of Warrington, and as a magistrate he shone conspicuous. Up to three or four months ago, when his health began to fail, he was most attentive to his magisterial duties— punctual and regular in his attendances. All cases that were brought before him had a patient and im- partial hearing, and his judgment -was always sound. In politics he was a zealous Conservative, and for several years he occupied the position of chairman of the Warrington Conservative Associa- tion, from which he retired about three months ago owing to ill-health, lie was so much esteemed as chairman of the Association, by the working men of the party as well as the leaders, that an intimation of his intended resigna- tion was received with the, deepest regret, and, after several meetings had been held to consider the sub- ject, he was urgently requested to re-considerhis deci- sion. Acting under medical ads ice, he was, however, unable to continue the duties of that position, and- his resignation was acoepted. lie had done good service for the party that had his political sympa- thies, and so much esteemed was he that a popular subscription list was opened, and in November of last year the late Mr. Warrington Wood was com- missioned to execute a bust, to cost about 150 guineas, to be placed in the Conservative Club. This bust, it is stated, arrived in London on Satur- day frcin Rome. It had been intended to publicly present it to Captain Reynolds, but owing to his lamentable death, the arrangements which wore in contemplation have, of course, fallen through. Many years ago the deceased gentleman was a mem- ber of the Corporation, and for a long time he was a prominent member of Christ Church, Latchford. At the time of his death he was 57 years of age, and his loss is mourned by a widow and twelve children who survive him. A permanent and beautiful memorial of the generosity of Captain Reynolds will be found in a handsome stained glass window which he, in conjunction with Mrs. Reynolds, caused to be placed at tha east end of Christ Church, Latchford, little more than a month ago. The window bears a fine representation of the Adoration of our Lord, and beneath is the following inscription on brass:—" To the glory of God, and in thankfulness to Him for all His goodness this window was given by Syl- vanus and Jane Reynolds on the 2nd Oct., 1887." MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES.

Before the commencement of the ordinary business of,. the Borough Court, on Monday, the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), who presided over an unusually large attendance of magistrates, said that he very much regretted that his duty 6n his first appearance as Mayor in that court should be of such a painful nature. The death of Cap- tain Reynolds, a brother magistrate, which occurred on Saturday under such melancholy circumstances, had cast a gloom over the whole borough. Captain Reynolds was well known for his manly, honest, and impartial conduct as a magistrate for many years, and his thoroughly straightforward and generous disposition en- deared him to the hearts of everyone who knew him. The borough had suffered a very great loss in his death, and he was sorry to have to announce such a melancholy cir- cumstance on his first appearance there as Mayor.—Mr. H. Bleckly also referred to the sorrow that would be felt at the sad accident. Captain Reynolds, he said, was a man endeared to them—a mtn who endeavoured to per- form his duty to his fellow townsmen—and there was no one who had filled a larger space in the esteem of his fel- low townsmen than kad the late Captain Reynolds, who had been a courteous and conscientious worker in what- ever he believed was for the interest of the town in which he lived. He was sure that they all felt that they had lost a friend, and one of their, most valued townsmen.— Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, said that he had known Cap- tain Reynolds. a.s a most painstaking magistrate for the last ten years—honest and fair in his dealings there, as he had been outside the court. On behalf of himself and his brother members of the legal profession, he expressed deep sympathy with the bereaved widow and family.— Mr. H. B. White, the clerk to the magistrates, endorsed what had been said about the late Captain Reynolds, who, he remarked, had been one of the most regular at- tendants on the Bench, and who had in every way dis- charged his duty conscientiously and ably.—The busi- ness of the court then proceeded. REFERENCE BY MR. ROBERT DAVIES. _

On Tuesday evening, at a ineeting,of the Warringfon Literary and Philosophical Society, Mr. Robert Davies, the President, said that since they last met Warrington had lost another of her useful public men by the mi- timely death of Captain Reynolds, whose losS his sorrow- ing family and men of all shades of political feeling would most sincerely deplore. In the short space of twelve months their gifted townsmen, Mr. Warring-ton Wood, Mr. Peter Rylands m.r. and J.P., Mr. George Crosfield, J.P., Mr. Broadbent, .ore recently the Rev. R. Pitcher, and now Captain Jr.,Reynolds, J. 1.1 had been taken from, their midst. Thus their magisterial bench had in less than twelve months lost four of its 1 members, and it would not, he thought, be becoming to let that meeting pass over without expressing their sense of the loss their own town had sustained by the death of so many whose services in their, several spheres of life could so ill be spared. (Hear, hear). REFERENCES AT THE PUBLIC HALL. At a meeting. in favour of the Fair Trade movement, held in the Public Rail on Thursday evening, the chair- man, Mr. John White, said that that day there had been consigned to the grave One of Warrington's mast pro- minent men, and one of their greatest friends. Much had, been said about Captain Reynolds, but nothing too much had been said in his praise. He felt that the demonstration which waA made at the funeral that day was worthy of the man. The death of Captain Reynolds had left a void that would not readily, be filled up. Mr. George Woods also made reference to the sad subject. PULPIT REFERENCES.

The Rev. S. Wilkinson, Vicar of St. Paul's, at the con- clusion of his sermon on Sunday evening, said the name of Captain Reynolds was a household word in Warrington. They all knew how kind and generous he had been ; how willing to assist in-every good worlc. Only a few short hours ago he left his home at Latchford to 'enjoy that ' pleasure which was so dear to eve 6,. Englishman's heart —a day's shooting. Then he was strong and able. Now he was dead, and in a day, or two he would be laid be- neath the sod, and they should see him no more. These things should teach a solemn lesson, and be a reminder of those beautiful words,— Brief life is here our portion, Brief sorrow, short-lived care ; The life thit knows no ending, The teexless life is there.' • The Dead March in Saul was played on the organ after the benediction had been pronounced. ' At Christ Church, Latchford, on Sunday morning, and at Wycliffe Congregational Church, the prayers of the congregation were desired on behalf of the widow and family of Captiin Reynolds. VOTES OF CONDOLENCE.

On Tuesday evening, a well attended meeting of the Council of the Warrington Conservative Association was held in the Assembly Room of the Conservative Club. Mr. H. Pierpoint, chairman of the Association, presided, and many prominent local Conservatives were present. Letters were received from others who were unable to attend.—The CHAIRMAN said that was, he supposed, the saddest occasion on which they had met together. They had met in order that they might pay their tribute of re- spect, he might say of affection, for the leader who had : been so suddenly taken from them. Perhaps, before he went further, he should mention that Sir Gilbert Green- , all would have been present, only as a matter of fact he could not find it in his heart to face the meeting, fearing that his feelings would be so strong that he would break down. Though this was their immediate object, he felt that ho should be neglecting his duty if he were to let the occasion pass without saying some few, words attempting to express, however inadequately, the great less they had ustained in the death of their kiend and leader. He had gone from them, but it was not for thern to inquire into ttho inscrutable ways of Providence. They were lhere to express their sympathy with those whom he had eft behind. They could net pretend to assuage the grief of his widow or children; they could only say that they sympathised with them in their sorrow and their tears. They lamented the loss of a true hearted man, faithful and brave, working

for the' cause that they had at heart early and late, never discouraged, ever courteous and ever kind. It was only a few months since, from failing health, he had to give up the position of command that he had filled so well. They knew perfectly well that Captain Reynolds was a strong party man. He had in Warring- ton strong political opponents, but amongst them, he was sure, there was not one pertional enemy. He felt sure that there were many among their opponents who shared their sorrow, and were at one with them in their grief. They could erect no more fitting memorial to Captain , Reynolds and his work than by catching the blazing ' torch that had fallen from his cold hand, and carrying it high in the everlasting race, letting their cry be what might have been his motto "Faithful and true."—Mr. JOHN WHIM said that he was sure' that they all deeply echoed 'over), sentiment that had fallen from the chair- man's lips. • Associated as he had been with Captain Reynolds for so long he could say for himself how deeply he felt his loss. The loss to the association, he +felt, was irreparable ; how much greater must it be to those nearer and dearer to them. He believed that if the , wishes of their late chairman could at the moment be known they would, be that they could not shew greater respect to his memory than to carry on the work of the organisation and to keep it in as perfect a condition as he laboured so long to ptomote. He then proposed—" That this meeting of the Council of the Warrington Conservative Association deeply deplores the sad and sudden death of Captain Reynolds, and desires, on behalf of the Members of the Association, to each and all of whom his memory will ever be affectionately endeared, to convey heartfelt sympathy to Mrs. Reynolds and her family in the afflic- tion that has fallen on them, and the irreparable loss they have sustained."—Alderman HARRISON seconded the re- solution which was supported by Alderman,Webster and Councillor Jolley, and carried unanimottsly.—A resolution of condolence on behalf of the club committee was then carried, on the proposition of Councillor Francomb, seconded by Mr. William Taylor, and supported by Councillor Wright.—Arrangements were made for at- tending the funeral, and it was decided that the Conser- vative Club should be closed on the day of the sad ceremonial.

At a Liberal meeting held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Knutsford-road, on Tuesday evening, the sad death of Captain Reynolds was alluded to by the chair- man (Councillor W. Pierpoint). M. Pierpoint said that before commencing their business that night he thought it was only a fit and ptoper thing that they, as a portion of the Liberal party of Latchford assembled together, should take some notice of the sad affair which had hap- pened in their midst within the past few days—(hea.t, hear)—and he need not tell them that he alluaed to the _ _ .

sad and unfortunate accident which had happened toMr. Sylvanus Reynolds. Every- one of them in that room knew as well as he knew that in Mr. Reynolds the Li- beral party, not only of .Latchford, but of Warrington, had a very strong and powerful antagonist, but, with all his strength and power, he always fought in a true and manly fashion—(hear, hear)—and in such a manner as none of them could take exception to. Many words of his on that point would be perfectly unneccessary. • Ile had known Mr. Reynolds even from boyhood, and before he (Mr. Pierpoint) became an inhabitant of Latchford: and during the whole of that time he had been one of his warmest friends—always ready to give him a kind word of good advice in reference to business matters. when he asked font. (Hear, hear.) Hethought, therefore, it was a duty he owed to the memory of that gentleman to join with them in forwarding the following resolution of condolence to Mrs. Reynolds :—" Resolved—That this meeting of the Liberals of Latchford receives with [ deep regret the announcement of the death of Sylvanus ' Reynolds, Esq., J.P., and desires to express its sincere sympathy with Mrs. Reynolds and family in the great bereavement which they have sustained." (Hear, hear.) The resolution embodied pretty much his feelings in con- nection with the melancholy occurrence, but if there were at ny of their friends present who could say anything whidh would add to its impressiveness they had only to mention it, and he was sure it would be acted upon. (Ap- plause.)—Dr. Gornall said it was a painful privilege for him to second the resolution which had been proposed. He had had the privilege of knowing Mr. Reynolds for a great number of yearS,and to a great extent he looked upon him as a personal friendof hisown. Itwasonlyafortnight ago the previous Sunday when he met Captain Reynolds for the first time since he came to live in Latchford, and he moved out of the circle of friends and relatives with whom he was walking to grasp him by the hand and welcome him to Latchford. (Hear, hear.) He felt that they had lost in Mr. Reynolds a worthy man, an honour- able opponent, and a generous friend, and in conclusion he would say, "May his bodyhe buried in peace, and the memory of his name live for evermore." (Loud ' applause.)—The vote of condolence was then unanimously agtOecl to.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

On Tuesday afternoon the inquest as to the death ea Captain Reynolds was held at Roe Farm, the house of Mr. E. Sankey, Culeheth;before Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner. The Rev. Dr. Black, rector of Newchurch, was chairman of the jury. Dr. Sephton was also present. The Coroner said they were there to inquire into the death of Captain Reynolds, of Latchford, Cheshire, who was na doubt very well known to them and others ,in that neighbourhood as a justice of the peace. .He came by his death on Sunday through Injuries received on .the previous day whilst shooting with the Town Clerk of Warrington. They would hear the evidence,. and when they had heard that they would say whether they thought it was articcident or not. Mr. W. H. Brook said: lam the town clerk of War,. rington. I knew the deceased perfectly. His name was Sylvanns Reynolds, and he lived at Latchford, Cheshire, and Was a justice of the peace. He was's7 years of age on the 13th December last. He and I came out here about one o'clock on Saturday afternoon, and we went down to the willows, a pidee where we expected to find • pheasants. Mr. Reynolds went on one side and I went on • the other, the keeper beating through the' willows and working up a ditch which is a likely place for them On the side with me, when we heard a gun. The keeper called "Look out," thinking something might come over. The shot , was immediately followed •by a cry "which the keeper thought was the usual cry to the !deceased's dog which was named "Joe," but I thought there was a cry of pain' in it, and that it was not "Joe," but "Oh." That was ' followed by another shout, and I rushed round the willows about 1.50 yards, and found deceased lying on the ground just by the side of the fence. I fund his left leg shattered to pieces at the knee. For not more than two seconds he was un- conscious, and immediately regained'. consciousness and know me. Ile told roe he had fallen over the fence. ! I Frit the keeper for a trap, and Captain Reynolds was i brought to this hOuse. I, of course, bandaged up his ! leg as well as I could. .1 sent some one for Dr. Sepliton, ! and he was at this house before we arrived. Other ! medical men came in the course of the day—Dr. White- ! • • head who was sent for from Manchester, Dr, White, ! deceased's own medical man, Dr. Starkey Smith, and Dr. !Richmond. The leg was amputated, and deceased re- mained conscious up to that time, but I' think never regained consciousness after the chloroform. I was present at his death at a quarter-past three o'clock on Sunday morning. I should add that it was purely, acci- dental, for although none of' us saw it all the cireum- stances .pointed to that. James Jackson, the keeper referred to, said: On Saturday I accompanied deceased, and Mr. Brook, of Warrington, when they were shooting here. Mr. Brook was on one 'side of the willows and the deceased on the other. I was beating through the willows. This was about half-past two or three o'clock in- the afternoon. I heard a shot about seven yards from us and I then heard a cry and then another shot. I went in the direction of the shots and, found deceased lying down with his left knee shattered. I heard him make a iktatenient,. but I could not catch everything he said. I was present when he was removed to this house and when • the doctors came. I saw nothing to lead me. to believe it was other than an accident. • ! The Coroner said it was scarcely necessary to call the doctor.

Mr. Brook said the deceased made a statement to the doctor. The Coroner then briefly suMmecl up. He said that the facts were very painful but-at the same time very clear. He was a gentleman who went out in good 1 health intending to enjoy some sport, when unfortu- nately his gun went off and shattered his leg. It was certain that no one saw *hat happened, amt deceased was in good spirits and there was nothing to lead them to suppose that it had been other than an accident, and indeed deceased made a statement to that effect directly afterwards. It was a questipn of fact, and it was for the jury to say on the evidence whether it was an acci- dent or not. The Foreman said that as far as he was concerned it was as clear as could be that it was an accidebt, The rest of the jurymen concurred. The following verdict was then agreed to, via. On the 13th day of November in this year at this township! the said deceased, being of tlic;' age of 57 years, died at the house of Mr. Enoch Sankey from a: gun-shot wound received on the preirious day,. ,whilst out shooting, and so the jurors say that the said deceased came by his death accidentally and not otherwise. IMPOSING FUNERAL.

All that was mortal of the late Captain Reynolds was I reverentially placed in the grave at Grappenhall church- yard shortlz,after noon on Thursday. The funeral pro- cession, which formed at Radddn Court at about half- past eleven o'clock in the morning, was of an imposing nature, the long array of mourning coaches being joined , by a number of private carriages. The sides of the road II for a length extending from lia,ddon Court to beyond the Cheshire Cheese were, crowded with sympathising specta- tors, and when the procession ,reached the church at Grappenhall a large number of people had there a.,q,sem- bled. Leading the procession were a number of repre- sentatives of both political parties, and other admirers of the deceased ° gentleman, next came the ' hearse, then a carriage containing Dr. White, Dr. Star- key ' Smith, and Dr. Richmond, and the mourn- ing and private coaches followed. On the hearse had been placed several magnificent wreaths sent by' sorrowing friends, and in these a melancholy interest ! was taken. Ott arrival at the church the coffin was carried into the sacred edifice by the ,bearers, all old and trusted workmen of the deceased, aud a shortand solemn service was conducted by the Bev. B. B. Prescott (vicar of Christ Church, Latchford), and the Rev. J. M. Pros-

cott. Thence the coffin was slowly borne to the family vault, and the remains were consigned, amidst many manifestations of grief, to their last resting place. The sides of the grave were beautifully and artistically lined with moaS, on a trellis work of wire, relieved witi carnelias, white roses and ferns. After the coffin had been lowered,/ and • the . mourners had departed, crowds of people came to see the vault and to examine the many and beautiful wreaths that had been sent is respect to the memory of the deceased. The mourning coaches were occtipied .by the following relatives and near friends of the deceased "'gentlemen :—(1) Mrs 6- Reynolds, the widow, Miss Francis Reynolds, Mr. S. Reynolds, and Mr. P. G.
