THE FOOTBALL FATALITY AT ST. HELENS. Sir,—The sad death which resulted from the accident on the St. Helens Recreation football field last Saturday has naturally raised attention to the dangers attending the Rugby game, and I, for one, think that the Coroner was quite right, and strictly to the point, when he said at the inquest that it must be admitted by everyone that the Rugby rules were yen- dangerous to play under, and that the Association rules were the safest. I don't see how there can be two opinions about the matter; and, in fact, I am surprised that Rugbyism, the relict of a rough and tumble period, should so long have survived in these days. I have heard it rumoured that the Lowe House True Blues have decided to disband themselves as a Rugby club, and I hope it is correct. I have been an admirer of the Rugby game but no longer shall Ibe so. What a pity it is that there is not a strong and powerful club in St. Helens playing under the Asso- ciation rules! lam sure it would become very popular, and it should be well supported. Hoping steps will be staken to secure this end,—l remain, yours, ko., GLASS-BLOWER. St. Helens, November 18th.

THE PENICETH MUTUAL IMPROVEME.NT ASSOCIATION. Sir,—Last night (Wednesday) I had the honoUr of reading an essay on "The Text, or its Expounders; Which?" before the members of the above association, and as you have usually been kind enough to insert a short notice of previous meetings I think it likely you will be asked to do so on this. Now, as I consider, not my- self but my subject, to have been unfairly treated at that meeting, I ask you to insert this resolution, which I had intended to have proposed had it not been vetoed by the chairman, at the whispered suggestion of Mr. Chas. Par- ker, who seemed to judge it more expedient to smother inconvenient facts and statements than to meet them openly with reason assigned. This obnoxious resolution , so much dreaded by Mr. Parker was worded as follows: —" That this meeting of the P.M.1.A., believing that ! what it has pleased God to do or to say, with a definite object, cannot be changed or improved for the better by man, think it incumbent upon all believers in the divine , inspiration of Genesis to accept and to teach literally the Mosaic account of creation as given by Moses, and reiterated o solemnly by God Himself in the command- ments; Exod. xxii." Such, sir, was this terrible resolu- tion, Which, by an unfair use of the ear of the chairman, I was prevented from submitting to my audience, thereby rendering the paper to that extent pointless and incon- sequent. Surely. this is a resolution which may be, with the Utmost propriety, proposed and carried by any assem- blage of professing Christians ? And I hereby challenge Mr. C. E. Parker to show openly any valid reason against its being so read and passed. Failing this I can supply him with one good reason—good to him that is—why he took this underhand course to stifle discussion—a hazy and uneasy feeling that he, as an expounder of a doc- trine at once unscriptuml andimseientific, might not have come out of it with flying colours.—! am. Sec., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, November 17, 1837.

CALIFORNIA AND BRITISH WOMEN. Sir,—l gladly send you one of the letters from Los Angeles, by Miss WainwrOit, who went on her own re- sponsibility before I had time to form Committees of Re- ception in California. A pleasing incident occurred just after I had finished my lecture at Southport in the draw- ing-room of the Smedley -Hydrovathic Institution. A lady came up to me, and said : "Mrs. Parker, did you see miss in Los Angeles ?" I said, "Yes." "Well," she said, "I know her friends, and I have heard her letters to her home read, and they are so glowing with happiness that her sister has gone out to her. She says that her work is done by noon every day, and she has the rest of the day for herself." Ido not, of course, sayi that all will be equally fortunate, but I do say that suit- I able sensible women will find pleasant homes, and be I treated in a manner that our poor governesses might envy. Another lady, a Miss McLachlan, from Glasgow, ar- rived the dayl left. A lady physician was waiting to engage her, and I hear from Pasadena that she dzives out with her mistress, reads with her, and is having a good time generally. At least 50 similar places are wait- ing at Pasadena. No one who goes under my auspices need fear having to wait a single day betore being suited. Ladies there are becoming impatient. They know that they can offer pleasant homes and good pay. This is the finest season there. My son writes me that 138,000 people are booked to ~spend their winter in Southern California, so as to escape the rigours of a win- ter elsewhere. No frost and snow, but fruits and flowers abound. Indeed, it seems as if God had lavished more beauty on Southern California than any spot upon earth. On Saturday, the 19th inst, I •go to Liverpool to see I the first party of ladies off. They are to sail by the Servia, (Cunard), and go second class by rail to Los Angeles. A little over a fortnight will, I expect, see them in that paradise of all the earth. We shall doubt- less hear from them ere long. MARGARET E. PARKER.

The Home Lea, Penketh. P.S.—The following is a copy of a letter I have received since reaching home [cowl Depot Boarding House, Loa Angeles, Sept. 6th, 1887. Dear Mrs. Parker,—My brother and I went over to Pasadena (7 miles) the Sunday after you left, and very much we enjoyed the visit. We were made to feel at home at once, Mr. aid Mrs. Nelms being exceedingly kindland pleasant. I call the life lived by them an ideal life. Miss McLachlan, the young lady who came on the , Thursday after you had gone, was there. What with the friends, the fruit, scenery, and flowers, it was a most enjoyoble afternoon. I thought Los Angeles a beautiful Place, but Pasadena exceeds it. Not one word too much fias been said in praise of the loveliness, fertility, and fine climate; indeed, not enough. I came with great expectations, but it is all, and much more, than I imagined. When I admire the country, people all say— " This is the worst part of the year; wait till winter to see everything at its best." It seems to melhere is work for any number if they will only put away their pride, and go into homes as helps. They will get good wages, and be treated as kindly as if doing a daughter's work in their own homes. The only difficulty will be the Ameri- can style of cooking and manner of serving meals. There are so many different kinds of dishes and vegetables it is appalling at first, but a week or two will make any- one who gives her mind to it a proficient cook. The stoves used here make cooking easy. Women are greatly needed in the laundries. You are, I know, tryingito arrange to send out women here. They Must make up their minds to work hard; but they will have good wages and pleasant homes, and have plenty of liberty. kind treatment, not being treated as inferiors, but being made to feel at home. As to clothing, light coiours are best, the dust in summer being such a nuisance. Simply made washing dresses are much worn, and keep clean a long time. Gloves, stockings, and flannels are dear here, and a plain dress costs 8 dollars, or 32.5. to make. I hope all who come will be of the right kind, willing to adapt themselves to American manners and customs. I think they will not regret coming here, but will enjoy the life and climate. I. for one, have no wish to come back to England.—With best wishes, yours very sin- cerely,
E. WAINWRIGHT.

div.head: LATE FATHER FENNELLEY, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE LATE FATHER FENNELLEY, OF RUNCORN.

The mortal remains of the Rev. W. Fennelley, pastor of St. Edward's Catholic Chapel, Runcopt, whose death was announced last week, were conyey6d to the Chapel on Sunday and placed in the chancel. The body was enclosed in a handsome oak coffin, which was almost hidden by floral wreaths and crosses that had been con- tributed by sorrowing members of the congregation. The pulpit, the chancel, and other portions of the sacred edifice were draped in black. During the day solemn services in accordance with the custom of the CathOlie Church were held. In the evening the chapel was crowded, and after the service the Rev. Father Stanisla.s Bdsvrin, of Ditton College, who had conducted the mission during Father Fennelley's itlness, preached an appropriate sermon in which he said he thanked their separated brethren for the kindly spirit With which they had always favoured Father Fenneilev, and also for the truly kind memory which they still bore for him. Those who were not in the church agreed that great blessing and great pleasure had been thrown upon .the town of Runcorn by the ministry of their departed pastor, and they, as Catholic children, frankly ayowedthat amongst theserviceshe had rendered to the community, this one might be considered the fore- most, that he had shown the community outside the Church the real personal value and dignity of a Catholic priest ; and how a faithful Catholic priest could exert a good moral influence upon all sections of the popula- tion.—During the night a watch was kept over the body, 12 zealous members of the church undertaking this last duty toward their late pastor. On Monday the remains of the deceased gentleman were conveyed to Pantasaph, near Holywell, for burial. Prior to the removal of the coffin mass was celebrated in the chapel, which was crowded with a devout congregation. Shortly after ten o'clock the procession started for the railway station. In front were the members of the School Board: Messrs. J. Pritchard (chairman), Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. E. 'liai- son, F.. A. Lake, .7. R. Frith, accompanied by Messrs. Cr. Moss (cleric), W. Hankin.son, T. Bowyer, W. Sutton, and R. Wright. Then came the hearse containing the coffin, which was covered with the floral tributes of the teachers and scholars and of Mr. and Mrs Mutch, Mr. and Mrs Byrne, Mr. and Mrs Kelly, Mrs Massey, and Mrs Nick- son. Then came the mourning coaches, which were occupied by the Rev. Father Boswin, Mr. J. Barker, Mr. J. Dutton, &c. Following were a number of the mem- bers of the congregation, amongst whom were Messrs. J. Dugmore, Byrne, Nixon, P. Collins, Peck, Reilly. Peek, Keogh, Phillips. Massey, Birchall, Costello, and Finegan. The blinds of the houses along the route were drawn, and in some instances the places of busi- ness were closed. The Rev. Father Boswin, and Mr. 'James Peck accompanied the corpse to Chester, where it was handed to the Rev. Father Tench, who proceeded with the body to Holywell. The interment took place at Pantasnph on Tuesday morning, The eofais bore the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1887.
THE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A

WARRINGTON GIRL. At the Manchester County Police Court on Thursday, before the stipendiary magistrate (Mr. Leresche), Samuel Evans, aged thirty-fouz, warehouseman, living in Can- ute-street, Withington-street,yendleton, was charged on suspicion with having caused the death of Elizabeth Ellison, aged twenty-two, of Warrington, under circum- stances recorded in another column. •

Mr. Superintendent Bent stated the facts of the case. He added that the prisoner, in his (Mr. Bent's) opinion alked a very suspicious question. He asked Mrs. Colton whether she thought Lizzie had been drowned. Mrs. Colton replied, "Not unless you have drowned her." He then said, "Can I hide here ?" Mrs. Colton replied, "No. If you are a man you can face it out." He then obtained the address of the young man to whom the deceased had been engaged at Warrington, and left. It was afterwards discovered that he went to , the address at Warrington, and after asking whether the deceased had been there, he remarked, "Well, if she is not here she must be dead." He would, therefore, ask that the prisoner should be remanded for a week, which would give the police time to make further inves- tigations. The prisoner was a married man with fivje children, and had been married about fifteen years. He had, however, led the deceased to believe that he was single, and ad actually taken her to a house in Pendle- ton where he said he lodged. Mr. Leresche said the application :for a remand was a most reasonable one, and /would be granted. The prisoner is of dark com- plexion, and slightly built. On leaving the dock he was heard in a low tone to say that he was not guilty. We understand that although the deceased young woman's parents live, as stated, at 36, Dial-street, War- rington, she has not lived with her parents for the last six years though she occasionally visited her parents at Warrington.
LATEST NEWS.
The report of the West Cumberland Iron and Steel Company just issued states that the loss on the year was £28;2413._

Lnrd Stair, Chancellor of Glasgow University, has given his casting vote in the election of Lord Rector to the Earl of Lytton. Mr. Parnell's health has improved since the rising of Parliament; but he will, by medical advice, take no part in public affairs during the recess. On Friday a boiler exploded on the premises of Mr. Foley, gingerbeer manufacturer, Cradley Heath. The factory was wrecked, three men narrowly escaping being killed.
Mr. Doughty, the British labour delegate, was on Fri- day sentenced at the Six Mile Bridge (Limerick) Petty Sessions to a month's imprisonment for an offence under the Primes Act.

BUCKSHOT FOR LONDONERS,—,SIT Charles Warren has issued another proclamation under another Act of Par- liament prohibiting meetings and processions in Trafal- gar-square and the vicinity. Government 'orders have been received at Woolwich Arsenal for an immediate supply of buckshot cartridges for the use of the Guards in London.

ANOTHER MURDER IN SHROPSHIRE.—On Thursday night another dreadful murder was committed in Shrop- shire. The murdered man is John Powell, a well-to-do- farmer residing at the Round Thorn, Whixall, some six miles from Whitchurch, and the suspected murderer is his brother-in-law, Elijah Bowers Forester, a farmer who lives only a short distance away. They had not been on good terms for a long time. About half-past seven on Thursday night, as Powell was sitting in his house with his wife and family, they heard Forester singing outside. Powell went out and walked along in the direction Fores- ter had taken for about sixty yards, it being dark. All at once the singing stopped, and the report as of a double-barrelled gun was distinctly heard. PowelPs son rushed outside and found his father dead on the road, Some neighbours were quickly on the spot, and he was carried into his house. Powell presented a terrible sight, the internal organs protruding. Death must have been instantaneous. Proceeding to Forester's house the police found him in the custody of P.C. Bowen, who had also taken charge of the gun. Both barrels presented the ap- pearance of having been recently fired out of. Superin- tendent Edwards arrested Forester, and having charged him with the murder, which he neither denied or ad- mitted, brought him to Whitchurch, and locked him up. He will be brought before a magistrate this (Saturday) afternoon.

SHOCKING FOOTBALL FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

A painful sensation has been occasioned through- out St. Helens and district by an occurrence on the Recreation football ground, Boundary-road, on Saturday afternoon, • which, unfortunately, had a fatal termination on the following day. The second or " A " terms of the Recreation and Widnes clubs were engaged playing one of their ordinary club fixtures; and one of the home team's 'players was William Edward Taylor, 27 years of age, residing at 102, Croppers Hill, and employed AS -.9; clerk at Messrs. Pilkington Brothers glass works. During the course of the game the deceased was attempt- ing to kick the leather, when he was seized from behind by an opponent, and he fell heavily on his back. He rose from his feet, and played for a few minutes, when he was seen to fall. Several persons at once went towards him, but he became insensi- ble. He was conveyed to the pavilion, and Dr. Knowles was sent for. Efforts to restore conscious- ness was unavailing, and Taylor was removed to his home, where he was several times visited by Dr. Knowles, and on Sunday afternoon by Dr. Garton also. Notwithstanding every attention, however, the young man died about seven o'clock on Sunday night. The deceased was of a quiet and unassum- ing nature, and was extremely popular among his friends and acquaintances. The news of his death cast a gloom over the neighbourhood; especially his football comrades and companions being affected.

INQUEST AND VERDICT. An inquest on the body of the 'deceased was held be- fore Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, on Tuesday morning, at the Town Hall. Among those present were Dr. Knowles, Chief Constable Wonris, Inspector , Bond, and several members of the Widnes team and club. The, jury com- prised Messrs. James Latham, Wm. Windlehurst, George Hoult, James Broadbent, Daniel Green, William Nash, George Harris, Thomas Fairclough, Joseph Lee, Matthew Whalley, Wm. Brown and Wm. Thompson. Evidence having been given as to the facts stated, Jesse Sampson, captain of the Widnes A team, stated that, although inquiries had been made, the name of the Widnes player who pulled at deceased had not been as- certained.

The Coroner said the question before them was one of fact, and it rested entirely with the jury to find a verdict upon this evidence. Perhaps they understood the game a good deal more than he did, but as he understood it they could play either under Rugby or Association rules. Under Rugby rules any player could get hold of the ball and hold of each other, and this fatality and other fatali- ties which had occurred showed quite clearly how very dangerous it was to play under these rules. Then, as he understood it, under Association rules the 'player could not take hold of the ball, but only the goalkeeper could, and players could only shoulder and push one another with their bodies. He (the corouer)thought it must be admitted on all hands that the Association rules were the safest to play under. It came to this. Had the deceased received injuries, and did the man who caused the inju- ries do anythir7 that was contrary to the rules of the game? if he did not, then their verdict must be one of misadventure. If he did something not allowed, then the inquest imtst be adjourned, and the man must attend and give evidence. The jury retired, and in a few minutes returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death."

THE VYRNWY WATER SCHEME AND THE RIVER '.MERSEY. Rear-Admiral Sir George Strong Nares, K.C.B. on be- half of tie Board of Trade, held an inquiry, on Tuesday, in the Bethesda Lecture Hall at Runcorn "for the pur- pose of enabling the Board of Trade to exercise the powers vested in them by section 18 of the Liverpool. Corporation Waterworks Act, 1880, with respect to the. depth at which the aqueduct authorised by that Act had been laid under the bed of the river Mersey." The -Cor- poration of Liverpool was represented by Mr. French,, Q.C. ; and there were also present Mr. Alderman Bower (chairman of the Water Committee), Sir Frederick Brain- well; the Manchester Ship Canal Company by Mr. Fern- her, QC.; the Manchester Corporation by Mr. Talbot (deputy town clerk) ; and the Warrington Corporation by Mr. Sutton (barrister), and on their behalf there were also present Mr. W. H. Brook (town clerk), Mr. Alderman Davies, Mr. Alderman Crosfield, and others.— The Commissioner said he understood that the Manches- ter ship Canal Company were practically in possession ef the waters of the Mersey above Runcorn and up to War- rington. They had statutory powers over that channel, and if they wished to do so could dredge it without go- ing to Parliament for further powers at the present moment.—Mr. Pember : Certainly, at the present mo- ment. He added that the Mersey Conservancy Board had also powers to dredge.—Witnesses were then called on behalf of the Corporation of Liverpool.— Mr. G. F. Deacon was first examined. He said they pro- posed to cros.s the river just below the lowest part of the river bed. It was usual to lay pipes crossing the river in the bed of the river. There was not a single exam- ple, either in this country or in America, of a tunnel be- in e- constructed for the purpose. In his opinion, the utility of the deepening of the channel between Runcorn and Warrington would be almost nil unless the channel of the estuary were dealt with. It would certainly be absolutely nil at neap tides. His first objection to carry- ing the pipes under the river in a tunnel was the cost, which, of course, could be got over. Having regard to the Strata, they would, in order to make a tunnel, have to go down 150 ft. below the proposed level of the pipes. Then there had to be faced the difficulty not merely of making the pipes stronger, but of maintaining the tunnel. By Mr. Pember : It was propoSed to place the pipes under the Manchester Ship Canal in a culvert, at if depth of 31 feet below ordnance datum. But there was a dif- ference in this case, because the levels were very differ- ent. The one was 34 feet below ordnance datum, and the other was over 150 feet below ordnance datum. The whole of Mr. Barry's scheme could be carried out, so far as the improvement of the river went,by putting the top of the pipes at 21 feet below ordnance datum.—Mr.Wm. H. Wallstead, C.E., engineer to the Hull Water Com- pany, testified to pipes having been carried across the Humber in the same way as they-are now proposed to be carried across the Mersey at Fialer's Ferry.—Sir Fredk. B ramwell corroborated the evidence of Mr. Deacon.— This concluded the case for the Liverpool Corporation.— Mr. Pember, Q.C., then stated the ground of opposition of the Manchester Ship Canal Company and the Man- chester Corporation. In view of the probability or pos- sibility of Warrington spending £130,000 in..improving the river, and in view of thelprobable usefulness of the river, either as a separate navigation or as an adjunct to the Manchester Ship Canal, it was highly important that it should not be interfered with in the manner proposed. It would not entail much extra cost to follow the wiser plan of putting the pipes in a tunnel, and even if it did, he submitted that £50,000 or £lOO,OOO more or less was not of much account in connection with so gigantic :a scheme as that which the Liverpool Corporation had in hand.—Mr. Sutton, in stating the case for the Warring- ton Corporation, severely criticised the conduct of the Liverpool Corporation. He held that the laying of the pipes at the place proposed would not only prevent any improvement in the Mersey between Runcorn and War- rington, but would be a great source of danger te,the 'navigation aS it at present exists. —The inquiry was then adjourned. On Wednesday Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal, examined by Mr.'Pember, said the Ship Canal Company had powers to dredke the river between Bank Quay and the east point of Warring- ton, and he considered it very important that nothing should be done to interfere with the navigation of the river lower down. Widnes was the centre of the greatest chemical industry in the world, and bad grown to that position in spite of very defective navigation, and seeing that the means of navigation would be immensely im- proved, there was every reason to anticipate that the chemical industry of Cheshire would now be immensely. developed. It was of immense importance to the Ship Canal to have the opportunity 'of using an alternative water-way in case of the canal becoming overcrowded with traffic. The shifting of the channels, which went on to an extraordinary extent in the Upper Mersey, would be a source of danger, and the grounding of any ship over the pipes would be a source of further risk, even though the pipes were sunk a !few feet in the river

Mr. John Crosfield, soap manufacturer, of Warrington, was next called by Mr. Pember, and said he was an alderman of that. town and ex-mayor. He employed steam barges on the Upper Mersey, which conveyed 1000 tons of goods per month at a much less cost than they could be conveyed by rail. The difference of carriage by river and rail upon wire he considered would make a I handsome profit now, and to his firm it was worth £l,OOO a year that the river should be kept wide open, besides' the convenience of having their goods landedon the quay at their ownmorks. They had been making use of the river since, 1815, and it would be a great shame to have the navigation interfered with or the prospective im- provement of it interfered with. At present his barges could pass up and down every other week with the spring tides. An eight-foot channel could be dredged Out for.£loo,ooo, and would enable barges to pass all the year round. He thought if the pipes were laid, as pro- posed by the Corporation of Liverpool, there would be great danger from the dragging of anchors and the pos- sible grounding of vessels on the top of the pipes.—ln cross-examination by Mr. French the witness said if the river werOdeepened to Bft. at low water that would-be very good, and no danger deed be anticipated from grounding. He had no objection to the Corporation scheme so long as the pipes were laid deep enough not to interfere with the navigation of the river. Mr. George Henry Hill, C.E., examined by Mr. Pem- her, said he was of opinion the proper thine," was to make a subway under the river for the pipes, and this could be done without difficulty in either the boulder clay or red sandstone at a cost. of £25,000. Mr. Pember then summed up the case on behalf of his clients, and Mr. G. H. Hill, C.E., and Mr. H. M. Brunel, C.E., having given evidence in favour of the tunnel scheme, Mr. Sutton, on behalf of the Corporation of Warrington, urged that, in the event of the Commis- sioner not seeing his way to recommend the formation of the tunnel, he should at all events report in favour of the placing of the pipes at a very much greater depth than the ICorporation of Liverpool Proposed, arid also that the pipes should be encased in a strong cover. Mr. French replied on behalf of the Liverpool Corporation, and the inquiry terminated, the Commissioner stating that he should give close attention to the case, and that the Board of Trade was fully alive to the great import- ance of the decision they would have to arrive at.

SINGULAR •6 DOG AT LARGE" CASE.-At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs.lt.Houghton, W. P. Gooch, and A. C. McCorquodale, James Mather, of Earle-street, Earlestown, was stimmOned for allowing his dog to beat -large and iinmuzzled in Junction-lane, Earlestown, on the Bth inst.—P.G. Cameron stated that he found the dog running at large without a muzzle.. It had a muzzle -hanging by a strap round its neck.—Mr: A. C. .MeCorquodale, J.P. How did it get the muzzle off? Witness : I don't know—it was off. —Mr. Houghton T.P. : The muzzle must have been put on too slack, and the dog slipped it off.—Mrs. Mather (defend- ant's wife) said the muzzle, which she produced, was , fastened on firm by her husband, and it prevented the dog from biting.—The Bench dismissed the ease. . MISSIONARY SERMONS AND METING.—The annual Ser- mons in aid of they Primitive Methodist Home and Foreign Mission Fund were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Earlestown, on Sunday, : when the pulpit in the morning was occupied by the Rev. E. Ilancox, of Liverpool, and in the' evening by the Rev. R. Carr, resident minister. There were large congregations at each service. The annual public meet- ing,was held in the same place of worship on Wednesday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr. F. J. Holmes, of Newton, occupied the chair. Appropriate addresses were delivered by .the chairman, the Rev. E. Haneox (who attended as a deputation from the Parent Society), Rev. R. Carr (resident minister), and Rev. T. Vaughan (of Golborne). Mr. T. Ormand read extracts from the annual report showing that the mission work was progressing in many parts. At each service, and at the meeting, a collection was made in aid of the mission fund, and the total amount raised, including the contents of the children's boxes, was a little over £8 3s.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

_ The interment of the . remains of the deceased took place at Old Windleshaw Abbey onWeditesday afternoon, and there was a marked public testimony to the respect in which the deceased was held and the general sym- pathy felt for his relatives in their sad loss. The cortege left deceased's late home about half-past two o'clock, Cropper's-hill, Westfield-street, &c., being thickly lined with spectators. In front was a procession of about 150 gentlemen, comprising the members of the Lowe House Senior Boys' Guild, and the members of the Lowe House Men's Guild in their regalia; the members, of the Lowe House True Blues Football Club; the members of the Recreation Football Club; the clerks from the department of Messrs. Pilkington's • glassworks in which the deceased was employed, representatives from the St. Helens and Widnes football dubs, and Mr. F. T. Parry, secretary of the West Lancashire Rugby Union. The hearse was followed by five coaches con- taining the relatives and intimate friends of the deceased: There was a large crowd of people at the Abbey, where in the mortuary chapel the service was read by the Rev. Father Father Mordaunt, assisted by the Rev. Fathers Kenny and Dobson; and at the grave side the service was read by the Rev. Fathers Mordaunt and Kenny. Fhe coffin was covered with beautiful wreaths contribu- ted by sorrowing friends, football clubs, and the Lowe House Guild.
MASONIC BANQUET AND PRESENTA-
TION AT NEWTON.

The brethren of the Makerfield Lodge, No. 2,155, of Freemasons, held their first anniversary since its consecration at their Masonic Rooms, the Pied BUll Hotel, Newton, on Tuesday .evening, under the presidency of their W.M. Brother R Brierley. The lodge was opened in masonic form, and a candidate was initiated by the W.M. A hoard of instal mas- ters was formed, and Brother Henry. Stones was in- stalled W.M. for the ensuing year by Brother W. Goodall,P.G.S.. B.Prov.G.Sec.. who was supported by Brother Murray. P.Prov., D. of C.; W. 11. Robin- son, Prov., D. of C.; Brother D. M. 'F. Gaskin, Prey. G.Treas.: Brother R. Brierley, P. Prim, G. S. of W.; and a numerous retinue of past masters from neighbouring towns. After the W.M. was in- stalled in solemn form he proceeded to invest his officers far the ensuing year, as follows :—J.P.M. Brother Richard Brierley; S.W., Brother James Blundell: J.W., Brother James 'Lambert; Treas., Brother S. Hewitt; Secretary, Brother J. Adams; SD, Brother P. Hall (whose investiture was de- ferred through Brother Hall's illness) ; J.D., Bro. Peter Garton; J.G. Brother E. L. Bent; Stewards, Brothers T. Ormand and E. Fairclongly; organist Brother C. E. Arnott ; and Tyler, Brother John Devereux. The Installing Master ('Brother Good- acre) then gave the usual charge to the W.M., offi- cers, and brethren; and the lodge afterwards pro- ceeded .to elect Brother Daniel,' P.M., as its representative, on the Masonic Charities Committee. The eports of the treasurer and audi- Itors were deferred to a future meeting. An inter- esting presentation then took place ; this consisting of the presentation to the Immediate Past 'Master (Brother Brierley) of the " Jewel " of 'his office. The " Jewel " was of an extremely pretty descrip- tion, being in the form of a medal, containing a design of the Makerfield crest, enclosed in a scroll, upon the latter being the words, Founder, Ashton- in-Makerfield Lodge, 2,155." On the reverse side was engraved the sentence, "Presented to Brother R. Brierley, P.M., first W.M. of the ledge, Newton- le-Willows. Nov. 15th, 1887." The " Jewel" was attached to a ribbop. above which were the masonic emblems, and the whole were encloeedi in a hand- some case. The presentation was made by the W.M., who spoke very highly of Brother Brierley's services as tha founder of that lodge and as its first W.M.—Brother Brierley acknowledged the gift in appropriate terms.---The lodge was then closed in Masonic form.

The members subsequently commemorated the festival of St. John by holdibg a banquet in the large room of the Pied Bull Hotel. The repast, provided ty Mr H. J. Bond. was ot a first-class character. The W.M., Brother Stone, was supported by the Grand Provincial Officers and others, and about fifty gentlemen sat down. The usual loyal toasts were honoured with tpusical accompani- ments. The W.M. proposed "The healths of the Hon. the Earl of Camarvon, W.M., Provincial Grand Master, and the rest of the Grand Officers\ present and past ; " and Brother Goodacre responded. The W.M. also gave 'The healths of the Earl of Lathom, Deputy Grand Master. Provincial Grand Masters, and the Provincial Grand Officers, past and pre- sent ; " and this was responded to by Brother D. M. F. Gaskin. The "Masonic Charities" was proposed by the W.M., and ably responded to by Brother Murray. The toast of the evening, "The health of the was given by Brother R. Brierley, and responded to by Brother Henry Stones, W.M. The W.M. next gave "The health of the I.P.M. (Brother Brierley)," and the latter, in responding, thanked the members of the lodge for their attendance and support during the year, and hoped they would give the same attention and care to thee W.M. for the ensuing year. The toast of "The healths of the Officers of the Lodge" was next given, and re- sponded to; after which Brother Brierley, 1.P.M., proposed "The visiting brethren," of whom there was a goodly representation, and Brothers Rigby, McLellan, and others responded. The concluding toast was "All poor and distressed Masons," and this was appropriately honoured. The proceedings Were interspersed with musical selections efficiently rendered by Brothers W. H. Young, W. D. Burdis, Evans, and others.

At the Warwickshire Assizes, on Thursday, Thomas Payne, labourer, was sentenced to death for die murder of his sister-in-law, Charlotte Taylor, at Coventry, in August last. " Marriage," says ohn Seiden, "is a desperate thing: the frogs in ,Esop were extremely wise; they had a great mind to some water, but they would not leap into the well, because they could not get out again."

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.]
23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

The first three days of the week the chief attention of members of the Stock Exchange has been devoted to the settlement, although this is, as a rule, an all-absorb- ing mattes, to the limitation of other business. Consi- derable attention has been given to the markets, with the natural result that the prices have been very firm. So strong, indeed, has been the " bull " feeling, that a few days ago certain stocks; which are regarded as almost dead, show considerable improvement. Last week hol- ders of Rio Tinto' s were advised to realise the profit; and those who accepted this advice have been fortunate in securing a handsome profit. Another rebound has since taken place in these , stocks, and holders should lose no time in again realising the present prices as the upward movement is regarded as purely artificial and the outcome of a market rig." This re- mark applies with equal force to copper which, it is sta- ted, has been artificially stimulated. The American mar- ket has continued uncertain and the immediate future does not seem to predict any stability, and it would be rash for speculators not on the spot to touch scarcely a single one of these stocks. The one exception, perhaps, and the only one at the time of writing is Eries. Inve,s- -' tors in milling shares have been inundated with the pro- spectuses of a company called the Kilkinan Mines, Limi- ted, which has been formed with a capital of £120,000 to worka property in Queensland. Out of this sum the venders are to receive £90,000 in cash and shares. Comparison is Made by the promoters to prove what they call the moderate amount paid for the property. The KaboOnga mines shareholders, how- ever,. should carry the comparison raised by the pro- moters still further, and they will see that the difference upon nominal shares of the Kaboongn losses which they have done, and promoters would not attempt to foist on them doubtful schemes and shelter themselves behind concealed contracts. The only company,- brougtit put within. the last week which has commanded serioua at- tention has been R. Bell and Co., the well-known match and vesto Makers. The public in this case have been induced more by the reputation of the firm than.' iv any merits of a prospectus which is silent on the profit earned, and says nothing as to any report or examina- tion having been made of the books of the firm whose business has been acquired. These shares have be run up to a premium, and we should advise thop who have obtained an allotment to take advantage at the premium without delay. , The action, between the London. Chatham, and ,Dover Railway, and the South Pastern Railway, which termin- ated on Thursday in favour of the first-named company, caused the shares of that company to go up two, while the South Eastern fell one. It is earnestly hoped by the shareholders of the South Eastern Company that an end has now been put to further litigation on the part of Sir Edward 'Watkin, the chairman.
LYMM.

WESLEYAN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday the Rev. E. H. Jackson, of Warrington, preached the annual foreign missionary sermons iu the Wesleyan Church, morning and evening.. The collections were in aid of the Wesleyan foreign mission. - MUTUAL TAIPROYEMENT ASSOCIATION. —On Monday evening the, usual weekly meetmg of this Association was held, when wings and readings were contributed by Messrs. Cross and Street, of Manchester, a very pleasant evening being spent. Miss L. Greeb accompanied on the pianoforte. VAGRANCY.—During the week, two va.grants, Thoinas. Lambert and Thomas Jackson (alias Skim th' Daisy "), have been charged at Lymm Police Court, before Mr. T. P. Norris, with having slept in outhouses at Bollington. Lambert was sentenced to fourteen days' hard labour, , but," Skim th' Daisy" was discharged on promising to go to the workhouse. ,

_ PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE.—Theppening public meeting in connection with this Band ot BiNpe was held in the Chapel, Eagle-brow, Lvmm, on Monday, when addresses Were given by Mr. W. Windsor, of Man- chester, and the Rev. W. Evans. Mr. Cr. L. Welford occupied the chair. Selections were rendered by the choir and brass band at intervals, and gave great satis- faction. •

BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT.-011 Monday evenin,, an entertainment was given in the Congregational Schools by some of the members of .the Band of Hope and friends. Mr. R. Dutton took the chair, and there was a very large attendance of adults as well as chil- dren. Mx. Edward Brown, senior, gave an address, and songs were rendered by Mr. Murry and Miss Moston. Two dialogues, entitled "The doctor's prescription" and "When we shall be men," the latter being perfor- med by ten boys dressed in the costumes of various tradesmen. A laughing chorus given by members bf the choir was re-demanded by the audience. At the close several persons signed the pledge,

NEW MEMO;4AL TAIIIIT IN LtiM CHURCH.—A new memorial plate has during the week been placed in position in the -14rnm Parish Church, bearing the following inscription :---•• To the glory of God, and in affectionate remembrance of Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart W. 'Mclver, who fell from sunstroke September 026th, 1886, at Taginet Upper Burmah, whilst in command of a detachment on a forward march to the relief of Taindah. 'Ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.' (1 Them. iv. 13.)" The deceased gentleman was the second son of the late Rev. William Maclver, a'former rector of Lymm, and brother of Mr. Colin Maclver, of Lymm and Warrington. The inscription is handsomely engraved on a brass tablet, with a black polished , marble border.

TUE PARISH Cnumcm.—On Saturday afternoon a meet- ing of parishioners was held in the vestry of the Parish Church to hear a report by Mr. Crowther, architeoW Manchester, as to the repair of the tower of the church, which has recently bore signs of dislocation. The Rev.' (I. W. Guest presided. Mr. Crowther stated that the tower was settling down on the west side owing to the formation of the ground, a portion of the masonry being thereby dislocated. To set this right about forty feet of the south-west angle and buttress—the whole of the winding staircase and where it terminates just below the belfry stage—would require to be taken down to the foundation.—ln the course of some conversation it was stated that it would take about £l,OOO to repair the tower, and about £2,000 to build a new tower. It was ultimately agreed that the architect should be " asked to prepare plans and, specifications for the taking' down and rebuilding of the tower, and also plans and specifications for its restoration. The tender of Mr. Ardern to remove the bells for £25 was accepted. •

LIVERPOOL PROVLSIONS, PRIDAT.-Beef rules very quiet. Pork meets a slow sale at unaltered figures. Bacon has ruled quiet, but prices of some cuts are rather higher, in sym- pathy with the American adsices. Trams are firm. Shoulders are dearer from scarcity. Butter continues steady. Cheese firm but quiet. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. - There is 110 buoyancy in any department of the market and only a small business going through. Cotton has recovered the 1-164. loss`on Wednes- day. • Cloth is particularly slow. There seems now to be no connection between cloth and cotton, There is little workable business offering in any department.
